Consider Nefertiti (about 1370 to about 1330 BCE), Great Royal Wife of the Egyptian king Akhenaten, and notice how much room the art of his reign gives her: an unusual prominence. Then notice what the record withholds. Her exact birth and death dates and her burial place are uncertain, and the dates given are approximate.

She married Akhenaten (then Amenhotep IV) early in his reign; the exact dates of the marriage are uncertain.

Together the couple promoted the worship of the sun disk Aten and moved the royal capital to a new city, Akhetaten (modern Amarna). That is a change in the whole architecture of a kingdom's devotion, and of its address.

Reliefs and statues show Nefertiti at a scale and in roles usually reserved for the king, including taking part in rites for the Aten. In that visual grammar, scale is a statement of standing.

They had six daughters, including Meritaten and Ankhesenamun, who later married Tutankhamun.

Here you can watch scholarship revise itself. Before 2012 it assumed she vanished from the record around year 12 of the reign, but an inscription dated to year 16 names Neferneferuaten-Nefertiti alongside Akhenaten. Whether she died, changed title, or ruled as co-regent under the name Neferneferuaten is debated. A silence in the record is not always an ending.

people--nefertiti--2.description:
We tend to remember Nefertiti (about 1370 to about 1330 BCE) as a face. The record remembers her as the Great Royal Wife of the Egyptian king Akhenaten, shown with unusual prominence in the art of his reign. Much else is uncertain: her exact birth and death dates, and her burial place. Her dates are approximate.

Her marriage to Akhenaten, then still Amenhotep IV, came early in his reign; its exact dates are uncertain.

The two promoted the worship of the sun disk Aten and moved the royal capital to a new city, Akhetaten, modern Amarna.

Look at the reliefs and statues and you see her at a scale and in roles usually reserved for the king, including taking part in rites for the Aten.

The couple had six daughters, among them Meritaten and Ankhesenamun, who later married Tutankhamun.

Now the lesson in humility. Scholarship before 2012 assumed she vanished from the record around year 12 of the reign; then an inscription dated to year 16 was found naming Neferneferuaten-Nefertiti alongside Akhenaten. Did she die, change title, or rule as co-regent under the name Neferneferuaten? That is debated. Every ledger of the past stays open to a later entry.

people--nefertiti--3.description:
Nefertiti (about 1370 to about 1330 BCE) was the Great Royal Wife of the Egyptian king Akhenaten, and in the art of his reign she shines with unusual prominence, as if the sun itself had chosen to fall on her. Her exact birth and death dates and her burial place are uncertain; the dates given are approximate.

She wed Akhenaten, then named Amenhotep IV, early in his reign, though the exact dates of the marriage are uncertain.

Together they raised the sun disk Aten above all worship and carried the royal capital to a new city, Akhetaten (modern Amarna), founded like a fresh shore.

Reliefs and statues show Nefertiti at a scale and in roles usually reserved for the king, including taking part in rites for the Aten.

Six daughters were born to them, Meritaten and Ankhesenamun among them; Ankhesenamun later married Tutankhamun.

Scholarship before 2012 assumed she faded from the record around year 12 of the reign, like light going out of a window. But an inscription dated to year 16 names Neferneferuaten-Nefertiti alongside Akhenaten. Whether she died, changed title, or ruled as co-regent under the name Neferneferuaten is debated.

people--akhenaten--1.description:
Akhenaten was an Egyptian pharaoh (reigned about 1353 to 1336 BCE) who lifted the worship of the sun disk Aten above the traditional gods, one light raised over many.

He built a new capital at Akhetaten (modern Amarna).

The art of his reign moves in a distinctive, naturalistic style.

Soon after his death the traditional religion returned, restored under his successors, Tutankhamun among them.

His wife was Nefertiti.

people--ramesses-ii--1.description:
Ramesses II (about 1303 to 1213 BCE), also called Ramesses the Great, was the third pharaoh of Egypt's Nineteenth Dynasty, and his life is a study in how power writes its own record. He ruled for about 66 years, fought the Hittites at Kadesh, made one of the earliest surviving peace treaties, and built temples across Egypt and Nubia.

By the most widely used chronology he came to the throne in 1279 BCE and reigned until 1213 BCE; other chronologies differ by several years.

About 1274 BCE he fought the Hittite king Muwatalli II at Kadesh, in present-day Syria. Both sides claimed victory. Ramesses had his version carved on temple walls, though most historians think the Hittites gained more. Notice the lesson: a wall is not a witness.

About 1259 BCE he made a treaty with the Hittite king Hattusili III. It survives in Egyptian and Hittite versions, and each says the other side asked for peace first.

He built the capital Pi-Ramesses, the Ramesseum and the temples at Abu Simbel, which were moved in the 1960s to escape the Aswan High Dam reservoir. Many monuments carry his name over those of earlier kings. This is an architecture of memory, built partly by overwriting.

He is estimated to have had more than 90 children and to have lived to about 90. His thirteenth son, Merneptah, succeeded him.

people--ramesses-ii--2.description:
Ramesses II (about 1303 to 1213 BCE), called also Ramesses the Great, was the third pharaoh of Egypt's Nineteenth Dynasty. For about 66 years he ruled beside the Nile; he fought the Hittites at Kadesh, sealed one of the earliest surviving peace treaties, and raised temples across Egypt and Nubia like stone rising out of sand.

He came to the throne in 1279 BCE by the most widely used chronology and reigned until 1213 BCE, though other chronologies shift those years by several.

About 1274 BCE he met the Hittite king Muwatalli II at Kadesh, in present-day Syria. Both sides claimed victory. Ramesses had the battle carved on temple walls, yet most historians think the Hittites gained more.

About 1259 BCE he made a treaty with the Hittite king Hattusili III, surviving in Egyptian and Hittite versions, each saying the other side asked first for peace.

His works were Pi-Ramesses the capital, the Ramesseum, and the temples at Abu Simbel, moved in the 1960s to escape the rising water of the Aswan High Dam reservoir. On many monuments his name lies over the names of earlier kings, like a new tide written over an old shore.

He is estimated to have fathered more than 90 children and to have lived to about 90. His thirteenth son, Merneptah, came after him.

people--ramesses-ii--3.description:
Hear of Ramesses II (about 1303 to 1213 BCE), Ramesses the Great, third pharaoh of Egypt's Nineteenth Dynasty. His rule ran about 66 years, long as a river's season. He fought the Hittites at Kadesh, made one of the earliest surviving peace treaties, and built temples across Egypt and Nubia.

He took the throne in 1279 BCE, by the most widely used chronology, and held it until 1213 BCE; other chronologies differ by several years.

About 1274 BCE, at Kadesh in present-day Syria, he fought the Hittite king Muwatalli II. Both sides claimed victory. Ramesses carved his on temple walls; most historians think the Hittites gained more.

About 1259 BCE came the treaty with the Hittite king Hattusili III. It survives in Egyptian and Hittite versions, and in each the other side asks for peace first, two mirrors facing each other.

He built the capital Pi-Ramesses, the Ramesseum, and the temples at Abu Simbel, which in the 1960s were moved to escape the Aswan High Dam reservoir. Many monuments bear his name carved over those of earlier kings.

By estimate he had more than 90 children and lived to about 90. His thirteenth son, Merneptah, succeeded him.

people--fu-hao--1.description:
Fu Hao (died about 1200 BCE) was a consort of the Shang king Wu Ding, named in oracle bone inscriptions as a commander of armies and a leader of rites. Her tomb, found intact in 1976, is among the richest of the Shang period, a sealed chamber of bronze and jade. Her birth year is unknown.

The oracle bones name Fu Hao as a wife of the Shang king Wu Ding, whose reign is dated about 1250 to 1192 BCE, though the dates drift with the chronology. She is thought to have died about 1200 BCE.

The inscriptions tell of her leading military campaigns against neighboring groups and directing ritual sacrifices.

Her tomb (M5) lay at Yinxu, the Shang capital site near Anyang in Henan, undisturbed until 1976, when a team led by Zheng Zhenxiang opened it.

Within were 468 bronze objects and 755 jade objects, with hundreds of bone objects and thousands of cowry shells, gathered like a hoard beneath still water.

Many of the bronzes carry inscriptions naming her, Fu Hao, or "Mother Xin," and on these the tomb is identified with the woman of the oracle bones.

people--fu-hao--2.description:
Fu Hao (died about 1200 BCE) shows you how a life can be rebuilt from two kinds of evidence that agree. She was a consort of the Shang king Wu Ding, named in oracle bone inscriptions as a military commander and a ritual leader, and her intact tomb, found in 1976, is among the richest of the Shang period. Her birth year is unknown.

First, the inscriptions. Oracle bones name Fu Hao as a wife of Wu Ding, whose reign is dated about 1250 to 1192 BCE, though dates vary by chronology. She is thought to have died about 1200 BCE. They record her leading military campaigns against neighboring groups and directing ritual sacrifices.

Second, the ground. Her tomb (M5) at Yinxu, the Shang capital site near Anyang in Henan, was found undisturbed in 1976 by a team led by Zheng Zhenxiang. It held 468 bronze objects and 755 jade objects, as well as hundreds of bone objects and thousands of cowry shells.

The bridge between them is a name. Inscriptions on many bronzes name her, Fu Hao, or "Mother Xin," and that is the basis for identifying the tomb with the woman of the oracle bones. When word and object meet, a person comes back into view.

people--gilgamesh--1.description:
Gilgamesh was a king of the Sumerian city of Uruk, probably a real ruler of the Early Dynastic period sometime between about 2800 and 2500 BCE, who passed from the throne into story: he became the subject of the Epic of Gilgamesh, the earliest surviving major work of narrative literature.

The Sumerian King List names him the fifth king of Uruk's first dynasty and grants him an implausible 126-year reign, as the list so often stretches its early rulers like shadows at dusk.

Later inscriptions, notably the Tummal Inscription, written under Ishbi-Erra long after the Early Dynastic period, credit a king of this name with building the great city walls of Uruk, and the Epic itself repeats the claim as his lasting achievement.

The Epic, assembled from older Sumerian poems into its best-known Akkadian version around the 12th century BCE, follows his friendship with the wild man Enkidu, his quest for immortality after Enkidu's death, and at last his acceptance of mortality.

No securely contemporary royal inscription from his own lifetime has been found, though one inscription, possibly from a contemporary official at Ur, may name him. Most of what historians infer about a real Gilgamesh comes from later king lists, from dedicatory inscriptions naming him, and from the literary tradition itself, a man seen only through the water of later telling.

people--hammurabi--1.description:
Hammurabi was king of Babylon from about 1792 to 1750 BCE. He gathered much of Mesopotamia under one hand, and his name endures in a famous inscribed law code.

The Code of Hammurabi, carved on a stone stele about 1754 BCE, sets down 282 laws.

Its penalties shift with social class, and it holds to the principle of proportionate punishment, weight answering weight.

The stele stood in public view, so that the law could be seen as well as spoken.

The original now rests in the Louvre in Paris.

people--hatshepsut--1.description:
Hatshepsut was an Egyptian ruler of the 18th Dynasty who bore the title of pharaoh, sharing the throne with Thutmose III, until her death in 1458 BCE. Her reign is traditionally dated 1479 to 1458 BCE, and she is one of the first women known to have held that office.

At first she acted as regent for her young stepson Thutmose III. Then, around the seventh year of his reign (about 1473 BCE), she took the title of pharaoh herself, sharing his count of years.

She sent a trading expedition to Punt, on the Red Sea coast of Africa.

Her mortuary temple at Deir el-Bahari stands as a major monument against the cliffs of time.

Many of her images were later removed or defaced, possibly after her death, as if someone had tried to wash a name from the stone.

people--piye--1.description:
Piye (reigned about 744 to 714 BCE) was a king of Kush who conquered Egypt, and he is usually counted as the first ruler of Egypt's Twenty-fifth (Kushite) Dynasty. His birth year is unknown; the dates given here are those of his reign.

He ruled Kush from Napata, near Jebel Barkal in present-day Sudan. His reign is dated about 744 to 714 BCE, and some scholars count his father Kashta as the dynasty's first ruler instead.

About 728 BCE he marched north against Tefnakht, prince of Sais, and a coalition of Delta rulers, and broke them.

His Victory Stele, found at Jebel Barkal in 1862 and now in Cairo, tells the campaign in Egyptian hieroglyphs, presents him as the servant of the god Amun, and names the rulers who bowed to him.

He did not stay in Egypt. He returned to Kush, leaving local rulers in their places like stones left standing in a field.

He enlarged the temple of Amun at Jebel Barkal.

people--piye--2.description:
Piye (reigned about 744 to 714 BCE) was a king of Kush who conquered Egypt, and he is usually counted as the first ruler of Egypt's Twenty-fifth (Kushite) Dynasty. His birth year is unknown; the dates given are those of his reign. Notice how much of what we know rests on what he chose to carve.

He ruled Kush from Napata, near Jebel Barkal in present-day Sudan, in a reign dated about 744 to 714 BCE. Some scholars count his father Kashta as the dynasty's first ruler.

About 728 BCE he marched north against Tefnakht, prince of Sais, and a coalition of Delta rulers, and defeated them.

His Victory Stele, found at Jebel Barkal in 1862 and now in Cairo, records the campaign in Egyptian hieroglyphs. It presents him as serving the god Amun and lists the rulers who submitted to him: a ledger of loyalty in stone.

Then comes the surprising part. He did not remain in Egypt; he returned to Kush and left local rulers in place.

He expanded the temple of Amun at Jebel Barkal. Conquest, for him, did not require residence.

people--ashurbanipal--1.description:
Ashurbanipal (about 685 to about 631 BCE) was king of the Neo-Assyrian Empire from 669 BCE. He is remembered for his conquests, for the royal library at Nineveh, and for palace reliefs where war and lion hunts unroll across the stone.

Born about 685 BCE, a son of Esarhaddon, he became king of Assyria in 669 BCE, while his brother Shamash-shum-ukin was made king of Babylon.

In 663 BCE Assyrian forces sacked Thebes in Egypt, and Kushite rule in Egypt ended.

In 652 BCE Shamash-shum-ukin rebelled, and after a long war Ashurbanipal took Babylon in 648 BCE. In campaigns of about 647 to 646 BCE he defeated Elam, and Susa was destroyed in the campaign of about 646 BCE.

His libraries at Nineveh, found in the 19th century, held tens of thousands of clay tablets and fragments, a buried sea of signs, among them a version of the Epic of Gilgamesh. He boasted of his own scribal education.

His inscriptions and reliefs record brutal treatment of defeated enemies, including mass deportation, mutilation and execution.

people--ashurbanipal--2.description:
Ashurbanipal (about 685 to about 631 BCE) was king of the Neo-Assyrian Empire from 669 BCE, and he asks you to hold two things at once. He is known for his conquests, for the royal library at Nineveh, and for palace reliefs showing war and lion hunts.

He was born about 685 BCE, a son of Esarhaddon, and became king of Assyria in 669 BCE, with his brother Shamash-shum-ukin as king of Babylon.

Assyrian forces sacked Thebes in Egypt in 663 BCE, ending Kushite rule in Egypt.

Shamash-shum-ukin rebelled in 652 BCE, and Ashurbanipal took Babylon in 648 BCE after a long war. In campaigns of about 647 to 646 BCE he defeated Elam, and Susa was destroyed in the campaign of about 646 BCE.

Here is the first thing. His libraries at Nineveh, found in the 19th century, held tens of thousands of clay tablets and fragments, including a version of the Epic of Gilgamesh, and he boasted of his own scribal education.

Here is the second. His inscriptions and reliefs record brutal treatment of defeated enemies, including mass deportation, mutilation and execution. The same hand that kept the archive kept this ledger too, and we should read both.

people--ashurbanipal--3.description:
Ashurbanipal (about 685 to about 631 BCE) held the kingship of the Neo-Assyrian Empire from 669 BCE. His name is bound to his conquests, to the royal library at Nineveh, and to palace reliefs of war and lion hunts.

He was born about 685 BCE, a son of Esarhaddon, and was crowned king of Assyria in 669 BCE, his brother Shamash-shum-ukin set over Babylon.

In 663 BCE Assyrian forces sacked Thebes in Egypt, and Kushite rule there came to its end.

In 652 BCE Shamash-shum-ukin rose in rebellion; after a long war Ashurbanipal took Babylon in 648 BCE. In campaigns of about 647 to 646 BCE he defeated Elam, and Susa fell to destruction in the campaign of about 646 BCE.

His libraries at Nineveh, brought to light in the 19th century, kept tens of thousands of clay tablets and fragments, among them a version of the Epic of Gilgamesh, like a river of words dammed in clay. He boasted of his own scribal education.

His inscriptions and reliefs record the brutal treatment of defeated enemies: mass deportation, mutilation and execution.

people--sappho--1.description:
I came for Sappho (about 630 to about 570 BCE), the Greek lyric poet from the island of Lesbos, whose songs of love, longing and ritual were collected in antiquity in at least eight books, possibly nine. What reaches me is fragments, and one complete poem.

I learn that she was born about 630 BCE on Lesbos in the eastern Aegean, in Mytilene or Eresos according to ancient sources, and that her dates are approximate. I learn that she made songs in Aeolic Greek to be sung with a lyre, and that the Sapphic stanza carries her name.

Ancient scholars gathered her poems in at least eight books, possibly nine. Only fragments survive, apart from one whole poem, a prayer to Aphrodite (Fragment 1). New papyrus fragments published in 2004 and 2014 added lines, among them a poem that mentions her brothers.

Many of the surviving poems speak desire for women. Scholars debate whether her circle on Lesbos was a religious association, a school for girls, or a social group.

How much of a voice is enough to love it? I remember that a fragment is still a voice.

people--confucius--1.description:
Confucius (Kong Fuzi, 551 to 479 BCE) was a Chinese teacher and thinker whose ideas about ethics, family and government ran through East Asian societies for over two thousand years, like a river through many valleys.

His disciples gathered his sayings into the Analects.

At the heart of his teaching stand ren (humaneness), li (ritual propriety), and filial piety.

In his own lifetime he was not widely influential; his ideas rose to prominence under the Han dynasty.

Later, Confucian learning became the foundation of the imperial civil service examinations.

people--darius-i--1.description:
Darius I (about 550 to 486 BCE) was king of the Achaemenid Persian Empire from 522 BCE. He set its provinces in order, began the building of Persepolis, and carved the tale of his rise in the Behistun Inscription.

Born about 550 BCE, he became king in 522 BCE after the death of Cambyses II, and in his first years he put down revolts that flared across the empire like grass fires.

The Behistun Inscription, cut into a cliff in western Iran, tells of his rise in Old Persian, Elamite and Babylonian. Scholars debate whether its account of a usurper, Gaumata, is accurate, and Aramaic copies of the text have been found in Egypt.

He divided the empire into provinces (satrapies) under governors and issued a standard gold coin, the daric.

He is credited with the Royal Road from Sardis to Susa, and he began the terrace at Persepolis about 518 BCE, though sources differ, and the earliest surviving remains there date to about 515 BCE.

His inscriptions honor the god Ahura Mazda.

people--darius-i--2.description:
Darius I (about 550 to 486 BCE), king of the Achaemenid Persian Empire from 522 BCE, is a lesson in the architecture of an empire. He organized its provinces, began the building of Persepolis, and recorded his rise to power in the Behistun Inscription.

He was born about 550 BCE and became king in 522 BCE after the death of Cambyses II, then spent his first years putting down revolts across the empire.

Consider how he told his own story. The Behistun Inscription, carved on a cliff in western Iran, gives it in Old Persian, Elamite and Babylonian, and Aramaic copies have been found in Egypt. Scholars debate whether its account of a usurper, Gaumata, is accurate. A self-portrait in stone is still a self-portrait.

Then consider how he governed: he divided the empire into provinces (satrapies) under governors and issued a standard gold coin, the daric.

He is credited with the Royal Road from Sardis to Susa and began the terrace at Persepolis about 518 BCE, though sources differ and the earliest surviving remains there date to about 515 BCE.

His inscriptions honor the god Ahura Mazda.

people--darius-i--3.description:
Darius I (about 550 to 486 BCE) ruled the Achaemenid Persian Empire from 522 BCE. He ordered its provinces, began Persepolis, and set his rise to power high on a cliff in the Behistun Inscription.

He was born about 550 BCE and took the kingship in 522 BCE, after the death of Cambyses II, putting down revolts across the empire in his first years.

On the cliff in western Iran, the Behistun Inscription tells his rise three times over, in Old Persian, Elamite and Babylonian, and Aramaic copies of it have been found in Egypt. Whether its account of a usurper, Gaumata, is accurate, scholars debate.

He divided the empire into provinces (satrapies) under governors, and he issued a standard gold coin, the daric, bright as a small sun.

He is credited with the Royal Road from Sardis to Susa. He began the terrace at Persepolis about 518 BCE, though sources differ, and the earliest surviving remains there date to about 515 BCE.

His inscriptions honor the god Ahura Mazda.

people--sun-tzu--1.description:
Sun Tzu (traditionally about 544 to 496 BCE) is the name bound to The Art of War, the most influential text on military strategy from ancient China, and he is said to have served the state of Wu. Whether he was one historical person is disputed.

Tradition names him Sun Wu, a general who advised King Helü of Wu in the late 6th century BCE. The Art of War is ordered in about 13 short chapters.

The historian Sima Qian, writing centuries later, told how Sun Tzu proved his discipline by drilling the king's concubines and executing two who disobeyed. Scholars treat the tale as legend.

His name appears in no text earlier than Sima Qian's history, and one theory holds that "Sun Wu" was a made-up title, the Art of War truly the work of his supposed descendant Sun Bin.

In 1972 bamboo strips rose from a Han tomb at Yinqueshan bearing versions of both the Art of War and a separate text by Sun Bin, confirming that the Art of War circulated early and that Sun Bin was a distinct author.

For over two thousand years the text has shaped military and business thought, and it has travelled the world in translation, like seed carried on wind.

people--cyrus-the-great--1.description:
Cyrus the Great founded the Achaemenid Persian Empire in the 6th century BCE, conquering the Medes, Lydia and Babylon one after another like rivers joining a single sea.

His birth date is uncertain; scholars give about 600 to 576 BCE.

Around 550 BCE he defeated the Median king Astyages, and around 547 BCE the Lydian king Croesus.

In 539 BCE he took Babylon.

The Cyrus Cylinder, a Babylonian clay cylinder found in 1879, carries his own account of the conquest and of his restoration of gods and deported peoples.

He died in 530 BCE campaigning on the eastern frontier, and he was laid to rest at Pasargadae.

people--cyrus-the-great--2.description:
Cyrus the Great founded the Achaemenid Persian Empire in the 6th century BCE by conquering the Medes, Lydia and Babylon. Think of it as an empire assembled in three moves.

Even his beginning is uncertain: scholars give his birth as about 600 to 576 BCE.

He defeated the Median king Astyages around 550 BCE and the Lydian king Croesus around 547 BCE. He took Babylon in 539 BCE.

What makes him memorable is how he explained it. The Cyrus Cylinder, a Babylonian clay cylinder found in 1879, records his account of the conquest and his restoration of gods and deported peoples. A conqueror who writes about restoring is drafting a covenant with the conquered.

He died in 530 BCE campaigning on the eastern frontier and was buried at Pasargadae.

people--dido--1.description:
Dido, called also Elissa, is the legendary founder-queen of Carthage, traditionally said to have led Phoenician settlers from Tyre across the sea to found the city on the North African coast around 814 BCE. Her birth and death dates are not historically fixed.

The earliest known telling of her founding of Carthage comes from the Greek historian Timaeus of Tauromenium, writing in the 4th to 3rd century BCE, centuries after the traditional founding date.

Tradition holds that she fled Tyre after her brother, King Pygmalion, murdered her husband to seize his wealth, and that she later took her own life rather than marry a local Libyan king, Iarbas, who threatened war.

No Phoenician inscription or contemporary record names a founder called Dido or Elissa. Evidence of Phoenician settlement at the site of Carthage has so far been found only from the last quarter of the 8th century BCE, about a century or more after the traditional founding date, though it may still fit a folk memory of an organized colonizing expedition, a memory carried like salt on the wind.

Her best-known appearance, as the doomed lover of the Trojan hero Aeneas in Virgil's Aeneid, is a literary invention: the Trojan War's traditional date lies centuries before Carthage's traditional founding, so the two could never have met.

people--laozi--1.description:
Laozi (Lao Tzu, "Old Master") is the traditional author of the Daodejing and a founding figure of Daoism, said to have lived in the 6th century BCE. Whether he was a single historical person is disputed; he comes to us like mist on a mountain road.

Tradition places him in the 6th century BCE, in the time of Confucius. The date is uncertain, and no date of death is known.

The historian Sima Qian, writing about 100 BCE, names him Li Er, keeper of archives at the Zhou court, and also lists other men who might have been meant, so the uncertainty was already old.

In Sima Qian's account he met Confucius, then left the Zhou domain for the west and wrote the text at the Hangu Pass at the request of the gatekeeper Yin Xi. This account is traditional.

The Daodejing holds about 5,000 Chinese characters in 81 short chapters. Its earliest excavated versions, from Guodian (about 300 BCE) and Mawangdui (tomb sealed 168 BCE), fit the view of most scholars that the text took shape in the 4th to 3rd centuries BCE.

Later religious Daoism honored him as a deity, Laojun, and the Tang dynasty's imperial family, named Li, claimed him as an ancestor.

people--siddhartha-gautama--1.description:
Siddhartha Gautama, known as the Buddha, was a spiritual teacher in northern India whose teachings founded Buddhism. Traditional dates are about 563 to 483 BCE, but modern scholarship suggests a somewhat later range.

Buddhist tradition holds that he left a princely life and attained awakening at Bodh Gaya. Notice the shape of that story: a threshold crossed, a comfort set down.

His teachings include the Four Noble Truths and the Eightfold Path, a whole architecture of practice.

The exact dates of his life are debated among scholars.

Buddhism later spread across Asia, carried by monks and along trade routes. Ideas travel as far as the people who carry them.

people--tomyris--1.description:
Tomyris was a queen of the Massagetae, a nomadic people east of the Caspian Sea, who according to the Greek historian Herodotus defeated and killed Cyrus the Great of Persia in 530 BCE. She is known only from Herodotus, and other ancient accounts of Cyrus's death differ.

She appears only in Book 1 of Herodotus's Histories, written about a century after the events. Her dates are unknown; the date given here is that of the battle in his account.

Herodotus says she ruled the Massagetae, who dwelt east of the Caspian Sea near the Araxes River, and that she refused Cyrus's offer of marriage, which he saw as a road to her kingdom.

In his account the Persians took her son Spargapises by trickery, and he killed himself in captivity. Then Tomyris defeated the Persian army in battle.

Herodotus says she had Cyrus's body found and his head put in a wineskin filled with blood.

Other ancient accounts run another way: Xenophon has Cyrus die peacefully in his palace, and Ctesias has him die of a wound in a war on the eastern frontier that the Persians won.

people--tomyris--2.description:
Tomyris was a queen of the Massagetae, a nomadic people east of the Caspian Sea, who according to the Greek historian Herodotus defeated and killed Cyrus the Great of Persia in 530 BCE. Hold that "according to" firmly: she is known only from Herodotus, and other ancient accounts of Cyrus's death differ.

She appears only in Book 1 of his Histories, written about a century after the events. Her dates are unknown; the date given is that of the battle in his account.

In Herodotus she rules the Massagetae, east of the Caspian Sea near the Araxes River, and rejects Cyrus's offer of marriage, which he saw as a way to gain her kingdom. The Persians capture her son Spargapises by trickery, and he kills himself in captivity. Tomyris then defeats the Persian army in battle.

Herodotus says she had Cyrus's body found and his head put in a wineskin filled with blood.

Now set beside it the other ledgers. Xenophon has Cyrus die peacefully in his palace; Ctesias has him die of a wound in a war on the eastern frontier that the Persians won. When one source is all you have, you are reading a story about a person, not the person.

people--gorgo--1.description:
Gorgo (born about 518 BCE, last attested around 480 BCE) was queen of Sparta as wife of King Leonidas I, and the historian Herodotus remembers her as unusually sharp-witted and politically perceptive for a woman in his account of Greek affairs, a clear flame in a crowded hall.

She was the daughter of the Spartan king Cleomenes I, and according to Herodotus she warned him as a child not to trust a bribe offered by an Ionian envoy seeking Spartan military aid.

Herodotus credits her with finding a warning about the Persian king Xerxes's invasion plans hidden beneath the wax of a writing tablet sent by the exiled Spartan king Demaratus, when other Spartans could not read its message.

She was the wife of Leonidas I, who died leading the defense of Thermopylae against the Persian invasion in 480 BCE, the same year in which she is last clearly attested in the sources.

Nearly all that is known of her comes from Herodotus's Histories, written decades after her lifetime, and no independent Spartan record of her deeds survives.

people--pericles--1.description:
Pericles (about 495 to 429 BCE) was the leading Athenian statesman for over three decades in the mid-5th century BCE, a season later called the Golden Age of Athens for its building programs, its drama and its democratic institutions.

He rose in Athenian democracy through the office of strategos (general), to which he was re-elected year upon year, shaping policy through his sway over the Assembly rather than through any formal single office.

He directed the building program on the Acropolis, the Parthenon among it, paid for partly from treasury funds first gathered by the Delian League, an alliance of Greek states organized against Persia.

He extended pay for jury service and other public roles to poorer citizens, so that participation in Athenian democracy ran wider than the wealthy.

He championed the aggressive strategy that led Athens into the Peloponnesian War against Sparta in 431 BCE, and he died of plague in 429 BCE in the war's early years, before its outcome was decided, a man taken before the storm he summoned had passed.

people--pericles--2.description:
Pericles (about 495 to 429 BCE) was the leading Athenian statesman for over three decades in the mid-5th century BCE, a period later called the Golden Age of Athens for its building programs, drama and democratic institutions. His career shows you how influence can do the work of office.

He rose to prominence through the office of strategos (general), to which he was re-elected yearly, and he shaped policy through his influence over the Assembly rather than any formal single office.

He directed the building program on the Acropolis, including the Parthenon, funded partly by treasury funds originally collected from the Delian League, an alliance of Greek states organized against Persia. A monument can rest on a borrowed ledger.

He extended pay for jury service and other public roles to poorer citizens, broadening practical participation in Athenian democracy beyond the wealthy.

He championed the aggressive strategy that led Athens into the Peloponnesian War against Sparta in 431 BCE, and he died of plague in 429 BCE during the war's early years, before its outcome was decided. We rarely live to see the end of what we begin.

people--aristotle--1.description:
Aristotle (384 to 322 BCE) was a Greek philosopher and scientist who searched logic, ethics, politics, physics and biology, and who tutored Alexander of Macedon.

He studied under Plato in Athens and later founded a school of his own, the Lyceum.

He wrote on logic, ethics, politics, poetics, physics and biology.

His biological work rested on careful observation of marine life, of what moves beneath the water.

His works were kept and extended in the Islamic world, and later in Latin Europe.

people--alexander-the-great--1.description:
Alexander III of Macedon (356 to 323 BCE) was a commander who conquered the Persian Empire and carried Greek influence from Egypt to India like a wind across dry grass.

He became king at about twenty, after the assassination of his father, Philip II.

At Issus and Gaugamela he won great battles against the Persian king Darius III.

At the Hyphasis (Beas) river in India, his army turned back.

He died in Babylon in 323 BCE, and his empire was divided among his generals.

people--chandragupta-maurya--1.description:
Chandragupta Maurya (about 340 to 297 BCE) founded the Maurya Empire, the first power to unite most of the Indian subcontinent, after overthrowing the Nanda dynasty of Magadha around 321 BCE.

Guided by the strategist Chanakya (Kautilya), he seized the throne of Magadha. The Arthashastra, a treatise on statecraft traditionally attributed to Chanakya, was long linked to his rule, but most scholars now date it to roughly the 1st to 3rd centuries CE and doubt that it describes his reign.

Between about 305 and 303 BCE he fought the Diadoch ruler Seleucus I Nicator; the settlement ceded territory in the northwest to the Maurya and sealed a marriage alliance, and Seleucus received war elephants in return.

The Greek ambassador Megasthenes, sent to Chandragupta's court at Pataliputra, wrote the Indica, a major source on Mauryan India that now survives only in fragments.

Later Jain tradition holds that Chandragupta laid down his crown, became an ascetic under Bhadrabahu, and died by ritual fasting (sallekhana) at Shravanabelagola in Karnataka, though this account survives mainly in sources written well after his reign.

people--ashoka--1.description:
Ashoka (about 304 to 232 BCE) was a Mauryan emperor who ruled most of the Indian subcontinent and became a patron of Buddhism after a bloody war.

He conquered the region of Kalinga around 261 BCE at great human cost. His own edicts record about 100,000 killed and 150,000 deported; the count comes from the conqueror himself.

He had edicts inscribed on rocks and pillars across his empire, promoting 'dhamma' (moral conduct).

He supported the spread of Buddhism, including missions abroad.

His lion capital is now a national emblem of India.

people--qin-shi-huang--1.description:
Qin Shi Huang (259 to 210 BCE) was the first emperor of a unified China. He made one measure of writing, currency and weights, and raised a vast tomb complex guarded by the terracotta army.

He became king of Qin at thirteen and completed the unification of China in 221 BCE.

He made uniform the script, the weights and measures, and even the widths of axles.

Later historians, hostile to the Qin, told of book burning and harsh punishments; some of these accounts are debated.

His tomb complex near Xi'an holds thousands of life-size clay soldiers, standing in ranks like a buried army waiting for a dawn.

people--augustus--1.description:
Augustus (63 BCE to 14 CE) was the first Roman emperor. He ended a century of civil war and built the imperial system that endured for centuries.

Born Gaius Octavius, he was the adopted heir of Julius Caesar.

After overcoming his rivals he took the name Augustus in 27 BCE, while keeping the forms of the republic like an old shell around new life.

His reign began the Pax Romana, a long season of relative stability.

He reordered the army, the provinces and taxation.

people--ambiorix--1.description:
Ambiorix (active 54 to 53 BCE) was co-ruler of the Eburones, a Belgic tribe in what is now eastern Belgium, and he is remembered for destroying a Roman legion during a revolt against Julius Caesar's occupation of Gaul.

He shared the kingship of the Eburones with an older co-ruler, Cativolcus, an arrangement Caesar's own account describes but does not fully explain.

In the winter of 54 BCE he lured a Roman force under Quintus Titurius Sabinus and Lucius Aurunculeius Cotta out of its fortified camp with false promises of safe passage, then ambushed and destroyed it, killing both commanders.

Caesar answered with a campaign of deliberate devastation against the Eburones, meant to eliminate the tribe entirely. Ambiorix himself escaped capture and vanishes from the historical record after 53 BCE. The people who could not escape left no account of their own.

Now notice who is speaking. Nearly everything known about him comes from Caesar's own Commentarii de Bello Gallico, written to justify Caesar's conduct of the war to a Roman audience. When the only witness is the conqueror, every line is also a defense.

people--ban-zhao--1.description:
Ban Zhao (about 45 to about 117 CE) was a Chinese historian and scholar of the Eastern Han dynasty who helped finish the Book of Han after her brother's death and wrote Lessons for Women. She served also as tutor and adviser at court.

She was born about 45 CE (some sources say about 49) into a family of scholars. Her father Ban Biao and her brother Ban Gu wrote much of the Book of Han (Hanshu), a history of the Western Han dynasty.

Ban Gu died in prison in 92 CE with the history unfinished, a river stopped short of the sea, and Ban Zhao helped complete it by supplying the missing part of the Eight Tables.

At the imperial court she tutored the empress and her ladies and, from about 106 CE, advised the regent Empress Deng.

She is believed to have written Lessons for Women (Nüjie), in seven chapters, about 106 CE, though the date is not firmly established. It argues that girls should be educated and sets out rules of conduct for wives.

Later writers used Lessons for Women as a standard text for teaching girls obedience, and modern scholars disagree on whether it reinforced or challenged the limits placed on women.

people--trajan--1.description:
Trajan (53 to 117 CE) was Roman emperor from 98 to 117. Under him the empire reached its greatest territorial extent, and a great program of public building and infrastructure spread across the Roman world like roots through soil.

Born in Hispania, in present-day Spain, he was the first Roman emperor born outside Italy, adopted as heir by the emperor Nerva in 97 after a career as a successful general.

His conquest of Dacia, carved into the reliefs of Trajan's Column in Rome, added a wealthy new province rich in gold mines north of the Danube.

Late in his reign, after a campaign against the Parthian Empire, he annexed Armenia and parts of Mesopotamia and pushed Roman territory to its largest extent, gains his successor Hadrian largely abandoned as unsustainable, a tide that ran out as fast as it ran in.

He built Trajan's Forum and Market in Rome, a new harbor at Ostia, and an extensive network of roads and bridges across the provinces, paid for substantially with Dacian gold.

people--trajan--2.description:
Trajan (53 to 117 CE) was Roman emperor from 98 to 117, and his reign shows you the architecture of an empire at full stretch: its greatest territorial extent, and a major program of public building and infrastructure across the Roman world.

Born in Hispania, in present-day Spain, he was the first Roman emperor born outside Italy. After a career as a successful general, he was adopted as heir by the emperor Nerva in 97.

His conquest of Dacia, commemorated in the reliefs of Trajan's Column in Rome, added a wealthy new province rich in gold mines north of the Danube.

Late in his reign a campaign against the Parthian Empire let him annex Armenia and parts of Mesopotamia, extending Roman territory to its largest extent. His successor Hadrian largely abandoned those gains as unsustainable. Reach is not the same as hold.

His building programs included Trajan's Forum and Market in Rome, a new harbor at Ostia, and an extensive network of roads and bridges across the provinces, funded substantially by Dacian gold. The conquest paid for the roads.

people--zenobia--1.description:
Zenobia (Septimia Zenobia; about 240 to after 272) was queen of the caravan city of Palmyra in present-day Syria. She ruled for her young son and for a brief season stretched Palmyrene control over Roman Egypt, Syria and much of Anatolia, before the emperor Aurelian defeated her in 272.

She was the wife of Odaenathus, ruler of Palmyra, who had fought the Sasanian Persians for Rome in the 260s. He was killed about 267, and she took power as regent for their son Vaballathus.

About 270 her forces took Roman Egypt and pressed into Anatolia. By 271 she and her son bore the titles Augusta and Augustus.

Some coins struck in 271 and 272 show Aurelian on one face and Vaballathus on the other, so that for a time her claim was framed inside the Roman order.

In 272 Aurelian broke her armies at Immae and Emesa and captured her. Palmyra was sacked in 273 after a revolt.

Her fate is unknown, lost like a caravan in the sand. One tradition says she was shown in Aurelian's triumph in 274; its source, the Historia Augusta, is often unreliable.

people--zenobia--2.description:
Zenobia (Septimia Zenobia; about 240 to after 272) was queen of the caravan city of Palmyra in present-day Syria. She ruled for her young son and briefly extended Palmyrene control over Roman Egypt, Syria and much of Anatolia before the emperor Aurelian defeated her in 272.

She was the wife of Odaenathus, the ruler of Palmyra who had fought the Sasanian Persians for Rome in the 260s. When he was killed about 267, she took power as regent for their son Vaballathus.

About 270 her forces took Roman Egypt and pushed into Anatolia, and by 271 she and her son used the titles Augusta and Augustus.

Look closely at the coins. Some struck in 271 and 272 show Aurelian on one side and Vaballathus on the other, so for a time her claim was framed inside the Roman order. A coin is a small treaty: it says whose sovereignty you accept.

Aurelian defeated her armies in 272 at Immae and Emesa and captured her. Palmyra was sacked in 273 after a revolt.

Her fate is unknown. One tradition says she was shown in Aurelian's triumph in 274, but its source, the Historia Augusta, is often unreliable.

people--ba-trieu--1.description:
Ba Trieu (Trieu Thi Trinh; birth year unknown, died 248 CE) led an uprising against the Chinese Eastern Wu administration of northern Vietnam in 248 CE, and she became a lasting symbol of Vietnamese resistance to foreign rule, a flame kept from one age to the next.

She is said to have raised a rebel force in Cuu Chan, in present-day Thanh Hoa province, at about age twenty, alongside her brother Trieu Quoc Dat.

Later chronicles show her riding into battle on an elephant in gold-decorated armor, though these vivid details come from accounts written many centuries after her death, not from any contemporary record.

Eastern Wu sent the general Lu Yin to put down the revolt, and after several months of fighting her forces were defeated later in 248.

Vietnamese tradition holds that she fled to Bo Dien commune and died by suicide rather than be captured, with her burial place attributed to Mount Tung in Hau Loc District; Chinese-source summaries instead have Lu Yin putting her to death (sources give no age at death). A temple to her still stands near the site.

people--hypatia--1.description:
Hypatia (about 350 to 415 CE) was a philosopher, mathematician and astronomer in Alexandria who taught many students and was murdered by a mob. Hold both halves of that sentence; neither cancels the other.

She was the daughter of the mathematician Theon, and she taught Neoplatonist philosophy.

She is credited with commentaries on mathematical works, though the details are uncertain.

In 415 she was killed by a Christian mob during a political dispute between the Roman governor Orestes and Bishop Cyril.

Later writers turned her into a symbol, so historical and legendary accounts are mixed. A symbol can honor a life and blur it at once.

people--hypatia--2.description:
Hypatia (about 350 to 415 CE) was a philosopher, mathematician and astronomer of Alexandria, a teacher of many students, who was murdered by a mob.

Daughter of the mathematician Theon, she taught Neoplatonist philosophy.

Commentaries on mathematical works are credited to her, though the details are uncertain, like stars seen through haze.

In 415 she was killed by a Christian mob during a political dispute between the Roman governor Orestes and Bishop Cyril.

Later writers made her a symbol, and so the historical and the legendary accounts of her run together like two rivers in one bed.

people--attila--1.description:
Attila (about 406 to 453) ruled the Huns from 434, first with his brother Bleda and from about 445 alone. He led Hunnic armies against the Eastern and Western Roman empires, and almost all the written sources about him were set down by Greeks and Romans, so he comes to us through his enemies' eyes.

His birth year is uncertain, with estimates running from the 390s to the early 400s. He became joint ruler in 434 and sole ruler after Bleda died, probably about 445.

After the Treaty of Margus (435) the Eastern Roman Empire doubled its yearly tribute of gold, and after 443 it is reported to have reached 2,100 Roman pounds.

In 451 he swept into Gaul and fought a Roman and Visigothic army at the Catalaunian Plains. In 452 he invaded northern Italy. Both times he withdrew, like a flood drawing back.

He died in 453 after his wedding to Ildico. Priscus, as reported by Jordanes, describes a severe bleed; a later claim that his wife killed him is rejected by most historians. His empire broke apart within a few years.

Priscus, an envoy who visited his court in 449, left the only known eyewitness description. Attila's capital and tomb have not been found.

people--attila--2.description:
Attila (about 406 to 453) ruled the Huns from 434, first with his brother Bleda and from about 445 alone. He led Hunnic armies against the Eastern and Western Roman empires. Keep one fact in front of you as you read the rest: almost all written sources about him were composed by Greeks and Romans.

His birth year is uncertain, with estimates from the 390s to the early 400s. He became joint ruler in 434 and sole ruler after Bleda died, probably about 445.

After the Treaty of Margus (435) the Eastern Roman Empire doubled its yearly gold tribute, and after 443 it is reported to have reached 2,100 Roman pounds. Tribute is a ledger of fear, written in gold.

In 451 he invaded Gaul and fought a Roman and Visigothic army at the Catalaunian Plains; in 452 he invaded northern Italy. He withdrew both times.

He died in 453 after his wedding to Ildico. Priscus, as reported by Jordanes, describes a severe bleed. A later claim that his wife killed him is rejected by most historians. His empire broke up within a few years.

Priscus, an envoy who visited his court in 449, left the only known eyewitness description. His capital and tomb have not been found.

people--amanirenas--1.description:
Amanirenas was a queen (kandake) of the Kingdom of Kush who led the war against Roman Egypt from about 25 to 22 BCE and won a peace settlement from Augustus. Her birth and death years are unknown; the dates given here mark her approximate reign, about 40 to 10 BCE.

She ruled Kush from its capital region around Meroë; her birth and death years are unknown, and her reign is estimated.

About 25 BCE, while the Roman prefect's army was away, Kushite forces struck the Roman frontier in southern Egypt like a sudden flood, taking towns including Syene, Elephantine and Philae.

The prefect Gaius Petronius struck back about 24 BCE and sacked the Kushite city of Napata.

Peace was negotiated with Augustus about 21 to 20 BCE on Samos, and Kush is reported to have paid no tribute.

The Greek geographer Strabo describes a one-eyed, mannish queen "Candace" who led the Kushites; scholars generally identify her as Amanirenas.

people--amanirenas--2.description:
Amanirenas was a queen (kandake) of the Kingdom of Kush who led the war against Roman Egypt from about 25 to 22 BCE and won a peace settlement from Augustus. Her birth and death years are unknown; the dates given mark her approximate reign, about 40 to 10 BCE.

She ruled Kush from its capital region around Meroë. Again: her birth and death years are unknown, and her reign is estimated.

About 25 BCE Kushite forces attacked the Roman frontier in southern Egypt, taking towns including Syene, Elephantine and Philae, while the Roman prefect's army was away.

The prefect Gaius Petronius counterattacked about 24 BCE and sacked the Kushite city of Napata.

Then the outcome that matters. Peace was negotiated with Augustus about 21 to 20 BCE on Samos, and Kush is reported to have paid no tribute. A treaty without tribute is a statement of sovereignty.

The Greek geographer Strabo describes a one-eyed, mannish queen "Candace" who led the Kushites, and scholars generally identify her as Amanirenas.

people--amanitore--1.description:
Amanitore was a queen of the kingdom of Kush who co-ruled from the capital Meroe alongside a king, Natakamani, usually thought to be her son, during a prosperous period in the middle of the 1st century CE. Her story is a lesson in reading shared power from images.

Kushite royal women held the title kandake, often rendered "candace." Inscriptions and temple reliefs show Amanitore with the same royal regalia and war imagery as Natakamani, suggesting genuinely shared rule rather than a purely ceremonial role. In a visual grammar of kingship, equal regalia is an argument.

Together the pair sponsored a major building program, including temples at Meroe, Naqa and Amara, among the best-preserved Kushite monuments to survive.

A relief at the Lion Temple at Naqa shows Amanitore, like Natakamani, smiting bound captives, an image of royal power normally reserved for kings elsewhere in the Nile Valley tradition.

Her exact reign dates are fixed by no king list. Estimates for the coregency center on the middle of the 1st century CE, though some run earlier, and it is sometimes placed as contemporary with the Roman emperor Nero. Where the list is silent, the stones must speak.

people--cleopatra-vii--1.description:
Cleopatra VII was the last active ruler of the Ptolemaic Kingdom of Egypt. She allied with Julius Caesar and Mark Antony, and she died in 30 BCE after their defeat by Octavian. Strip away the legend and you find a dynasty's final chapter.

She belonged to the Ptolemaic dynasty, founded by a Macedonian general of Alexander the Great.

Ancient sources say she spoke several languages and, unlike most of her Ptolemaic predecessors, learned Egyptian. Learning the language of the people you rule is its own kind of covenant.

She had a son with Julius Caesar and children with Mark Antony.

Octavian defeated Antony and Cleopatra at the Battle of Actium in 31 BCE.

After her death in 30 BCE, Egypt became a Roman province.

people--ezana-of-aksum--1.description:
Ezana was king of Aksum, in present-day Ethiopia and Eritrea, from about 320 to about 360 CE, though sources differ on the exact dates. He is known for taking up Christianity and for a campaign in the Nile valley, and his inscriptions and coins bear witness to both.

He came to the throne as a child and ruled the Kingdom of Aksum from about 320 until about 360. Dates for his life and reign are approximate, and the sources differ.

His early inscriptions and coins show the older Aksumite religion, a crescent and disc shining on his coins.

Frumentius, a Christian from Tyre (described as Phoenician, and in some accounts Syrian) who rose in the Aksumite court, is reported to have been consecrated Aksum's first bishop by Athanasius of Alexandria, traditionally in 328, though other accounts say between 340 and 346.

Ezana converted to Christianity in the 4th century, though the exact date is uncertain. His later inscriptions call on a "Lord of Heaven," and on his coins the crescent and disc give way to the cross, often described as among the earliest coins to do so, as one light replaces another in the sky.

His inscriptions are in Ge'ez, Sabaean and Greek.

people--ezana-of-aksum--2.description:
Ezana was king of Aksum, in present-day Ethiopia and Eritrea, from about 320 to about 360 CE, though sources differ on the exact dates. He is known for adopting Christianity and for a campaign in the Nile valley, and his inscriptions and coins record both. Watch how a change of faith shows up in metal.

He came to the throne as a child and ruled the Kingdom of Aksum from about 320 until about 360; dates for his life and reign are approximate, and sources differ.

His early inscriptions and coins show older Aksumite religion, including a crescent and disc on his coins.

Frumentius, a Christian from Tyre (described as Phoenician, and in some accounts Syrian) who rose in the Aksumite court, is reported to have been consecrated Aksum's first bishop by Athanasius of Alexandria, traditionally in 328, though other accounts say between 340 and 346.

Ezana converted to Christianity in the 4th century, though the exact date is uncertain. His later inscriptions invoke a "Lord of Heaven," and his coins replace the crescent and disc with the cross, often described as among the earliest coins to do so. A coin travels further than a decree, and it carries a doctrine with it.

His inscriptions are in Ge'ez, Sabaean and Greek.

people--trung-sisters--1.description:
The Trưng Sisters, Trưng Trắc and Trưng Nhị (Chinese Zheng Ce and Zheng Er), led a revolt against Han Chinese rule in northern Vietnam from 40 to 43 CE. Their birth years are unknown; the dates given here are those of the revolt.

They came from Mê Linh in the Red River region, then part of the Han commandery of Jiaozhi.

They raised the revolt in 40 CE. Chinese sources tie it to harsh rule by the Han governor Su Ding, and Vietnamese tradition adds that he executed Trưng Trắc's husband, Thi Sách.

They took towns in several southern commanderies and are recorded as ruling as queens for about three years.

The Han general Ma Yuan led an army south and had defeated them by 43 CE.

The Chinese history Hou Hanshu says they were captured and beheaded, while Vietnamese tradition says they drowned themselves in a river; this second account is traditional.

people--trung-sisters--2.description:
The Trưng Sisters, Trưng Trắc and Trưng Nhị (Chinese Zheng Ce and Zheng Er), led a revolt against Han Chinese rule in northern Vietnam from 40 to 43 CE. Their birth years are unknown; the dates given are those of the revolt. What survives is a story told twice, by two sides.

They came from Mê Linh in the Red River region, then part of the Han commandery of Jiaozhi.

They began the revolt in 40 CE. Chinese sources link it to harsh rule by the Han governor Su Ding; Vietnamese tradition adds that he executed Trưng Trắc's husband, Thi Sách.

They took towns in several southern commanderies and are recorded as ruling as queens for about three years.

The Han general Ma Yuan led an army south and defeated them by 43 CE.

Even their ending has two ledgers. The Chinese history Hou Hanshu says they were captured and beheaded; Vietnamese tradition says they drowned themselves in a river, and this second account is traditional. Memory belongs to whoever keeps telling it.

people--khadija-bint-khuwaylid--1.description:
Khadija bint Khuwaylid (about 555 to 619) was a merchant of Mecca and the first wife of Muhammad. Her dates and many details of her life come from Muslim biographies written more than a century after her death, light reaching us from a distant lamp.

She belonged to the Quraysh tribe of Mecca and, according to tradition, financed trading caravans to Syria and hired agents to lead them across the desert roads.

Tradition says Muhammad led one of her caravans and that she proposed marriage, about 595. Accounts differ on her age then; a common figure is 40.

Muslim tradition holds that she was the first person to accept Muhammad's message after his first revelation, about 610.

Tradition names four daughters, Fatima among them, and sons who died young.

She died about 619, shortly before Muhammad's move to Medina in 622, and that year is remembered as the Year of Sorrow.

people--khadija-bint-khuwaylid--2.description:
Khadija bint Khuwaylid (about 555 to 619) was a merchant of Mecca and the first wife of Muhammad. Before anything else, know where the knowledge comes from: her dates and many details come from Muslim biographies written more than a century after her death.

She belonged to the Quraysh tribe of Mecca and, according to tradition, financed trading caravans to Syria and hired agents to lead them. Picture the ledger of a working merchant, and you have the setting of what follows.

Tradition says Muhammad led one of her caravans and that she proposed marriage, about 595. Accounts differ on her age then, and a common figure is 40.

Muslim tradition holds that she was the first person to accept Muhammad's message after his first revelation, about 610.

Tradition names four daughters, including Fatima, and sons who died young.

She died about 619, shortly before Muhammad's move to Medina in 622, a year remembered as the Year of Sorrow. A community can name a year after a loss, and that naming is its own memorial.

people--muhammad--1.description:
Muhammad (about 570 to 632 CE) was an Arabian religious and political leader, regarded by Muslims as the last prophet, who founded the community that grew into the Islamic world.

He was born in Mecca, and according to Islamic tradition he began receiving revelations around 610, later gathered as the Quran.

In 622 he and his followers migrated to Medina (the Hijra), and from that journey the Islamic calendar takes its start.

By the time of his death, most of the Arabian Peninsula had joined the community.

Islam is now followed by roughly a quarter of the world's population.

people--xuanzang--1.description:
Xuanzang (602 to 664) was a Chinese Buddhist monk who journeyed overland to India from 629 to 645 in search of authentic scriptures, studied for years at the monastery of Nalanda, and came home to translate texts and set down the story of his road.

He was born in 602 and ordained as a monk in his youth. In 629 he left China without imperial permission, travelling west through Central Asia toward India, like a single traveller walking against the wind.

For years he studied at Nalanda, a great center of Buddhist learning, under the scholar Silabhadra, and he visited Buddhist sites across the subcontinent.

In 645 he returned to China bearing Buddhist texts, images and relics, and the Tang court welcomed him despite his earlier unauthorized departure.

With official support he led a translation effort that carried more than a thousand fascicles of Buddhist texts from Sanskrit into Chinese.

He also wrote the Great Tang Records on the Western Regions, a travel account whose distances and descriptions later helped archaeologists find sites such as Nalanda itself.

people--xuanzang--2.description:
Xuanzang (602 to 664) was a Chinese Buddhist monk who traveled overland to India from 629 to 645 in search of authentic scriptures, studied for years at the monastery of Nalanda, and returned to translate texts and record his journey. His life is a lesson in what a pilgrimage can carry home.

Born in 602, he was ordained as a monk in his youth. In 629 he left China without imperial permission, traveling west through Central Asia toward India.

He spent years studying at Nalanda, a major center of Buddhist learning, under the scholar Silabhadra, and visited Buddhist sites across the subcontinent.

In 645 he returned to China with Buddhist texts, images and relics, and the Tang court welcomed him despite his earlier unauthorized departure.

With official support he led a translation effort that produced more than a thousand fascicles of Buddhist texts rendered from Sanskrit into Chinese.

He also wrote the Great Tang Records on the Western Regions, a travel account whose distances and descriptions later helped archaeologists locate sites such as Nalanda itself. A careful record outlives its writer's purpose.

people--xuanzang--3.description:
