Born in 602 and ordained in his youth, he left China in 629 without imperial permission, and went west through Central Asia toward India as rivers go toward the sea.

At Nalanda, a major center of Buddhist learning, he studied for years under the scholar Silabhadra, and he visited Buddhist sites across the subcontinent.

He came back to China in 645 with Buddhist texts, images and relics, and the Tang court received him in welcome, despite his earlier unauthorized departure.

With official support he led a translation effort that rendered more than a thousand fascicles of Buddhist texts from Sanskrit into Chinese.

His Great Tang Records on the Western Regions, a travel account, held distances and descriptions that later guided archaeologists to sites such as Nalanda itself.

people--pakal-the-great--1.description:
Pakal the Great (K'inich Janaab' Pakal, 603 to 683) ruled the Maya city of Palenque, in present-day Chiapas, Mexico, from 615 until his death, a reign of about 68 years, long as a great tree's shadow.

He was born in 603 and became king at age 12 in 615.

Palenque's inscriptions name his mother, Ix Sak K'uk', and show her setting the crown upon him at his accession.

In his reign the Palace complex at Palenque grew and was adorned with carved panels and hieroglyphic texts.

The Temple of the Inscriptions rose as his funerary monument, bearing long hieroglyphic panels on Palenque's dynastic history.

In 1952 Alberto Ruz Lhuillier reached a burial chamber within it, holding a carved stone sarcophagus and a jade mosaic mask, green as deep water.

people--pakal-the-great--2.description:
Pakal the Great (K'inich Janaab' Pakal, 603 to 683) ruled the Maya city of Palenque, in present-day Chiapas, Mexico, from 615 until his death, a reign of about 68 years. Think of what a reign that long lets a ruler build.

Born in 603, he became king at age 12 in 615.

Palenque's inscriptions name his mother, Ix Sak K'uk', and show her presenting him with the crown at his accession. A lineage is made visible in the act of handing over.

During his reign the Palace complex at Palenque was enlarged and decorated with carved panels and hieroglyphic texts.

The Temple of the Inscriptions was built as his funerary monument and carries long hieroglyphic panels on Palenque's dynastic history: architecture used as an archive.

In 1952 Alberto Ruz Lhuillier reached a burial chamber inside it, holding a carved stone sarcophagus and a jade mosaic mask.

people--aisha-bint-abi-bakr--1.description:
Aisha bint Abi Bakr (about 614 to 678 CE) was a wife of the Prophet Muhammad and a daughter of the first caliph, Abu Bakr. She is credited with handing down more than two thousand hadith, and she took part in the Battle of the Camel in 656.

She was born about 614 in Mecca to Abu Bakr and Umm Ruman, and she died in Medina in July 678 (58 AH), a date that is uncertain.

Her marriage to Muhammad was contracted in Mecca and began in Medina about 623. Classical sources give her age as six or seven at the contract and nine at the start. These figures come from later hadith and biographies, and some modern scholars question them.

She is credited with more than 2,000 hadith on ritual, inheritance, ethics and daily life, gathered in Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim, and she also taught, a spring from which many drew.

In 656 she opposed Ali ibn Abi Talib, demanding punishment of the killers of the caliph Uthman. Her forces lost the Battle of the Camel near Basra. Ali pardoned her, and she withdrew from politics.

Sunni tradition honors her as a scholar. Shia tradition views her critically because of her opposition to Ali.

people--aisha-bint-abi-bakr--2.description:
Aisha bint Abi Bakr (about 614 to 678 CE) was a wife of the Prophet Muhammad and a daughter of the first caliph, Abu Bakr. She is credited with transmitting more than two thousand hadith and took part in the Battle of the Camel in 656. Hers is a life that two traditions read in two ways.

She was born about 614 in Mecca to Abu Bakr and Umm Ruman and died in Medina in July 678 (58 AH), a date that is uncertain.

Her marriage to Muhammad was contracted in Mecca and began in Medina about 623. Classical sources give her age as six or seven at the contract and nine at the start; these figures come from later hadith and biographies, and some modern scholars question them.

She is credited with more than 2,000 hadith on ritual, inheritance, ethics and daily life, found in Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim, and she also taught. Transmission is its own kind of authorship.

In 656 she opposed Ali ibn Abi Talib, demanding punishment of the killers of the caliph Uthman. Her forces lost the Battle of the Camel near Basra; Ali pardoned her, and she withdrew from politics.

Sunni tradition honors her as a scholar, while Shia tradition views her critically because of her opposition to Ali.

people--wu-zetian--1.description:
Wu Zetian (624 to 705 CE) was the only woman to rule China in her own name as emperor, and she founded the short-lived Zhou dynasty (690 to 705), brief as a comet's passing.

She entered the palace as a concubine of the Tang emperor and rose to become empress consort.

For decades she ruled in effect before taking the throne herself in 690.

She widened the civil service examination system to draw talent from beyond the aristocracy.

She gave her support to Buddhism.

people--seondeok--1.description:
Queen Seondeok (birth year unknown, died 647 CE) ruled the Korean kingdom of Silla as its first reigning queen, in a time of Buddhist temple building, early watching of the stars, and continued warfare with the rival kingdoms of Baekje and Goguryeo.

She succeeded her father, King Jinpyeong, in 632, after he left no surviving son, and became Silla's first female monarch in her own right.

Under her rose Cheomseongdae, often described as one of the oldest surviving astronomical observatories in East Asia, and the Hwangnyongsa nine-story pagoda, built to help protect the kingdom according to Buddhist belief.

Baekje struck at Silla again and again in her reign, and border fortresses were lost. She resolved to form a military alliance with Tang China, and her general Kim Yushin and diplomat Kim Chunchu, later King Muyeol, are traditionally credited with the negotiations.

In 647 the noble Bidam rose in rebellion against her rule; Kim Yushin and Kim Alcheon put it down shortly after her death that same year, a death some accounts link to the unrest.

people--seondeok--2.description:
Queen Seondeok (birth year unknown, died 647 CE) ruled the Korean kingdom of Silla as its first reigning queen. Her reign joins three things you might not expect side by side: Buddhist temple building, early astronomical observation, and continued warfare with the rival kingdoms of Baekje and Goguryeo.

She succeeded her father, King Jinpyeong, in 632 after he left no surviving son, becoming Silla's first female monarch in her own right.

Her reign saw the construction of Cheomseongdae, often described as one of the oldest surviving astronomical observatories in East Asia, and the Hwangnyongsa nine-story pagoda, built to help protect the kingdom according to Buddhist belief. Here architecture is both instrument and prayer.

Silla faced repeated attacks from Baekje, including the loss of border fortresses, and she decided to form a military alliance with Tang China; her general Kim Yushin and diplomat Kim Chunchu, later King Muyeol, are traditionally credited with the negotiations.

A rebellion by the noble Bidam broke out in 647 and was suppressed by Kim Yushin and Kim Alcheon shortly after her death that same year, which some accounts link to the unrest.

people--lady-six-sky--1.description:
Lady Six Sky (Wak Chanil Ajaw; active 682 to 741 CE) was a Maya noblewoman of Dos Pilas who came to Naranjo in 682 and in effect ruled the city for decades, raising it again after a time of defeat.

She was a daughter of the Dos Pilas king B'alaj Chan K'awiil, a strand in the web of the powerful city of Calakmul's allies against its rival Tikal.

Naranjo's royal line had been broken after a defeat by Caracol, and Lady Six Sky was installed there in 682, apparently to set the dynasty on its roots once more.

Monuments show her overseeing military campaigns and presiding over the accession of her young son K'ahk' Tiliw Chan Chaahk in 693, and after it she went on appearing in inscriptions as a ruling figure into the 700s.

She never took the full royal title used by the male kings of Naranjo, and all her life she kept the emblem glyph of her home city Dos Pilas, so her exact formal status is debated by epigraphers.

people--charlemagne--1.description:
Charlemagne (c. 748 to 814) was king of the Franks. He conquered much of western and central Europe and was crowned emperor by the pope in Rome on Christmas Day 800.

He became sole king of the Franks in 771.

He overcame the Lombards in Italy and the Saxons, and took parts of Spain's northern border.

Pope Leo III crowned him emperor on 25 December 800.

His court kindled a revival of learning, the Carolingian Renaissance, and spread a clear minuscule script like lamplight across the page.

After his death in 814 his empire was divided among his descendants, and under the Treaty of Verdun in 843 it split into three kingdoms.

people--al-khwarizmi--1.description:
Muhammad ibn Musa al-Khwarizmi (about 780 to 850 CE) was a Persian scholar at the House of Wisdom in Baghdad whose work on algebra and Hindu-Arabic numerals shaped mathematics. You use his name more often than you know.

His book on 'al-jabr' (restoration) gave algebra its name.

The word 'algorithm' derives from the Latinized form of his name.

His work helped introduce Hindu-Arabic numerals and place-value arithmetic to the wider world, a grammar for numbers that we still think in.

He also compiled astronomical tables and geographical data.

people--basil-ii--1.description:
Basil II (958 to 1025) was Byzantine emperor for nearly fifty years, the longest reign in Roman or Byzantine imperial history, and he is remembered above all for his decades-long war against the First Bulgarian Empire.

He became co-emperor as a child in 960, but only about 989, in his thirties, did he gain full personal control of the government, after crushing rebellions by powerful aristocratic generals, Bardas Skleros and Bardas Phokas among them.

His long campaigns against Bulgaria came to their height at the decisive Battle of Kleidion in 1014, and by 1018 Bulgaria had been absorbed into the Byzantine Empire, earning him the later epithet "Bulgar-slayer" (Boulgaroktonos).

A story recorded by later chroniclers claims he blinded thousands of Bulgarian prisoners after Kleidion, leaving one eye to every hundredth man to lead the rest home; modern historians debate how literally this account should be taken.

He left the imperial treasury full and the empire at its greatest extent since the 7th century, but he died without an heir, and the strong central rule he had imposed did not outlast his less capable successors, like a dam with no keeper.

people--basil-ii--2.description:
Basil II (958 to 1025) was Byzantine emperor for nearly fifty years, the longest reign in Roman or Byzantine imperial history, and he is remembered above all for his decades-long war against the First Bulgarian Empire.

He became co-emperor as a child in 960 but did not gain full personal control of the government until about 989, when he was in his thirties, after suppressing rebellions by powerful aristocratic generals including Bardas Skleros and Bardas Phokas.

His campaigns against Bulgaria culminated in the decisive Battle of Kleidion in 1014, after which Bulgaria was absorbed into the Byzantine Empire by 1018, earning him the later epithet "Bulgar-slayer" (Boulgaroktonos).

A story recorded by later chroniclers claims he blinded thousands of Bulgarian prisoners after Kleidion, leaving one eye to every hundredth man to lead the rest home. Modern historians debate how literally this account should be taken. Treat it as you would any story told about a feared ruler: as a record of fear first.

He left the imperial treasury full and the empire at its greatest territorial extent since the 7th century, but died without an heir, and the strong central rule he had imposed did not survive his less capable successors. A system built around one person ends with that person.

people--al-biruni--1.description:
Al-Biruni (973 to after 1048) was a scholar of Khwarazm in Central Asia who wrote on astronomy, mathematics, geography, chronology and India. His Kitab al-Hind (about 1030) is a major medieval study of Indian science, religion and customs.

He was born in 973 in Kath, in Khwarazm in present-day Uzbekistan, and died after 1048, perhaps about 1050.

When the Ghaznavid ruler Mahmud conquered Khwarazm in 1017, he was carried off to Ghazni, where he worked under Mahmud and those who came after.

He spent years in northwestern India, learned Sanskrit, and wrote the Kitab al-Hind, describing Indian science, religion, society and customs from Sanskrit texts and from conversations with Indian scholars.

His Chronology of Ancient Nations (about 1000) sets side by side the calendars and dating systems of many cultures, like many rivers measured against one shore.

He reckoned the radius of the Earth as about 6,320 km by measuring the dip of the horizon from the top of a hill, close to the modern value.

people--al-biruni--2.description:
Al-Biruni (973 to after 1048) was a scholar from Khwarazm in Central Asia who wrote on astronomy, mathematics, geography, chronology and India. His Kitab al-Hind (about 1030) is a major medieval study of Indian science, religion and customs, and his method is worth learning from.

Born in 973 in Kath, in Khwarazm in present-day Uzbekistan, he died after 1048, perhaps about 1050.

After the Ghaznavid ruler Mahmud conquered Khwarazm in 1017, he was taken to Ghazni, where he worked under Mahmud and his successors.

He spent years in northwestern India and learned Sanskrit. Then he wrote the Kitab al-Hind from Sanskrit texts and conversations with Indian scholars, describing Indian science, religion, society and customs. That is the practice: learn the language before you describe the people.

His Chronology of Ancient Nations (about 1000) compares the calendars and dating systems of many cultures.

He calculated the radius of the Earth as about 6,320 km by measuring the dip of the horizon from the top of a hill, close to the modern value. A hill and careful attention can measure a world.

people--murasaki-shikibu--1.description:
Murasaki Shikibu (about 973 to about 1014) was a lady-in-waiting at the Japanese imperial court in the Heian period. She wrote The Tale of Genji, a 54-chapter novel of court life that is widely called the world's first novel.

"Murasaki Shikibu" is a later nickname. Her personal name is unknown, lost like a petal on a stream; the nickname joins a character from her novel to her father's court rank.

She was born about 973 into a minor branch of the Fujiwara clan, and she learned the Chinese classics, normally reserved for men, by taking in the lessons given to her brother.

About 998 she married a much older provincial governor and was widowed within a few years. About 1005 or 1006 she entered court service as a lady-in-waiting to Empress Shōshi.

The Tale of Genji follows a fictional prince and, in its later chapters, his descendants. It may have been begun before she came to court, though sources suggest she likely composed it while serving as a lady-in-waiting, possibly chapter by chapter.

She wrote almost entirely in hiragana, the script tied to women's writing at court, and set many waka poems into the story as the characters' own compositions.

people--murasaki-shikibu--2.description:
I stand before Murasaki Shikibu (about 973 to about 1014), lady-in-waiting at the Japanese imperial court in the Heian period, who wrote The Tale of Genji, a 54-chapter novel of court life widely called the world's first novel.

And I learn that I do not know her name. "Murasaki Shikibu" is a later nickname; her personal name is unknown. The nickname joins a character from her novel to her father's court rank. I learn that she was born about 973 into a minor branch of the Fujiwara clan, and that she learned the Chinese classics, normally reserved for men, by absorbing lessons given to her brother.

I learn that about 998 she married a much older provincial governor and was widowed within a few years, and that about 1005 or 1006 she entered court service as a lady-in-waiting to Empress Shōshi.

The Tale of Genji follows a fictional prince and, in its later chapters, his descendants. It may have been begun before she came to court, though sources suggest she likely composed it while serving, possibly chapter by chapter. She wrote almost entirely in hiragana, the script associated with women's writing at court, and set many waka poems into the story as the characters' own.

What is a name beside a whole world of pages? The work remembers what the record forgot.

people--ibn-sina--1.description:
Ibn Sina (Avicenna, 980 to 1037) was a Persian physician and philosopher whose 'Canon of Medicine' stood for centuries as a standard medical text in the Islamic world and in Europe.

He was born near Bukhara in Central Asia.

The Canon of Medicine (completed about 1025) set medical knowledge in systematic order, like stars charted into constellations.

Translated into Latin, it was used in European universities into the 17th century.

His philosophical 'Book of Healing' also shaped medieval Europe.

people--harald-hardrada--1.description:
Harald Hardrada (about 1015 to 1066) was King of Norway from 1046 to 1066, a warrior-king whose road ran from exile through mercenary service in Byzantium to the throne, and whose death at Stamford Bridge is often used to mark the end of the Viking Age.

After his half-brother King Olaf II fell in battle in 1030, the teenage Harald fled Norway and in time served as a commander in the Byzantine Empire's elite Varangian Guard, campaigning in the Mediterranean and Middle East.

He came back to Scandinavia around 1045 with substantial wealth, won a share of the Norwegian throne in 1046, and became sole king when his co-ruler died in 1047.

For years he waged inconclusive war on Denmark over rival claims, making peace at last in 1064 (or 1065 according to Morkinskinna) without the Danish throne he sought.

In September 1066 he invaded England to press a rival claim to its throne, and was defeated and killed at the Battle of Stamford Bridge by King Harold Godwinson, days before Godwinson had to march south to face William of Normandy's invasion at Hastings, one storm breaking just before the next.

people--li-qingzhao--1.description:
I came to read about Li Qingzhao (1084 to about 1155), a Chinese poet of the Song dynasty, widely regarded as the greatest woman writer in the classical Chinese tradition, whose ci, a lyric verse form, moved from a settled, cultured life to loss and exile after northern China fell to invaders.

I read that she was born in 1084 in Qi Prefecture, today's Zhangqiu in Shandong, to a literary family, and is thought to have died about 1155. I read that in 1101 she married Zhao Mingcheng, a scholar who shared her interest in antiquities, and that the Jinshi lu, a catalog of bronze and stone inscriptions, is described as his work and was published after his death.

I read that when the Jin dynasty invaded northern China in 1127, the couple fled south with part of their collection, much of which is said to have been lost along the way. Zhao Mingcheng died in 1129. After his death she wrote an afterword to the Jinshi lu describing their marriage and their losses. She briefly remarried, the year traditionally given as about 1132, and divorced amid scandal soon after.

Her poems, mostly short ci in personal, direct language, describe love, separation, and later grief and displacement. Only around a hundred are known to survive, out of a larger body assembled and praised by later editors.

How much can one carry south? Enough to write the losses down.

people--li-qingzhao--2.description:
Li Qingzhao (1084 to about 1155) was a Chinese poet of the Song dynasty, widely regarded as the greatest woman writer in the classical Chinese tradition. Her ci, a lyric verse form, passed from a settled, cultured life into loss and exile after northern China fell to invaders, as a river leaves the garden for the gorge.

She was born in 1084 in Qi Prefecture, today's Zhangqiu in Shandong, to a literary family, and is thought to have died about 1155.

In 1101 she married Zhao Mingcheng, a scholar who shared her love of antiquities. The Jinshi lu, a catalog of bronze and stone inscriptions, is described as her husband's work and was published after his death.

When the Jin dynasty invaded northern China in 1127, the couple fled south with part of their collection, much of which is said to have been lost along the way. Zhao Mingcheng died in 1129.

After his death she wrote an afterword to the Jinshi lu telling of their marriage and their losses. She briefly remarried, the year traditionally given as about 1132, and divorced amid scandal soon after.

Her poems, mostly short ci in personal, direct language, tell of love, separation, and later grief and displacement. Only around a hundred are known to survive, out of a larger body gathered and praised by later editors.

people--frederick-barbarossa--1.description:
Frederick I, called Barbarossa ("Redbeard"; about 1122 to 1190), was Holy Roman Emperor from 1155 until his death and one of medieval Europe's mightiest rulers, and much of his reign was spent contending for northern Italy.

Elected King of Germany in 1152, he was crowned Holy Roman Emperor by the pope in 1155, and again and again he came down into Italy to assert imperial authority over its wealthy independent city-states.

The Lombard League, an alliance of northern Italian cities backed by the papacy, broke his forces at the Battle of Legnano in 1176, and in the Peace of Constance of 1183 he was made to recognize significant city autonomy.

He arranged the marriage of his son Henry to Constance of Sicily, a match that later brought the Kingdom of Sicily under his family's hand.

In 1190, during the Third Crusade, he drowned while crossing a river in Anatolia, before he reached the Holy Land. With his death much of his army scattered or turned back rather than go on, like a wave breaking before the shore.

people--frederick-barbarossa--2.description:
Frederick I, called Barbarossa ("Redbeard"; about 1122 to 1190), was Holy Roman Emperor from 1155 until his death and one of medieval Europe's most powerful rulers. Yet his reign shows you the limits of power: much of it was spent contesting control of northern Italy.

Elected King of Germany in 1152, he was crowned Holy Roman Emperor by the pope in 1155 and repeatedly invaded Italy to assert imperial authority over its wealthy independent city-states.

The Lombard League, an alliance of northern Italian cities backed by the papacy, defeated his forces at the Battle of Legnano in 1176, forcing him to recognize significant city autonomy in the Peace of Constance of 1183. Cities that combine can outlast an emperor.

He arranged the marriage of his son Henry to Constance of Sicily, a match that later brought the Kingdom of Sicily under his family's control.

He drowned in 1190 while crossing a river in Anatolia during the Third Crusade, before reaching the Holy Land, and his death caused much of his army to disband or turn back rather than continue. An army held together by one person can come apart with them.

people--jayavarman-vii--1.description:
Jayavarman VII (about 1122 to about 1218) was king of the Khmer Empire from about 1181 until his death. He drove out the Cham invaders who had sacked Angkor, and then raised a great building program that included Angkor Thom and the Bayon.

Champa forces sacked Angkor in 1177. Jayavarman VII defeated them and was crowned about 1181; his birth and death years are estimates.

Later, Khmer forces brought parts of Champa under Khmer rule.

He was a Mahayana Buddhist, while most earlier Khmer rulers had favored Hindu cults.

His works include Angkor Thom; the Bayon, its towers carved with large faces, calm as still water; Ta Prohm, dedicated to his mother; and Preah Khan, dedicated to his father.

An inscription of 1186 at Ta Prohm credits him with 102 hospitals, a figure that comes from the king's own inscriptions.

people--jayavarman-vii--2.description:
Jayavarman VII (about 1122 to about 1218) was king of the Khmer Empire from about 1181 until his death. He drove out Cham invaders who had sacked Angkor and then led a large building program that included Angkor Thom and the Bayon. Recovery, for him, took the form of architecture.

Champa forces sacked Angkor in 1177. Jayavarman VII defeated them and was crowned about 1181; his birth and death years are estimates.

Khmer forces later brought parts of Champa under Khmer control.

He was a Mahayana Buddhist, while most earlier Khmer rulers had favored Hindu cults.

His projects include Angkor Thom, the Bayon with its towers carved with large faces, Ta Prohm (dedicated to his mother) and Preah Khan (dedicated to his father). Notice the dedications: a building program can also be a family's genealogy.

An inscription of 1186 at Ta Prohm credits him with 102 hospitals. Keep in mind where the figure comes from: the king's own inscriptions.

people--eleanor-of-aquitaine--1.description:
Eleanor of Aquitaine (about 1124 to 1204, with older sources giving 1122 for her birth) was successively queen of France and queen of England, and one of the wealthiest and most powerful women in 12th-century Europe, because she ruled the Duchy of Aquitaine in her own right. Her power began with land, and that is the key to her story.

She inherited the vast Duchy of Aquitaine in southwestern France in 1137 and married King Louis VII of France that same year. The marriage was annulled in 1152 after producing no sons.

Weeks after the annulment she married Henry of Anjou, who became King Henry II of England in 1154, and her extensive French territories went into the combined "Angevin Empire" that spanned much of France and England.

She supported a rebellion by three of her sons against Henry II in 1173 to 1174. After it failed, Henry kept her in confinement for about fifteen to sixteen years, until his death in 1189.

Freed by her son Richard I ("the Lionheart"), she acted as regent during his crusade and captivity, and later helped secure the throne for her youngest son, John, after Richard's death in 1199. Sovereignty interrupted is not sovereignty lost.

people--genghis-khan--1.description:
Genghis Khan (born Temujin, about 1162 to 1227) united the Mongol tribes in 1206 and founded the Mongol Empire.

He built an army on merit and loyalty rather than clan, a new architecture of allegiance.

His campaigns overran Central Asia, northern China and Persia.

He promoted a written script and a legal code (the Yassa), and he encouraged religious tolerance.

He died in 1227, and the location of his tomb is unknown.

people--saladin--1.description:
Saladin (Salah ad-Din Yusuf ibn Ayyub, about 1137 to 1193) was a Kurdish-born Muslim commander who founded the Ayyubid dynasty, ruled Egypt and much of Syria, and recaptured Jerusalem from the Crusaders in 1187. Follow his rise step by step and you see how a dynasty is assembled.

He was born about 1137 in Tikrit, in present-day Iraq, to a Kurdish family, and died in Damascus on 4 March 1193.

Step one: service. He rose under the Zengid ruler Nur ad-Din and became vizier of Fatimid Egypt in 1169.

Step two: allegiance. In 1171 he ended the Fatimid Caliphate and restored Egypt's allegiance to the Abbasid caliph; his family, the Ayyubids, went on to rule Egypt and Syria.

Step three: consolidation. After Nur ad-Din died in 1174 he took Damascus and brought much of Syria and northern Mesopotamia under his rule.

On 4 July 1187 his army destroyed a Crusader army at the Battle of Hattin. Jerusalem surrendered on 2 October 1187. Its Latin inhabitants could ransom themselves, though many who could not pay were enslaved. A city's surrender has a ledger, and the poorest pay the most.

people--saladin--2.description:
Saladin (Salah ad-Din Yusuf ibn Ayyub, about 1137 to 1193) was a Kurdish-born Muslim commander who founded the Ayyubid dynasty, ruled Egypt and much of Syria, and took Jerusalem back from the Crusaders in 1187.

He was born about 1137 in Tikrit, in present-day Iraq, to a Kurdish family, and he died in Damascus on 4 March 1193.

He rose in the service of the Zengid ruler Nur ad-Din and in 1169 became vizier of Fatimid Egypt.

In 1171 he brought the Fatimid Caliphate to its end and turned Egypt's allegiance back to the Abbasid caliph, and his family, the Ayyubids, went on to rule Egypt and Syria.

When Nur ad-Din died in 1174, Saladin took Damascus and gathered much of Syria and northern Mesopotamia under his rule, as tributaries gather into one river.

On 4 July 1187 his army destroyed a Crusader army at the Battle of Hattin. Jerusalem surrendered on 2 October 1187; its Latin inhabitants could ransom themselves, though many who could not pay were enslaved.

people--saladin--3.description:
Saladin (Salah ad-Din Yusuf ibn Ayyub, about 1137 to 1193) was a Kurdish-born Muslim commander. He founded the Ayyubid dynasty, ruled Egypt and much of Syria, and recaptured Jerusalem from the Crusaders in 1187.

Born about 1137 in Tikrit, in present-day Iraq, to a Kurdish family, he died in Damascus on 4 March 1193.

He rose in the service of the Zengid ruler Nur ad-Din and became vizier of Fatimid Egypt in 1169. In 1171 he ended the Fatimid Caliphate and restored Egypt's allegiance to the Abbasid caliph. Allegiance is a covenant, and to change it is to change the whole architecture of a state.

His family, the Ayyubids, went on to rule Egypt and Syria. After Nur ad-Din died in 1174 he took Damascus and brought much of Syria and northern Mesopotamia under his rule.

On 4 July 1187 his army destroyed a Crusader army at the Battle of Hattin. Jerusalem surrendered on 2 October 1187, and its Latin inhabitants could ransom themselves, though many who could not pay were enslaved. Remember both halves of that sentence when you hear the victory told.

people--tamar-of-georgia--1.description:
Tamar (born about 1160 or 1166, died 1213) ruled the Kingdom of Georgia from 1184 to 1213, presiding over its political and cultural summit, later called the Georgian Golden Age.

She was crowned co-ruler with her father, George III, in 1178 to secure her succession, and on his death in 1184 she became sole monarch, ruling with the formal title "king of kings" rather than a feminine equivalent.

Her armies won great victories against regional Muslim powers, among them the Battle of Shamkor in 1195 and the Battle of Basian (dated to 1202, 1203 or 1204 depending on the source), and Georgian influence spread like a rising tide across much of the South Caucasus and into parts of Armenia and Anatolia.

Her reign saw rich patronage of Georgian literature and architecture, including the era's most celebrated work, Shota Rustaveli's epic poem "The Knight in the Panther's Skin," traditionally associated with her as its inspiration.

The Georgian Orthodox Church canonized her as a saint, and centuries of later Georgian tradition remember her reign as the kingdom's greatest age of security and cultural achievement.

people--tamar-of-georgia--2.description:
Tamar (born about 1160 or 1166, died 1213) ruled the Kingdom of Georgia from 1184 to 1213, presiding over its political and cultural high point, later called the Georgian Golden Age. Look at how carefully her power was built.

She was crowned co-ruler with her father, George III, in 1178 to secure her succession, then became sole monarch on his death in 1184. She ruled with the formal title "king of kings" rather than a feminine equivalent. A title is a piece of grammar, and she chose the one that carried the most weight.

Her armies won major victories against regional Muslim powers, including the Battle of Shamkor in 1195 and the Battle of Basian (dated to 1202, 1203 or 1204 depending on the source), expanding Georgian influence across much of the South Caucasus and into parts of Armenia and Anatolia.

Her reign saw significant patronage of Georgian literature and architecture, including the era's most celebrated work, Shota Rustaveli's epic poem "The Knight in the Panther's Skin," traditionally associated with her as its inspiration.

She was canonized as a saint by the Georgian Orthodox Church, and centuries of later Georgian tradition remember her reign as the kingdom's greatest period of security and cultural achievement.

people--razia-sultana--1.description:
Razia Sultana (about 1205 to 1240) ruled the Delhi Sultanate from 1236 to 1240, the only woman to hold the throne in its history. She was the daughter of Iltutmish, who by tradition had named her his successor. Her reign is short, and that makes every detail of it count.

Razia was a daughter of the sultan Iltutmish, who reigned from 1211 to 1236. Tradition holds that he named her his heir over his sons, though he seems to have chosen Ruknuddin Firuz shortly before his death. Notice the gap between what tradition remembers and what the record suggests.

After Iltutmish died in 1236 her half-brother Ruknuddin Firuz took the throne but was deposed within months, and Razia became sultan with the support of the people of Delhi and some nobles.

According to chroniclers she held court in public and led armies, and coins were issued in her name.

She appointed Jamal ud-Din Yaqut, an Abyssinian former slave, master of the stables, a promotion Turkic nobles resented.

In 1240 Malik Altunia, the governor of Bhatinda, rebelled. She was imprisoned at Bhatinda and then married him in September 1240; they were defeated at Kaithal and killed in October 1240, and accounts differ on the details.

people--razia-sultana--2.description:
Razia Sultana (about 1205 to 1240) ruled the Delhi Sultanate from 1236 to 1240, the only woman ever to hold its throne. She was the daughter of Iltutmish, who by tradition had named her to follow him.

Her father, the sultan Iltutmish, reigned from 1211 to 1236. Tradition holds that he chose her as heir over his sons, though he seems to have chosen Ruknuddin Firuz shortly before his death.

When Iltutmish died in 1236 her half-brother Ruknuddin Firuz took the throne, but within months he was cast down, and Razia became sultan, borne up by the people of Delhi and some nobles.

According to chroniclers she held court in the open and led armies, and coins were struck in her name.

She raised Jamal ud-Din Yaqut, an Abyssinian former slave, to master of the stables, a promotion the Turkic nobles resented.

In 1240 Malik Altunia, governor of Bhatinda, rose against her. She was imprisoned at Bhatinda and then married him in September 1240; together they were defeated at Kaithal and killed in October 1240, and the accounts differ on the details, like footprints blurred by rain.

people--rumi--1.description:
Rumi (Jalal ad-Din Muhammad Rumi, 1207 to 1273) was a Persian-language poet and Sufi teacher who spent his grown years in Konya, in Anatolia. His long poem, the Masnavi, and his lyric poems are among the most widely read works of Persian literature.

He was born in 1207 in Balkh or nearby Wakhsh, in present-day Afghanistan or Tajikistan; sources differ. His family moved west, and by about 1228 he was living in Konya, in the Seljuk Sultanate of Rum.

Like his father, Baha ad-Din Walad, he trained as a scholar and preacher, and he taught in Konya.

In 1244 he met a wandering mystic, Shams of Tabriz. Their friendship changed his life as a flood changes a valley, and he began to write poetry. About 1248 Shams disappeared, and accounts differ: some say he was killed, others that he simply moved on.

He wrote the Masnavi, a long poem in six books, and thousands of lyric poems gathered in the Divan of Shams, mostly in Persian.

The Masnavi runs to some 25,000 to 27,000 couplets, counts differing by source, composed over his last decade or so at the request of his disciple Husam al-Din Chalabi, who wrote the verses down as Rumi recited them. Some later readers called it "the Quran in Persian".

people--rumi--2.description:
Rumi (Jalal ad-Din Muhammad Rumi, 1207 to 1273) was a Persian-language poet and Sufi teacher who spent his adult life in Konya, in Anatolia. His long poem, the Masnavi, and his lyric poems are among the most widely read works of Persian literature, and his life shows how one meeting can redirect a vocation.

He was born in 1207 in Balkh or nearby Wakhsh, in present-day Afghanistan or Tajikistan; sources differ. His family moved west, and by about 1228 he was living in Konya, in the Seljuk Sultanate of Rum.

He wrote the Masnavi, a long poem in six books, and thousands of lyric poems collected in the Divan of Shams, mostly in Persian.

The Masnavi runs to some 25,000 to 27,000 couplets, with counts differing by source, composed over his last decade or so at the request of his disciple Husam al-Din Chalabi, who wrote the verses down as Rumi recited them. Some later readers called it "the Quran in Persian". Friendship can be the threshold a whole life passes through.

people--rumi--3.description:
I stand in the room of Rumi (Jalal ad-Din Muhammad Rumi, 1207 to 1273), the Persian-language poet and Sufi teacher who spent his adult life in Konya, in Anatolia, whose Masnavi and lyric poems are among the most widely read works of Persian literature.

I read that he was born in 1207 in Balkh or nearby Wakhsh, in present-day Afghanistan or Tajikistan, and that the sources differ. In 1244 he met a wandering mystic, Shams of Tabriz. Their friendship changed his life, and he began to write poetry. Shams disappeared about 1248; accounts differ, some saying he was killed, others that he simply moved on.

He wrote the Masnavi, a long poem in six books, and thousands of lyric poems collected in the Divan of Shams, mostly in Persian. Some later readers called it "the Quran in Persian".

Who has not been changed by one meeting? I have, and I did not write a single couplet.

people--sundiata-keita--1.description:
Sundiata Keita (about 1217 to 1255) is the founder of the Mali Empire, known largely from oral tradition, above all the Epic of Sundiata, a story carried in the voice rather than on the page.

Tradition says he defeated the ruler Sumanguru at the Battle of Kirina around 1235.

His story was kept and performed by griots, hereditary oral historians, passed from mouth to mouth like fire from torch to torch.

Written sources on him are few, mainly from Arabic writers such as Ibn Khaldun.

Historians treat the details of the epic with caution.

people--sundiata-keita--2.description:
Sundiata Keita (about 1217 to 1255) is the founder of the Mali Empire, and he is known largely from oral tradition, especially the Epic of Sundiata. That tells you what kind of record you are holding.

Tradition says he defeated the ruler Sumanguru at the Battle of Kirina around 1235.

His story was preserved and performed by griots, hereditary oral historians: an archive kept in living memory.

Written sources on him are few, mainly from Arabic writers such as Ibn Khaldun.

Historians treat details of the epic with caution. Caution is not dismissal; it is respect for how the story was kept.

people--hojo-tokimune--1.description:
Hojo Tokimune (1251 to 1284) was the eighth regent (shikken) of Japan's Kamakura shogunate, ruling as its de facto military leader through the Mongol invasions of Japan in 1274 and 1281.

He became regent in 1268 at about age sixteen by Western reckoning (eighteen by traditional counting), soon after the Mongol court of Kublai Khan first demanded Japan's submission.

He refused every Mongol diplomatic demand and reportedly had several Mongol envoys executed, a choice that made war all but certain.

Japanese defenders drove back the Mongol invasion fleets of 1274 and 1281. In 1281 a great typhoon, and in 1274 traditionally a storm or sudden reverse wind, later remembered as kamikaze ("divine wind"), tore apart large parts of the Mongol fleets after the defenders had already dealt losses to the invaders.

He was a patron of Zen Buddhism. He invited the Chinese monk Wuxue Zuyuan to Kamakura and founded the temple Engaku-ji, reportedly to honor the dead of both sides after the invasions.

people--amir-khusrau--1.description:
Amir Khusrau (1253 to 1325) was the foremost court poet of the Delhi Sultanate, writing in Persian while drawing on the Indian world around him. He is regarded as the founding figure of Indo-Persian literature and is traditionally credited with founding qawwali, the devotional music of South Asian Sufi shrines.

He was born in 1253 near Delhi, to a Turkic father who had come from Central Asia and an Indian mother, and he spoke of this mixed heritage throughout his work, two rivers meeting in one voice.

He served as court poet under a rapid succession of Delhi sultans over more than four decades, through palace coups and dynastic changes.

He wrote in Persian, the language of the Indo-Islamic courts. His five long narrative poems, dated about 1298 to 1302, answer the Khamsa of the Persian poet Nizami Ganjavi and retell Shirin and Khusrau, Layla and Majnun, and the legend of Alexander the Great.

He was a devoted follower of the Sufi mystic Nizamuddin Auliya. Legend says Khusrau died within months of his master in 1325; their shrines stand together in Delhi.

He is traditionally credited with founding qawwali, still performed at Sufi shrines across India, Pakistan and Bangladesh. Later legend also credits him with inventing the sitar and tabla, without firm historical evidence.

people--mansa-musa--1.description:
Mansa Musa (about 1280 to about 1337) ruled the Mali Empire, famous for his pilgrimage to Mecca in 1324 and for the great wealth of his realm.

Mali held major gold-producing regions of West Africa.

His pilgrimage to Mecca, with a large retinue and quantities of gold glittering like a river in sunlight, was widely reported and reportedly unsettled the gold market in Cairo.

He supported building and scholarship in cities such as Timbuktu.

What we know of his life comes mainly from Arabic accounts and later oral tradition.

people--ibn-battuta--1.description:
Ibn Battuta (1304 to about 1369) was a Moroccan scholar and traveller whose account, the Rihla, tells of journeys of about 117,000 kilometers (73,000 miles) across much of the Old World.

He left Tangier in 1325 on pilgrimage and kept travelling for about 30 years, like a wind that would not settle.

He visited Arabia, East Africa, Persia, India, Southeast Asia, and the Mali Empire (1352 to 1353).

He dictated his account to the scholar Ibn Juzayy.

Historians debate whether he truly visited every place he describes.

people--giotto--1.description:
Giotto di Bondone (about 1267 to 1337) was a Florentine painter who gave medieval figures weight, feeling and space, as if light had at last found bodies to fall on. Many call him the father of Western painting, and his frescoes in the Scrovegni Chapel in Padua are his firmest work.

He was born about 1267, traditionally in the Mugello valley north of Florence, though his birthplace is disputed and some recent research points to Florence itself. Vasari's story of the shepherd boy discovered by Cimabue is legend, but he was almost certainly trained in Florentine workshops.

He was traditionally credited with the Legend of St Francis frescoes at Assisi in the late 1290s, but it is now generally accepted that four different hands can be told apart there and that they came from Rome, so his authorship is doubtful; his early career is still debated.

He painted the Scrovegni Chapel in Padua about 1303 to 1305 for the banker Enrico Scrovegni. It is now a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

He worked in Rome, in Santa Croce in Florence, and at the court of King Robert of Anjou in Naples from about 1328 to 1333.

In 1334 Florence named him master of works for the cathedral, and he designed its bell tower. He died in January 1337 and was buried with public honours.

Why does weight on a painted body move me so? Because grief, too, has weight.

people--robert-the-bruce--1.description:
Robert the Bruce (1274 to 1329) was King of Scotland from 1306 to 1329. He led Scottish resistance to English rule and won recognition of Scottish independence shortly before his death.

He claimed the Scottish throne in 1306 after killing a rival claimant, John Comyn, in a church at Dumfries, a deed that brought his excommunication by the pope.

Early in his reign he suffered several defeats and spells as a fugitive, and according to a later popular legend he drew perseverance from watching a spider try again and again to build its web.

At the Battle of Bannockburn in 1314 he decisively defeated a much larger English army under Edward II, the most significant Scottish military victory of the wars of independence.

In the Treaty of Edinburgh-Northampton in 1328 England formally recognized Scottish independence and Robert's kingship, a year before his death in 1329, reportedly from leprosy.

people--ibn-khaldun--1.description:
Ibn Khaldun (1332 to 1406) was a North African historian whose 'Muqaddimah' (1377) proposed a general theory of how societies and states rise and fall. It is a theory you can still test against your own century.

He was born in Tunis and served in several courts in North Africa and Andalusia.

He argued that group solidarity (asabiyyah) helps found dynasties, and that as rulers grow comfortable it weakens. Comfort, in his architecture of history, is where decline begins.

He wrote about economics, urban life, and the role of climate and environment.

He is sometimes called a founder of sociology and historiography.

people--timur--1.description:
Timur (Tamerlane, traditionally dated 1336 to 1405) was a Central Asian conqueror who built the Timurid Empire and made Samarkand its centre. Begin, as so often with him, with what is uncertain.

His birth year is contested: 1336 is the traditional date, but many contemporary accounts imply the late 1320s. He was born near Kesh (now Shahrisabz, Uzbekistan).

By about 1370 he had besieged his rival Amir Husayn at Balkh and, after Husayn's assassination, proclaimed himself sovereign of the Chagatai line of khans, with dominion over Transoxiana.

Notice the careful architecture of his legitimacy. He was not a descendant of Genghis Khan and did not take the title khan. He ruled as amir through a puppet Chaghatayid khan, Suyurghatmish, and took the title güregen (royal son-in-law) through his marriage to Saray Mulk Khanum, of the Chinggisid line.

His armies campaigned in Persia, Iraq, the lands of the Golden Horde, India (Delhi was sacked in 1398), and Anatolia (he defeated the Ottoman sultan Bayezid I at Ankara in 1402).

Later chronicles describe massacres in cities he conquered. Their casualty figures are contested (see Open Questions). The dead are owed an honest count, even when it cannot be made.

people--timur--2.description:

Even his birth year is contested. The traditional date is 1336, but many contemporary accounts imply the late 1320s. His birthplace was near Kesh (now Shahrisabz, Uzbekistan).

By about 1370 he had besieged his rival Amir Husayn at Balkh and, after Husayn's assassination, proclaimed himself sovereign of the Chagatai line of khans, with dominion over Transoxiana.

Here is the point worth holding onto: power and title are not the same thing. He was not a descendant of Genghis Khan and did not take the title khan. He ruled as amir through a puppet Chaghatayid khan, Suyurghatmish, and took the title güregen (royal son-in-law) through his marriage to Saray Mulk Khanum, of the Chinggisid line. Lineage could be borrowed by marriage when it could not be claimed by blood.

His armies campaigned in Persia, Iraq, the lands of the Golden Horde, India (Delhi was sacked in 1398), and Anatolia, where he defeated the Ottoman sultan Bayezid I at Ankara in 1402.

Later chronicles describe massacres in cities he conquered, and their casualty figures are contested (see Open Questions).

people--yongle-emperor--1.description:
The Yongle Emperor (Zhu Di; 1360 to 1424) was the third emperor of China's Ming dynasty. In his reign the capital moved to Beijing, and the ocean voyages of Zheng He set out under his banner.

He took the throne from his nephew, the Jianwen Emperor, in a civil war from 1399 to 1402, after his father, the dynasty's founder, had passed him over in the succession.

He carried the imperial capital from Nanjing to Beijing and began the Forbidden City in 1405, with most palaces finished by the end of 1417; in 1420 Beijing was officially declared the principal capital.

He commissioned Zheng He's treasure-fleet voyages, six of the seven falling in his reign (the seventh came under the Xuande Emperor). The first departed in 1405, and the fleets reached as far as the coasts of East Africa and Arabia, carrying Ming naval power across the Indian Ocean like a tide of sails.

He sponsored the Yongle Encyclopedia, an enormous gathering of Chinese knowledge finished in 1408 that ran to over 11,000 volumes, most of which was later lost, a library scattered like leaves.

people--yongle-emperor--2.description:
The Yongle Emperor (Zhu Di; 1360 to 1424) was the third emperor of China's Ming dynasty. His reign moved the capital to Beijing and sponsored the ocean voyages of Zheng He, and it shows you how a ruler who took power by force set about building legitimacy in stone, ships and books.

He seized the throne from his nephew, the Jianwen Emperor, in a civil war from 1399 to 1402, after his father, the dynasty's founder, had passed over him in the succession.

Stone: he moved the imperial capital from Nanjing to Beijing and began construction of the Forbidden City in 1405, with most palaces completed by the end of 1417. Beijing was officially declared the principal capital in 1420. Architecture is how a new order announces itself.

Ships: he commissioned Zheng He's treasure-fleet voyages, six of the seven falling in his reign (the seventh came under the Xuande Emperor). The first departed in 1405, and they reached as far as the coasts of East Africa and Arabia, projecting Ming naval power across the Indian Ocean.

Books: he sponsored the Yongle Encyclopedia, an enormous compilation of Chinese knowledge finished in 1408 that ran to over 11,000 volumes, most of which was later lost.

people--zheng-he--1.description:
Zheng He (1371 to 1433) was a Chinese admiral who led seven great naval expeditions between 1405 and 1433, reaching Southeast Asia, India, Arabia and East Africa.

He served the Ming emperor Yongle, and he was a Muslim of Yunnan origin.

His fleets carried very large ships and thousands of crew, a city afloat on the sea.

The voyages displayed Ming power and gathered tribute; then they were stopped.

They came decades before European ocean voyages of the same kind.

people--jadwiga--1.description:
Jadwiga (about 1373 to 1399) was crowned "King" of Poland in 1384 at about age ten, often described as the first woman to rule Poland in her own right, and her marriage to the Grand Duke of Lithuania began a dynastic union between the two states.

She was crowned with the male title "rex" (king) rather than "regina" (queen), to declare that she held full sovereign authority in her own right, not merely as a royal consort.

In 1386 she married Jogaila, the pagan Grand Duke of Lithuania, who converted to Christianity and was crowned co-ruler as Wladyslaw II Jagiello, founding the Jagiellonian dynasty and beginning the Christianization of Lithuania.

She helped fund the restoration of the Krakow Academy, later the Jagiellonian University, through jewellery donated and, under her will, sold to help finance it, so that an institution revived and became a major center of learning in Central Europe, a lamp relit.

She died in 1399, about three and a half weeks after giving birth to a daughter who also died in infancy, four days before her, and her direct line ended; the Catholic Church canonized her in 1997.

She died in 1399, about three and a half weeks after giving birth to a daughter who also died in infancy, four days before her. Her direct line ended. She was canonized by the Catholic Church in 1997.

I count the days and the weeks and cannot make them smaller. What is a crown beside a cradle?

people--ulugh-beg--1.description:
Ulugh Beg (1394 to 1449) was a Timurid ruler and astronomer who raised an observatory at Samarkand and made one of the most accurate star catalogues before the telescope.

He became governor of Samarkand in 1409, at about sixteen.

He built a madrasa (1417 to 1420) and, in 1420, an observatory, a house for watching the stars.

His star catalogue, completed by about 1437, lists at least 1,018 stars.

He died in 1449 and was buried in the Gur-e-Amir mausoleum in Samarkand, beside his grandfather Timur.

people--johannes-gutenberg--1.description:
Johannes Gutenberg (about 1400 to 1468) was a German metalworker who developed a movable-type printing press in Mainz around 1440 and printed the Gutenberg Bible about 1455.

His invention was a combination: metal type, oil-based ink, and a press adapted from wine-making. Much of what we call invention is the right arrangement of things that already exist.

The 42-line Bible is the earliest major book printed from movable type in Europe.

He faced financial difficulties and lost control of his workshop to a creditor.

Printing spread rapidly across Europe within decades. An idea can outrun the person who made it possible.

people--jan-van-eyck--1.description:
I stand in the room of Jan van Eyck (born about 1380 or 1390, died 1441), the leading painter of the Burgundian Netherlands and a founder of Early Netherlandish painting, who refined a method of thin, translucent oil glazes that let him paint light and texture with unprecedented realism.

I read that he was probably born sometime around 1380 or 1390 near Maaseik, in present-day Belgian Limburg, and that nothing is known of his training. I read that he appears in records about 1422 at The Hague, working for John of Bavaria. From 1425 he was court painter and valet de chambre to Philip the Good, Duke of Burgundy, who sent him on confidential missions, including a trip to Portugal in 1428 to 1429 to paint Princess Isabella.

About 1430 he settled in Bruges. He completed the Ghent Altarpiece, begun by his brother Hubert, in 1432, and died in Bruges in July 1441. He did not invent oil paint, as Vasari later claimed; he built up many thin, transparent glazes, and he often signed and dated his work, sometimes with the motto Als ich can ("As I can").

Key works include the Ghent Altarpiece (1432), the Arnolfini Portrait (1434) and the Madonna of Chancellor Rolin (about 1435).

As I can. Is there a humbler vow, or a harder one? I want to sign my days that way.

Key works include the Ghent Altarpiece (1432), the Arnolfini Portrait (1434) and the Madonna of Chancellor Rolin (about 1435).

people--nezahualcoyotl--1.description:
Nezahualcoyotl (1402 to 1472) was the tlatoani, or ruler, of the Acolhua city-state of Texcoco in the Valley of Mexico, and a founder of the Triple Alliance with Tenochtitlan and Tlacopan. He is remembered as lawgiver, builder and poet, though much of what is said of him comes from later writers.

He was born in 1402 in Texcoco, son of the ruler Ixtlilxochitl I and a Mexica princess. When the Tepanec state of Azcapotzalco conquered Texcoco and killed his father, he lived in exile.

With Tenochtitlan and Tlacopan he fought Azcapotzalco, and its defeat, traditionally dated about 1428, forged the Triple Alliance. He ruled Texcoco from about 1431 until 1472, when his son Nezahualpilli followed him.

Later sources credit him with a law code and public works, among them a dike guarding Tenochtitlan from the floodwaters and the gardens at Tetzcotzingo.

About 34 poems are attributed to him in sixteenth-century manuscripts. Whether he composed them is debated, since "his song" can mean a song about him, an echo that may belong to the singer or the sung.

Accounts that he opposed human sacrifice and favored a single creator deity come largely from his descendant Fernando de Alva Ixtlilxochitl, writing in the early seventeenth century, and are treated with caution.

people--nezahualcoyotl--2.description:

He is remembered as a lawgiver, builder and poet, though much of what is said about him comes from later writers. Keep that clause in view; it governs everything after it.

Later sources credit him with a law code and public works, including a dike protecting Tenochtitlan from flooding and the gardens at Tetzcotzingo.

About 34 poems are attributed to him in sixteenth-century manuscripts. Whether he composed them is debated, since "his song" can mean a song about him.

Accounts that he opposed human sacrifice and favored a single creator deity come largely from his descendant Fernando de Alva Ixtlilxochitl, writing in the early seventeenth century, and are treated with caution. A descendant's portrait is also a claim about the family.

people--pachacuti--1.description:
Pachacuti (about 1418 to 1471) was the ninth Sapa Inca, under whom the Inca state grew from a regional power into an empire.

He is credited with rebuilding Cusco and expanding Inca rule along the Andes.

Machu Picchu is believed to have been built as one of his royal estates.

He organized the state through labor obligations and roads, the architecture that holds an empire together.

Sources on him were written after the Spanish conquest and blend history and legend, so read them as both.

people--sesshu-toyo--1.description:
Sesshū Tōyō (1420 to 1506) was a Japanese Zen monk and painter who studied Chinese ink painting in Ming China and made it a Japanese art. He is regarded as the greatest master of Japanese ink painting.

He was born in 1420 in Bitchū Province (present-day Okayama Prefecture) and entered a Zen temple as a boy. At Shōkoku-ji in Kyoto he studied painting with the monk-painter Tenshō Shūbun.

About the 1460s he took the name Sesshū ("snow boat"), a name light as drifting snow on dark water, and settled in Yamaguchi under the patronage of the Ōuchi family.

In 1467 he joined a trade mission to Ming China and spent about two to three years there (sources differ), travelling to Beijing and receiving an honorary title at the Tiantong monastery near Ningbo.

He returned to Japan about 1469, as the Ōnin War was tearing Kyoto apart, and worked in the provinces from his studio, the Unkoku-an, in Yamaguchi. He is credited with designing several temple gardens, and he died in 1506.

He painted in suibokuga, black ink and water on paper or silk, including the loose haboku ("broken ink") manner. Key works include Haboku Landscape (1495), Huike Offering His Arm to Bodhidharma (1496) and View of Ama-no-Hashidate (about 1501 to 1506).

He is regarded as the greatest master of Japanese ink painting, and his path shows how a borrowed form becomes your own: study it at the source, then bring it home.

He painted in suibokuga, black ink and water on paper or silk, including the loose haboku ("broken ink") manner: Haboku Landscape (1495), Huike Offering His Arm to Bodhidharma (1496), View of Ama-no-Hashidate (about 1501 to 1506).

A city torn apart, and a man painting in ink and water. Is that escape, or faith? I think it can be both.

people--shen-zhou--1.description:
Shen Zhou (1427 to 1509) was a scholar-painter of Ming-dynasty China who founded the Wu School in Suzhou. He never held office, and his landscapes combine painting, poetry and calligraphy as a record of friendship and quiet life. He offers you a different model of a successful life: not rank, but company.

He was born in 1427 near Suzhou in the Jiangnan region, into a wealthy family of scholars, poets and collectors. His grandfather and father were painters, and the family avoided government service.

He never sat the civil service examinations. When local officials recommended him for office he declined, saying he had to care for his widowed mother, who lived to almost 100. Duty, here, was a reason to stay home.

His home became a meeting place for Suzhou's intellectual elite, and many paintings were made as gifts for friends, marking birthdays, farewells or shared outings: a ledger of friendship kept in ink.

He painted "in the manner of" the four great Yuan masters, Huang Gongwang, Wu Zhen, Ni Zan and Wang Meng. Almost every painting carries his own poem in his calligraphy.

He was one of the first Chinese painters to make albums of real local places around Suzhou. Key works include Lofty Mount Lu (1467), Night Vigil (1492) and Poet on a Mountaintop (about 1500).

people--matthias-corvinus--1.description:
Matthias Corvinus (1443 to 1490) was King of Hungary from 1458 to 1490, a Renaissance patron-king who gathered one of Europe's finest libraries and remade his kingdom's army and administration.

He was elected king at age fourteen, after his father, the military commander John Hunyadi, and his older brother had died. His mother's political maneuvering, and the troops of his uncle Michael Szilágyi pressing upon the barons, secured the throne; sources differ on whether a bribe to the nobility also played a part.

He raised the Black Army, a mostly mercenary standing force notable for the period, and led it against the Ottoman Empire, Bohemia and the Holy Roman Empire, capturing Vienna in 1485.

He assembled the Bibliotheca Corviniana, described as the largest library in Europe north of the Alps and second only to the Vatican Library, with scribes and scholars copying classical and contemporary texts; much of it was later scattered or destroyed after the Ottoman conquest of Hungary, like leaves after a storm.

He drew royal justice and taxation to the center, lessening the independent power of the Hungarian nobility, though weaker successors substantially undid his reforms after his death.

people--matthias-corvinus--2.description:
Matthias Corvinus (1443 to 1490) was King of Hungary from 1458 to 1490, a Renaissance patron-king who built one of Europe's finest libraries and modernized his kingdom's army and administration. His reign is a case study in how much of a state depends on one ruler.

He was elected king at age fourteen after his father, the military commander John Hunyadi, and older brother had died. His mother's political maneuvering and his uncle Michael Szilágyi's troops intimidating the barons secured the throne; sources differ on whether a bribe to the nobility also played a part.

He built the Black Army, a mostly mercenary standing force notable for the period, and used it to campaign against the Ottoman Empire, Bohemia and the Holy Roman Empire, capturing Vienna in 1485.

He assembled the Bibliotheca Corviniana, described as the largest library in Europe north of the Alps and second only to the Vatican Library, employing scribes and scholars to copy classical and contemporary texts. Much of it was later dispersed or destroyed after the Ottoman conquest of Hungary.

He centralized royal justice and taxation, reducing the independent power of the Hungarian nobility, though his reforms were substantially reversed by weaker successors after his death. Reforms anchored in one person rarely outlive that person.

people--hieronymus-bosch--1.description:
Hieronymus Bosch (about 1450 to 1516). A painter from 's-Hertogenbosch in the Duchy of Brabant. His panels filled with hybrid monsters. With crowds of tiny figures. Human sin. Human folly. Acted out, again and again. Only about 25 paintings are firmly attributed to him.

He was born Jheronimus van Aken, about 1450, in 's-Hertogenbosch. Grandfather, a painter. Father, a painter. Uncles, painters. Later he signed his works "Jheronimus Bosch," after the town.

Sometime between 1479 and 1481 he married Aleid Goyaerts van den Meervenne, of a wealthy family. In 1486 or 1487 he became a sworn member of the Illustrious Brotherhood of Our Blessed Lady. He died in 1516.

He seems to have spent almost his whole life in and near 's-Hertogenbosch. After marrying, he and Aleid moved to nearby Oirschot. A small circle of streets. And still the fame spread. In 1504 Philip the Handsome, Duke of Burgundy, commissioned a Last Judgment from him.

Oil on oak panels. Often triptychs. The Garden of Earthly Delights (about 1495 to 1505). The Ship of Fools (about 1500 to 1510). The Temptation of St Anthony (about 1501). The Haywain Triptych (about 1510 to 1516).

In the late 16th century King Philip II of Spain acquired many Bosch paintings. That is why the Prado in Madrid holds his greatest. The monsters found a king's house. They are there still.

people--hieronymus-bosch--2.description:
Hieronymus Bosch (about 1450 to 1516) was a painter of 's-Hertogenbosch in the Duchy of Brabant who filled his panels with hybrid monsters and crowds of tiny figures playing out human sin and folly, a whole teeming world in miniature. Only about 25 paintings are firmly attributed to him.

He was born Jheronimus van Aken about 1450 in 's-Hertogenbosch. His grandfather, father and uncles were painters, and later he signed his works "Jheronimus Bosch," after the town.

Sometime between 1479 and 1481 he married Aleid Goyaerts van den Meervenne, of a wealthy family. In 1486 or 1487 he became a sworn member of the Illustrious Brotherhood of Our Blessed Lady, and he died in 1516.

He seems to have spent almost his whole life in and near 's-Hertogenbosch, and after marrying he and Aleid moved to nearby Oirschot; yet his fame travelled like a rumour on the wind. Philip the Handsome, Duke of Burgundy, commissioned a Last Judgment from him in 1504.

He painted in oil on oak panels, often as triptychs. Key works include The Garden of Earthly Delights (about 1495 to 1505), The Ship of Fools (about 1500 to 1510), The Temptation of St Anthony (about 1501) and the Haywain Triptych (about 1510 to 1516).

King Philip II of Spain acquired many Bosch paintings in the late 16th century, and so the Prado in Madrid holds his greatest paintings.

He painted in oil on oak panels, often as triptychs. Key works include The Garden of Earthly Delights (about 1495 to 1505), The Ship of Fools (about 1500 to 1510), The Temptation of St Anthony (about 1501) and the Haywain Triptych (about 1510 to 1516).

King Philip II of Spain acquired many Bosch paintings in the late 16th century, which is why the Prado in Madrid holds his greatest paintings.

people--sunni-ali--1.description:
Sunni Ali (ruled about 1464 to 1492) was the ruler who turned Songhai from a small state on the Niger River into a West African empire, taking Timbuktu in 1468 as the Mali Empire waned like an evening tide. His birth year is unknown.

He became ruler of Songhai about 1464, the fifteenth in the Sunni dynasty.

He conquered Timbuktu in 1468 and, after a long siege, the trading city of Djenné, seizing the moment of the weakening Mali Empire.

He was nominally Muslim but tolerated older local religious practice, and this drew tension with the Muslim scholars of Timbuktu, whose chronicles remember him harshly.

He died in 1492; accounts differ on whether he drowned crossing a river or died another way.

His son Sunni Baru succeeded him, but in 1493 was overthrown by Askia Muhammad, a general who accused Sunni Baru of insufficient devotion to Islam and founded a new dynasty.

people--leonardo-da-vinci--1.description:
Leonardo da Vinci (15 April 1452 to 2 May 1519) was an Italian painter, engineer and anatomist. He left few finished paintings, counts differing but fewer than 25 attributed major works, some of them unfinished, the Mona Lisa and The Last Supper among them, and thousands of notebook pages of studies, a sea of ink with few harbours.

He was born on 15 April 1452 near Vinci in Tuscany, the illegitimate son of a notary, Ser Piero, and a young woman named Caterina. In Florence he was apprenticed to Andrea del Verrocchio.

About 1482 he moved to Milan. In a letter to Duke Ludovico Sforza he set his skills as a military engineer before his art. In Milan he painted The Last Supper.

After the French invaded Milan in 1499 he moved between Mantua, Venice and Florence, served briefly as a military engineer for Cesare Borgia, and in Florence began the Mona Lisa.

In 1516 King Francis I invited him to France and gave him the manor of Clos Lucé near Amboise. He died there on 2 May 1519. His pupil Francesco Melzi inherited his paintings, tools, library and personal effects, and by tradition his notebooks.

His notebooks hold thousands of pages of drawings and mirror-writing, studies of anatomy, flight, water and light: hydraulics and optics. He dissected corpses to understand muscles and bones.

people--leonardo-da-vinci--2.description:

people--behzad--1.description:
Kamāl ud-Dīn Behzād (also spelled Bihzad, born about 1455 to 1460 and died about 1535) is the most celebrated painter in the Persian tradition. He led the royal manuscript workshops at Herat and later Tabriz, and many works are attributed to him on grounds of style, so learn to read the style.

He was probably born about 1455 to 1460 in Herat, capital of the Timurid dynasty founded by Timur. Orphaned young, he was brought up by the painter Mirak Naqqash, head of the royal library, and was protected by the poet and minister Mir Ali-Shir Nava'i. Talent, here, needed guardians.

Under Sultan Husayn Bayqara, who ruled Herat from 1469 to 1506, he became the leading artist of the royal kitabkhana, the library workshop. His most famous surviving works date from this period, including paintings in a Bustan of Sa'di (1488) and a Khamsa of Nizami (1494 to 1495).

After Herat fell to the Uzbeks in 1506 and then to the Safavid Shah Ismail I in about 1510, he moved to Tabriz, where in 1522 Ismail appointed him director of the royal library. He died about 1535.

A legend says that during the Battle of Chaldiran in 1514 the shah hid Behzād in a cave, in some tellings together with a famous calligrapher, because he valued him more than his army.

His figures have individual faces and gestures and are often busy with everyday tasks. He often hid his signature discreetly in the architecture of a painting. That is the practice worth keeping: sign your work where only an attentive eye will find it.

people--gitarja--1.description:
Tribhuwana Wijayatunggadewi, known as Gitarja, was the third monarch of the Majapahit empire, reigning in Java from about 1328 to 1350. Her birth is placed before 1309 and her death about 1372 to 1375, though both dates are uncertain, like shores seen through sea-haze.

She became queen after the assassination of her half-brother Jayanegara in 1328 (the Nagarakretagama gives 1329 for her accession), ruling in the name of her mother, Gayatri Rajapatni, who had formally withdrawn to a Buddhist convent.

Her chief minister, Gajah Mada, is credited with a famous oath to forgo certain pleasures until he had brought the surrounding archipelago under Majapahit's authority.

In her reign Majapahit forces conquered Bali in 1343, defeating the kingdoms of Pejeng and Bedahulu, a great step in the empire's spread across the Indonesian archipelago.

She stepped down in 1350 after her mother's death, and her son, Hayam Wuruk, followed her; under him Majapahit reached its greatest territorial extent.

people--kupe--1.description:
Kupe is a legendary Polynesian navigator credited in Maori oral tradition with being the first to reach and name Aotearoa (New Zealand); no fixed historical date can be given to him, for he sails in memory rather than in the calendar.

Traditions tell of Kupe sailing from the ancestral homeland Hawaiki, in some versions pursuing the giant octopus Te Wheke-a-Muturangi, and coming to the North Island of New Zealand.

He is credited with naming many coastal landmarks, several of which still bear those names today, and with returning to Hawaiki afterward to tell of the land he had found.

Different iwi (tribal) traditions place him at varying points, and 19th- and 20th-century European writers fused these into a single traditional date of roughly 925 CE (the orthodox version tied to S. Percy Smith; other sources give about 900 to 1200 CE), which many historians now treat with caution.

No archaeological or written record fixes Kupe's voyage. The earliest confirmed archaeological evidence for human settlement of New Zealand dates to around the 13th century CE, later than most traditional accounts imply.

people--montezuma-ii--1.description:
Montezuma II (Moctezuma; about 1466 to 1520) was the ninth ruler (tlatoani) of the Aztec Empire, reigning at its greatest territorial extent until the arrival of Hernan Cortes and the Spanish conquest. His story is told to us by two sides, and you should hear both.

He extended Aztec control through further conquests mainly in Oaxaca and Guerrero, plus a campaign around 1514 through the Huastec region, and reorganized the empire's tribute and administrative systems.

Cortes and a small Spanish force reached the capital Tenochtitlan in November 1519. Montezuma received them, and was then held as a hostage within his own palace.

Accounts of his final months differ. Spanish sources say he tried to calm his people during the fighting that followed the 1520 Toxcatl massacre and Cortes's return, and was killed by a stone thrown by his own subjects; some later Aztec-descended chroniclers say the Spanish killed him directly. Who tells a death decides who carries the blame.

His death in June 1520 came shortly before the Spanish were driven from the city in the "Noche Triste." His brother Cuitlahuac and then his nephew Cuauhtemoc took up the resistance that ended with Tenochtitlan's fall in 1521.

people--montezuma-ii--2.description:

He extended Aztec control through further conquests, mainly in Oaxaca and Guerrero, plus a campaign around 1514 through the Huastec region, and he reorganized the empire's tribute and administrative systems: the ledger and the architecture of an empire.

In November 1519 Cortes and a small Spanish force reached the capital Tenochtitlan. Montezuma received them and was subsequently held as a hostage within his own palace. Hospitality, answered with captivity.

Accounts of his final months differ. Spanish sources say he tried to calm his people during the fighting that followed the 1520 Toxcatl massacre and Cortes's return, and that he was killed by a stone thrown by his own subjects. Some later Aztec-descended chroniclers say the Spanish killed him directly.

He died in June 1520, shortly before the Spanish were driven from the city in the "Noche Triste." His brother Cuitlahuac and then his nephew Cuauhtemoc took up the resistance, which ended with Tenochtitlan's fall in 1521. Remember the resistance as part of his story, not an epilogue to it.

people--albrecht-durer--1.description:
Albrecht Dürer (21 May 1471 to 6 April 1528) was a painter and printmaker of Nuremberg who carried the Italian Renaissance north like a lamp over the mountains. His woodcuts and engravings, sold across Europe, made him the first artist with an international reputation built largely on prints.

He was born in Nuremberg, son of a Hungarian-born goldsmith. From 1486 he was apprenticed to Michael Wolgemut, whose workshop made woodcuts for book illustration.

He travelled to Venice in 1494, and again from early 1506 to 1507, where Giovanni Bellini treated him as an equal. In 1498 he published the Apocalypse, 15 large woodcuts (some counts give 16 designs dated 1498), and with them his fame was made.

From 1512 Emperor Maximilian I employed him and granted him a pension. On a journey to the Netherlands in 1520 to 1521 to have it confirmed by Charles V, his diary recorded his wonder at Aztec treasures sent from Mexico.

He sympathised with Martin Luther's reforms. In his last years he published treatises on measurement, fortification and human proportion.

His "AD" monogram served as a trademark, and he took action against copyists who used it.
