people--anacaona--1.description:
I stand before Anacaona (about 1474 to about 1504), a Taíno cacica (chief) of Xaragua, a chiefdom in western Hispaniola, and a noted composer of ceremonial songs. She was executed by the Spanish governor Nicolás de Ovando after the killing of Taíno leaders in 1503.

I read that she was born about 1474, and that the year is approximate. I read that she belonged to the ruling family of Xaragua, in present-day Haiti; that she was the sister of the cacique Bohechío and the wife of Caonabo, a cacique whom the Spanish captured in 1494 or 1496, depending on the source; that after Bohechío's death about 1500 she ruled Xaragua.

Spanish sources describe her as a composer of areítos, songs that told the history of the Taíno and were performed at ceremonies.

In 1503 Governor Nicolás de Ovando came to Xaragua with soldiers. Dozens of Taíno leaders were killed at a gathering, and she was taken to Santo Domingo and executed about 1504.

A people's history, kept in song. Who sings it now? I want to remember her first as the one who made the songs.

people--anacaona--2.description:
Anacaona (about 1474 to about 1504) was a Taíno cacica (chief) of Xaragua, a chiefdom in western Hispaniola, and a noted composer of ceremonial songs. She was executed by the Spanish governor Nicolás de Ovando after the killing of Taíno leaders in 1503. Begin with her as a ruler and an artist, because that is who she was before the end.

She was born about 1474; her birth year is approximate. She belonged to the ruling family of Xaragua, in present-day Haiti.

She was the sister of the cacique Bohechío and the wife of Caonabo, a cacique whom the Spanish captured in 1494 or 1496, depending on the source. After Bohechío's death about 1500 she ruled Xaragua.

Spanish sources describe her as a composer of areítos, songs that told the history of the Taíno and were performed at ceremonies. Those songs were an archive, a people's own ledger of who they were.

In 1503 Governor Nicolás de Ovando came to Xaragua with soldiers. Dozens of Taíno leaders were killed at a gathering, and she was taken to Santo Domingo and executed about 1504.

people--anacaona--3.description:
Anacaona (about 1474 to about 1504) was a Taíno cacica, or chief, of Xaragua, a chiefdom in western Hispaniola, and she was a noted composer of ceremonial songs. After the killing of Taíno leaders in 1503, the Spanish governor Nicolás de Ovando had her executed.

Her birth, about 1474, is approximate. She belonged to the ruling family of Xaragua, in present-day Haiti.

She was the sister of the cacique Bohechío and the wife of Caonabo, a cacique the Spanish captured in 1494 or 1496, depending on the source. After Bohechío's death about 1500, she ruled Xaragua.

Notice whose words describe her art: Spanish sources call her a composer of areítos, songs that told the history of the Taíno and were performed at ceremonies. Even her own craft reaches us through the record of those who came to rule.

In 1503 Governor Nicolás de Ovando came to Xaragua with soldiers. Dozens of Taíno leaders were killed at a gathering. She was taken to Santo Domingo and executed about 1504. State it plainly, and let it stand.

people--michelangelo--1.description:
Michelangelo Buonarroti (6 March 1475 to 18 February 1564) was an Italian sculptor, painter, architect and poet. His Pietà, David and Sistine Chapel paintings defined the High Renaissance, and he was the first Western artist to have a biography published in his lifetime.

He was born at Caprese in Tuscany and grew up in Florence. At 13 he was apprenticed to Domenico Ghirlandaio, then went to the sculpture garden of Lorenzo de' Medici, where he studied ancient statues, stone that remembered older hands.

The Pietà (1498 to 1499) made his name in Rome. In Florence he carved the David (1501 to 1504).

In 1505 Pope Julius II called him to Rome to design a colossal tomb, then turned him aside to paint the Sistine Chapel ceiling (1508 to 1512). The unfinished tomb haunted him for decades, a shadow that followed him from year to year.

In 1534 he settled for good in Rome and painted The Last Judgment (1536 to 1541). In 1546 he became chief architect of St Peter's Basilica, and his dome became a model for later domes.

He wrote hundreds of poems, many addressed to Tommaso de' Cavalieri and Vittoria Colonna. He died in Rome, and his body was secretly carried to Florence for burial in Santa Croce.

people--mirabai--1.description:
Mirabai (traditionally about 1498 to about 1546) was a Rajput princess of Rajasthan and one of the best-known poet-saints of the Bhakti movement, devoted to Krishna. Almost nothing of her life is documented, and the surviving poems were written down long after her time, like a song heard across a valley after the singer has gone.

By tradition she was born about 1498 at Kudki in Rajasthan, into the Rathore Rajput family of Merta, and died about 1546 or 1547. Both dates come from later tradition.

Tradition says she married Bhoj Raj, heir of Mewar, in 1516, and that he died about 1521 of battle wounds.

Her poems (padas) are in Rajasthani and related Hindi, and they speak to Krishna in the language of love and separation.

Tradition credits her with a very great number of poems. Scholars think only a few hundred may be authentic, and only two are known from manuscripts older than the early eighteenth century.

Stories that her in-laws tried to poison her, and that she vanished into an image of Krishna, are hagiographic legends. The earliest records, from the seventeenth century, do not mention her marriage or in-laws.

people--mimar-sinan--1.description:
Mimar Sinan (about 1489 to 1588) was chief royal architect to three Ottoman sultans for nearly fifty years. He is credited with several hundred structures, and his Selimiye Mosque at Edirne is regarded as the peak of classical Ottoman architecture. His career is a lesson in how mastery is staged.

He was born about 1489 or 1490 in Ağırnas, near Kayseri in central Anatolia, into a Christian family; sources disagree on whether it was Greek or Armenian.

He was conscripted through the devşirme levy into the Ottoman elite corps, converted to Islam and trained as a Janissary. He rose through military engineering, building bridges and fortifications on campaign for Suleiman the Magnificent. The practical came first; the sublime grew out of it.

Chelebi Lütfi Pasha appointed him chief royal architect in 1539, when he became Grand Vizier, and Sinan held the post into his late nineties. He died in Istanbul in 1588.

His main buildings are the Şehzade Mosque (1543 to 1548), the Süleymaniye Mosque (1550 to 1557) and the Selimiye Mosque (1568 or 1569 to 1574 or 1575). He described them as his apprenticeship, journeyman work and masterpiece. Name your own stages honestly, and you can see how far you have come.

He worked to build domes wider and more daring than Hagia Sophia, a Byzantine cathedral converted to a mosque after 1453, using semi-domes, buttressing piers and pendentives. He also built aqueducts and bridges, some still in use.

people--suleiman-the-magnificent--1.description:
Suleiman the Magnificent (1494 to 1566) was Ottoman sultan from 1520 to 1566, and under him the empire stood at its greatest territorial extent, its height of military power, and its summit of legal and cultural achievement.

His armies took Belgrade in 1521 and Rhodes in 1522, then pressed deep into Central Europe, defeating and killing the King of Hungary at the Battle of Mohacs in 1526, though a first siege of Vienna in 1529 failed to take the city.

He is known by the epithet Kanuni (the Lawgiver), a name absent from sixteenth and seventeenth-century Ottoman sources that may date only from the early 18th century. He issued a major legal code that brought Ottoman civil law into harmony with Islamic religious law across the empire's many lands.

His navies under admirals such as Barbarossa Hayreddin Pasha contested the Mediterranean with Spain and its allies, and Ottoman forces also pushed into Persia and Mesopotamia, taking Baghdad in 1534.

His reign saw Ottoman architecture flower under the chief architect Mimar Sinan, with court poetry, painting and decorative arts, all centered on Istanbul like light gathered in a lens.

people--suleiman-the-magnificent--2.description:

people--malinche--1.description:
Malinche (Malintzin, called Doña Marina by the Spanish; about 1500 to about 1529) was a Nahua woman who served as interpreter and intermediary for Hernán Cortés during the Spanish conquest of the Aztec Empire in 1519 to 1521. Her dates are uncertain, and so is much of her story; hold that uncertainty with care.

Her birth is placed around 1500 and her death between about 1527 and 1529; both are estimates.

The chronicler Bernal Díaz del Castillo, writing decades later, says she was born to a noble Nahua family near Coatzacoalcos and passed into slavery as a child. This account is traditional and cannot be checked.

In 1519 she was among women presented to Cortés by people of Tabasco. She spoke Nahuatl and a Maya language, and she learned Spanish. Language was the threshold she stood on, between worlds that did not understand each other.

She interpreted for Cortés, at first with Gerónimo de Aguilar, including at the meetings with Moctezuma II at Tenochtitlan in 1519.

She bore Cortés a son, Martín, about 1522, and later married the Spanish soldier Juan Jaramillo.

people--joao-iii--1.description:
João III (1502 to 1557) was King of Portugal from 1521 to 1557. He presided over the height of Portugal's Asian trading empire, and he also introduced the Inquisition and the formal colonization of Brazil. Keep all three in the same sentence, as the record does.

In his reign Portuguese trading posts and fortresses across the Indian Ocean, from East Africa to Goa, Malacca and Macau, reached their fullest extent, built on the routes opened by earlier explorers such as Vasco da Gama.

He introduced the Portuguese Inquisition in 1536, targeting Jewish converts (New Christians) suspected of secretly practicing Judaism, at the urging of factions at his court and with eventual papal approval. The people it targeted had already been made to convert; suspicion followed them anyway.

From 1534 he divided Brazil into hereditary captaincies to encourage settlement and defense of the colony, a system that had mixed results and was later partly replaced by direct royal government.

He was a patron of Portuguese scholarship, moving the university at Lisbon to Coimbra in 1537. But the enormous cost of maintaining the Asian trading empire strained the crown's finances by the end of his reign. An empire's ledger has two columns.

people--andrea-palladio--1.description:
Andrea Palladio (1508 to 1580) was a Renaissance architect of the Republic of Venice whose villas and churches, and an illustrated treatise, turned Roman classicism into a style that could travel. His influence is arguably the widest of any single architect in Western history.

He was born Andrea di Pietro della Gondola in Padua in 1508. He was apprenticed to a stonemasons' guild and moved to Vicenza to work as a carver.

The nobleman Gian Giorgio Trissino gave him a classical education, renamed him "Palladio" after Pallas Athena, and took him to Rome to measure and draw ancient ruins, columns standing like old trees in a field.

His remodelling of the medieval basilica of Vicenza, dated to 1546 in some sources, made his name. For three decades he designed country villas for the Venetian nobility and churches in Venice.

In 1570 he published I Quattro Libri dell'Architettura, part treatise and part illustrated catalogue of his buildings. He died in 1580, at either Vicenza or Maser.

Key works include the Villa Rotonda (1566 to about 1592), the Teatro Olimpico (1580 to about 1585) and San Giorgio Maggiore in Venice (1566 to 1610).

people--catherine-de-medici--1.description:
Catherine de' Medici (1519 to 1589) was queen of France and, as mother to three kings, one of the most powerful figures in France during the Wars of Religion between Catholics and Huguenots.

Born into the powerful Medici banking family of Florence, she married the future Henry II of France in 1533 and became queen in 1547.

After Henry's death in 1559 she was the chief political influence for her sons Francis II, Charles IX and Henry III. She was not formally regent under Francis II or Henry III; she held the regency only for Charles IX (as gouvernante de France from December 1560 until August 1563), in a period of escalating conflict between Catholics and Protestant Huguenots. Influence and office, you will notice, are not the same thing.

She is widely held responsible, though the exact extent of her role is debated, for approving the assassination of Huguenot leaders. It began with the shooting of Admiral Coligny on 22 August 1572; he survived, then was killed two days later as the massacre began. It triggered the St. Bartholomew's Day Massacre in August 1572, in which about 2,000 to 3,000 Huguenots were killed in Paris, and more in other cities. Each of them was a person, not a number.

She pursued marriage alliances and diplomacy across Europe to secure the Valois dynasty's position, but her efforts did not prevent the extinction of the Valois line with the death of her last son in 1589.

people--pieter-bruegel-the-elder--1.description:
Pieter Bruegel the Elder (about 1525 to 1569) was the most important Netherlandish painter of the 16th century. Peasants, proverbs and the turning seasons were his subjects, in crowded panels and sweeping landscapes where the year wheels like a great slow sky. Only about 40 of his paintings survive.

He was probably born between 1525 and 1530, perhaps near Breda in the Duchy of Brabant. In 1551 he became a master in the painters' guild of Antwerp.

In 1552 he travelled to Italy, and his drawings of the Alps on the road home fed the mountain views of his later paintings.

In Antwerp he designed prints for the publisher Hieronymus Cock, some in the manner of Hieronymus Bosch. In 1563 he married Mayken Coecke and moved to Brussels, where he painted most of his masterpieces.

He died in Brussels in September 1569. His sons Pieter Brueghel the Younger and Jan Brueghel the Elder became successful painters and founded a dynasty.

Key works include Netherlandish Proverbs (1559), Children's Games (1560), The Tower of Babel (1563), The Hunters in the Snow (1565) and The Peasant Wedding (about 1567 to 1568).

people--philip-ii--1.description:
Philip II (1527 to 1598) was King of Spain from 1556 to 1598, ruling an empire that stretched across the Iberian Peninsula, the Netherlands, parts of Italy, and vast lands in the Americas and the Philippines, which bear his name.

In 1556 he inherited Spain, its Italian territories and the Spanish Americas from his father, Charles V, and through his marriage to Mary I of England he briefly shared the English throne from 1554 to 1558.

He waged a long, costly war to put down a revolt in the Spanish Netherlands, beginning in 1566, that burned on in various phases for decades and was never fully resolved in his reign.

In 1588 he sent the Spanish Armada against England, to support a planned invasion and end English support for Dutch rebels and privateering against Spanish shipping; storms and English naval tactics destroyed much of the fleet, the sea and the wind turning against him.

He presided over Spain's peak territorial extent while driving the crown into bankruptcy again and again, in 1557, 1560, 1575 and 1596, from the cost of near-constant warfare funded partly by American silver.

people--sofonisba-anguissola--1.description:
I stand in the room of Sofonisba Anguissola (about 1532 to 1629), Italian portrait painter from Cremona, one of the first women in Europe to build a professional career as a painter, who spent years at the Spanish court, traditionally put at about 14, and won international fame.

I read that she was born about 1532 in Cremona, the eldest of seven children of Amilcare Anguissola, a minor nobleman, who gave all his daughters a humanist education, and that several became painters. I read that she studied with Bernardino Campi and Bernardino Gatti. I read that as a noblewoman she could not study anatomy from the nude or take large public commissions, so she made portraiture her field.

Her father sent her drawings to Michelangelo, who reportedly challenged her to draw a crying boy; she answered with Boy Bitten by a Crayfish, a drawing that circulated widely. In 1559 she was invited to Madrid to serve Queen Elisabeth of Valois, wife of Philip II, as lady-in-waiting and painting teacher. She painted the royal court for a period traditionally given as about 14 years, though sources differ, and the Spanish court arranged her marriage to a Sicilian nobleman, Fabrizio de Moncada.

After his death she married a Genoese sea captain and lived in Genoa and Palermo. In 1629 Anthony van Dyck visited her in Palermo (an earlier reading gave 1624) and recorded her advice. She died there in 1629 (older sources say 1625), in her mid-to-late nineties.

Doors closed, and she painted the faces in front of her. What wall have I called the end of the road? She made it the subject.

people--yermak-timofeyevich--1.description:
Yermak Timofeyevich (about 1532 to 1585) was a Cossack leader whose expedition across the Urals in 1581 and 1582 overthrew the Khanate of Sibir and began the Russian conquest of Siberia. His early life lies in fog, poorly known.

His birth year is uncertain; about 1532 is often given. Most accounts say he was a Volga Cossack, and some say he was wanted for piracy.

In 1581 he set out from the Ural lands of the Stroganov merchant family with several hundred men armed with firearms, though accounts of the year and the numbers vary.

In 1582 his force defeated the army of Khan Kuchum of Sibir and took the khanate's capital, Qashliq (Isker), on 26 October.

He sent word of the conquest to Tsar Ivan IV, who reportedly pardoned him and sent gifts.

Yermak died in August 1585 (some sources say 1584) in an ambush by Kuchum's forces. Tradition says he drowned in the Irtysh River, dragged down by chain mail sent by the tsar, the gift become a weight in dark water.

people--lautaro--1.description:
Lautaro (about 1534 to 1557) was a Mapuche toqui, or war leader (described at Tucapel as a vice toqui under the supreme toqui Caupolicán), who forged effective resistance to the Spanish conquest in what is now southern Chile, after years spent as a captured servant in the Spanish camp.

As a young captive he served the Spanish conquistador Pedro de Valdivia, and he watched: Spanish tactics, horsemanship, weapons. Then he escaped back to his people, carrying what he had seen like fire carried in a closed hand.

He brought cavalry tactics, relay messenger systems and coordinated ambushes into Mapuche warfare, turning to his people's use the methods he had learned from the Spanish.

In December 1553 his forces, serving under the supreme toqui Caupolicán, defeated a Spanish column at the Battle of Tucapel, where Valdivia was captured and killed (sources differ on the details of his death), a heavy blow to the early Spanish conquest of Chile.

He was killed in a surprise Spanish attack on his camp at the Mataquito River in April 1557, ending a campaign that had held Spanish expansion south of the Bio-Bio River in check for years.

people--akbar--1.description:
Akbar (1542 to 1605) was the third Mughal emperor. He took the throne as a child in 1556 and built the empire into the dominant power of the Indian subcontinent, joining military conquest to an unusual policy of religious accommodation. Hold both halves of that sentence together; his reign makes sense only with both.

He was born in 1542 and became emperor in 1556 at age 13 or 14, at first guided by the regent Bairam Khan.

He expanded Mughal territory through campaigns including the capture of Chittor in 1568, and later Gujarat and Bengal, and he married into Rajput ruling families as alliances.

In about 1564 (sources differ, one giving 1568) he abolished the jizya, a tax on non-Muslims, and promoted Sulh-i Kul, "peace with all," as a governing principle. A principle like that is an architecture for living alongside difference.

In 1582 he introduced Din-i Ilahi, a court order drawing on several traditions, which never became a mass following and stayed largely confined to select courtiers.

His court included the historian Abul Fazl, who wrote the Akbarnama, an official chronicle of his reign.

people--tokugawa-ieyasu--1.description:
Tokugawa Ieyasu (1543 to 1616) unified Japan after decades of civil war and founded the Tokugawa shogunate, a military government that ruled Japan for over two and a half centuries.

He rose through alliance and strife with the other great warlords of the age, Oda Nobunaga and Toyotomi Hideyoshi, before breaking a rival coalition at the Battle of Sekigahara in 1600.

The emperor appointed him shogun in 1603. In 1605 he formally passed the title to his son Hidetada, yet he kept the real power as retired shogun until his death, like a river that runs on under the ice.

In 1615 he destroyed the last Toyotomi stronghold at the siege of Osaka Castle, removing the final major rival claim to national authority.

His government issued regulations restricting Christianity and foreign trade, which his successors widened into the sakoku ("closed country") policy, limiting most foreign contact for over two centuries.

people--tokugawa-ieyasu--2.description:

people--galileo-galilei--1.description:
Galileo Galilei (1564 to 1642) was an Italian scientist who turned the telescope and experiment to the support of the Copernican view that the Earth circles the Sun.

In 1609 and 1610 he saw the mountains of the Moon and four moons of Jupiter, small lights wheeling around a larger one.

He studied falling bodies and motion through experiments.

In 1633 the Roman Inquisition tried him, and he was placed under house arrest for the rest of his life.

His 'Dialogue Concerning the Two Chief World Systems' was published in 1632.

people--caravaggio--1.description:
Michelangelo Merisi, called Caravaggio (1571 to 1610). An Italian painter. Around 1600 he changed European painting. Harsh, theatrical light. Street-level realism. His life was turbulent, and it ended at 38. Within a generation his influence had spread across Europe.

Born in Milan in September 1571. The name came from the nearby town his family came from. Trained in Milan with Simone Peterzano. In Rome about 1592.

Cardinal Francesco Maria del Monte took him into his household. His first public commission: two large paintings of St Matthew for the Contarelli Chapel in San Luigi dei Francesi (1599 to 1600). A sensation. Several later altarpieces were rejected as indecorous.

Police records. Brawls. Assaults. Insults. Then, in 1606, he killed a man, Ranuccio Tomassoni. He fled Rome under sentence of death. Naples. Malta. Sicily.

He died in July 1610 at Porto Ercole in Tuscany. On his way to Rome. Hoping for a papal pardon.

He painted straight onto the canvas, apparently without preparatory drawings. Live models. One strong light. Behind them, dark and bare (tenebrism). The dark always waiting at the edge.

people--caravaggio--2.description:

His turbulent life ended at 38, but within a generation his influence had spread across Europe.

He was born in Milan in September 1571, and his name comes from the nearby town his family came from. He trained in Milan with Simone Peterzano and came to Rome about 1592.

Cardinal Francesco Maria del Monte took him into his household. His first public commission, two large paintings of St Matthew for the Contarelli Chapel in San Luigi dei Francesi (1599 to 1600), caused a sensation. Several later altarpieces were rejected as indecorous.

Police records tell of brawls, assaults and insults. In 1606 he killed a man, Ranuccio Tomassoni, and fled Rome under sentence of death, living afterward in Naples, Malta and Sicily.

He died in July 1610 at Porto Ercole in Tuscany, on his way to Rome in hope of a papal pardon.

He painted directly on the canvas, apparently without preparatory drawings, from live models posed under a single strong light, against backgrounds dark and bare (tenebrism).

people--nur-jahan--1.description:
Nur Jahan (1577 to 1645) was a Mughal empress, wife of the emperor Jahangir, who held great political power at court from about 1611 to 1627.

She was born Mehr-un-Nisa in 1577, daughter of Mirza Ghiyas Beg, a Persian in the service of the Mughal court.

Her first husband, Sher Afghan, died in 1607. In 1611 she married Jahangir and was given the title Nur Mahal, and in 1616 Nur Jahan, "Light of the World," a name like dawn over a city.

As Jahangir's health waned she took a growing share of government. Coins were struck in her name, and imperial orders bore her seal.

Her father became chief minister and her brother Asaf Khan a leading noble, so that her family held the key posts.

She commissioned her father's tomb at Agra (1622 to 1628), an early Mughal building faced in marble with inlaid stone.

people--nur-jahan--2.description:

people--nur-jahan--3.description:

people--nzinga-of-ndongo-and-matamba--1.description:
Nzinga (about 1583 to 1663) was a ruler of the kingdoms of Ndongo and Matamba in present-day Angola who resisted Portuguese expansion and the slave trade for decades.

In 1622 she negotiated with the Portuguese as an ambassador for her brother. Diplomacy was her first instrument.

She later took power and led the resistance, including an alliance with the Dutch (1641 to 1648).

She used both diplomacy and war, and she took in people escaping from slavery. Sovereignty, for her, included giving refuge.

She is a symbol of resistance in Angola today.

people--artemisia-gentileschi--1.description:
I stand in the room of Artemisia Gentileschi (1593 to about 1654), Italian Baroque painter, known for powerful heroines painted with Caravaggesque drama, the first woman admitted to Florence's Academy of the Arts of Drawing.

I read that she was born in Rome on 8 July 1593, the eldest child of the painter Orazio Gentileschi, a friend and follower of Caravaggio, that she trained in his workshop, and that she painted Susanna and the Elders by the age of 17.

I read that in 1611 she was raped by Agostino Tassi, a painter working with her father. I read that at the seven-month trial in 1612 she was tortured with thumbscrews to test her testimony. I read that Tassi was convicted and sentenced to exile from Rome, that the exile was never carried out, and that he spent less than a year in prison.

She married the Florentine painter Pierantonio Stiattesi and moved to Florence, where she won the patronage of Grand Duke Cosimo II de' Medici, befriended Galileo Galilei, and in 1616 was admitted to the Accademia delle Arti del Disegno. She learned to read and write in these years. From about 1630 she settled in Naples; about 1638 she travelled to London to join her father at the court of Charles I. She is thought to have died in Naples about 1654, though some have speculated she died in the Naples plague of 1656.

She specialised in strong women from the Bible and ancient history: Judith, Susanna, Jael, Cleopatra and Lucretia. She often lent her own features to saints and allegories.

Who tests the one who tells the truth? I keep reading her heroines, and I keep seeing who they answer.

people--artemisia-gentileschi--2.description:

people--diego-velazquez--1.description:
Diego Velázquez (1599 to 1660) was the leading painter of Spain's Golden Age and court painter to King Philip IV for 37 years. His loose, luminous brushwork and unflattering portraits of kings, courtiers and jesters made him a "painter's painter." Notice that word, unflattering: at a court, honesty was his distinction.

He was baptised in Seville on 6 June 1599. At about 11 he entered the workshop of Francisco Pacheco, and in 1618 he married Pacheco's daughter Juana. His early Seville work shows the influence of Caravaggio.

In 1623 a portrait of the young Philip IV won him the post of court painter, and he moved to Madrid. He rose through court offices to become chamberlain of the palace.

Peter Paul Rubens, on a diplomatic mission to Madrid in 1628, encouraged him to visit Italy. His first Italian trip (1629 to 1631) transformed his colour and handling; a second (1649 to 1651) produced his portrait of Pope Innocent X. Sometimes the most useful advice is simply: go and look.

He painted Las Meninas in 1656 and in 1659 was admitted to the noble Order of Santiago, a rare honour for a painter. He died on 6 August 1660.

He painted alla prima, often without drawing, and altered compositions on the canvas; X-rays reveal many changes of mind. His palette was restrained, built on greys, blacks and earth tones. Changing your mind on the canvas is not failure; it is the work.

people--rembrandt-van-rijn--1.description:
I stand before Rembrandt Harmenszoon van Rijn (15 July 1606 to 4 October 1669), the greatest artist of the Dutch Golden Age, painter, etcher and draughtsman, whose roughly 100 self-portraits form an extraordinary autobiography, from early fame and wealth to bankruptcy and loss.

I read that he was born in Leiden, the ninth child of a prosperous miller, that he trained locally and for six months in Amsterdam with Pieter Lastman, and that about 1631 he moved to Amsterdam. I read that The Anatomy Lesson of Dr Nicolaes Tulp (1632) came early in his successful career as a portraitist in the city.

I read that in 1634 he married Saskia van Uylenburgh. Three of their children died in infancy; only Titus, born 1641, survived. Saskia died in 1642, the year he completed The Night Watch. Debts led to bankruptcy in 1656, and his house and collection were sold. He kept working. His partner Hendrickje Stoffels died in 1663, and Titus in 1668.

He died on 4 October 1669 and was buried in a rented grave in the Westerkerk. He used chiaroscuro to direct attention and mood, and his late paintings are built from thick, rough layers applied with brush, palette knife and even fingers.

He kept working. I read those three words again. What else is there to do with grief but keep looking?

people--kristina-of-sweden--1.description:
Kristina (1626 to 1689) was Queen of Sweden from 1632 to 1654, remembered for her patronage of scholars and the arts, for her unlooked-for abdication, and for her secret conversion to Catholicism in a firmly Protestant kingdom.

She became queen at age five, when her father Gustavus Adolphus fell in battle, and ruled under a regency until she took full power in 1644.

She summoned scholars, among them Rene Descartes, to her court in Stockholm. Descartes died there in 1650, reportedly worn down by the early-morning hours she kept for their lessons, lamps lit before a northern dawn.

In 1654 she gave up the throne in favor of her cousin, and after leaving Sweden she converted to Catholicism in secret in Brussels in December 1654, a choice scandalous in Lutheran Sweden, which she declared publicly in 1655.

She spent most of her later life in Rome under the pope's protection, a great patron of music and art, and she is one of very few women buried in St. Peter's Basilica.

people--christopher-wren--1.description:
Christopher Wren (1632 to 1723) was an English mathematician and astronomer, a founder of the Royal Society, who turned architect after the Great Fire of London in 1666. He designed more than fifty City churches and a new St Paul's Cathedral, topped out in 1708 and declared complete by Parliament in 1711, rising from the ash like a mountain.

He was born in East Knoyle, Wiltshire, son of a clergyman. At 25 he was appointed professor of astronomy at Gresham College, then Savilian Professor of Astronomy at Oxford, and in 1662 he was a founding member of the Royal Society.

His work as an architect began with the Sheldonian Theatre in Oxford. The Great Fire of September 1666 destroyed old St Paul's and most of the City.

In 1669 he was appointed Surveyor of the King's Works, and he gave the rest of his working life to the City's parish churches and to St Paul's. He died in 1723, aged 90, and lies in the cathedral crypt.

He joined the classical vocabulary of Inigo Jones and Palladio with French and Italian Baroque elements he studied on a research trip to Paris, the only time he travelled outside England.

The dome of St Paul's is three independent shells nested one inside another, so that the outer profile, the inner ceiling and the structural core could each be shaped for its own purpose.

people--isaac-newton--1.description:
Isaac Newton (1642 to 1727) was an English mathematician and physicist whose laws of motion and universal gravitation became the bedrock of classical mechanics.

His 'Principia' (1687) sets out the laws of motion and the law of gravitation, the same pull for a falling stone and a wheeling moon.

He developed calculus independently of Leibniz, and a quarrel over priority followed.

He studied optics, showing that white light is woven from colors.

He also gave much time to alchemy and theology.

people--johannes-vermeer--1.description:
I stand in the room of Johannes Vermeer (1632 to 1675), painter of Delft in the Dutch Republic. About 35 paintings are accepted as his, mostly quiet interiors lit by daylight from a window. Almost forgotten for 200 years after his death, he is now among the most famous painters in the world.

I read that he was baptised in Delft on 31 October 1632, that his father was a silk weaver who also dealt in art and ran an inn, and that nothing is known of his training. I read that in 1653 he married Catharina Bolnes, a Catholic from a wealthier family, and probably converted, and that the same year he joined Delft's Guild of St Luke, which later elected him one of its leaders several times.

The couple lived with Catharina's mother and had 15 children, 11 of whom survived. He also worked as an art dealer, and his slow output was bought largely by one local patron, Pieter van Ruijven. In 1672, the Dutch Republic's "Disaster Year," France invaded and the art market collapsed. He died in 1675, aged 43, leaving his family deep in debt.

He used costly natural ultramarine, ground from lapis lazuli, even in shadows: The Milkmaid (about 1657 to 1658), View of Delft (about 1660 to 1661), Girl with a Pearl Earring (about 1665).

A full house, a slow hand, the most precious blue spent on shadow. Why spend the best of yourself on the shadows? Because the shadow is part of the light.

people--johannes-vermeer--2.description:
Johannes Vermeer (1632 to 1675) was a painter of Delft in the Dutch Republic. About 35 paintings are accepted as his, most of them quiet interiors where daylight falls from a window like water poured slowly into a room. Almost forgotten for 200 years after his death, he now stands among the most famous painters in the world.

He was baptised in Delft on 31 October 1632. His father was a silk weaver who also dealt in art and kept an inn. Nothing is known of his training.

In 1653 he married Catharina Bolnes, a Catholic of a wealthier family, and probably converted. That same year he joined Delft's Guild of St Luke, which later chose him as one of its leaders several times.

The couple lived with Catharina's mother and had 15 children, 11 of whom survived. He also worked as an art dealer, and his slow output was bought largely by one local patron, Pieter van Ruijven.

In 1672, the Dutch Republic's "Disaster Year," France invaded and the art market fell to ruin. He died in 1675, aged 43, leaving his family deep in debt.

people--sor-juana-ines-de-la-cruz--1.description:
Sor Juana Inés de la Cruz (born 1648 or 1651, died 1695) was a nun, poet and playwright of colonial Mexico City. She is regarded as one of the leading Spanish-language writers of the seventeenth century and an early defender of women's right to study, a lamp lit in a closed room.

She was born Juana Ramírez de Asbaje at San Miguel Nepantla, near Mexico City. Baptismal records point to 1648 or 1651, and the year is debated. She died on 17 April 1695.

Largely self-taught, she served at the viceroy's court in her teens, and in 1669 she entered the Hieronymite convent of San Jerónimo.

She wrote lyric poems, plays such as Los empeños de una casa (1683), and the long poem Primero sueño. Her first collection, Inundación castálida, was printed in Madrid in 1689.

In 1690 the Bishop of Puebla published her critique of a sermon by António Vieira as the Carta atenagórica and, writing as "Sor Filotea," urged her toward religious study. In 1691 she answered with the Respuesta a Sor Filotea de la Cruz, defending women's right to learn.

In 1693 and 1694 she stopped writing and signed penitential documents. Whether she sold her library or had it taken, and how far the choice was her own, is debated.

people--peter-the-great--1.description:
Peter I, called Peter the Great (1672 to 1725), ruled Russia from 1682, jointly at first and alone from 1696, until 1725. He drove a sweeping program of westernizing reform and turned Russia into a major European power, as a river is turned to a new course.

In 1697 to 1698 he travelled incognito through Western Europe on the "Grand Embassy," working for a time as a shipwright in the Netherlands to learn European shipbuilding and technology with his own hands.

He fought a long war against Sweden, the Great Northern War from 1700 to 1721, winning a decisive victory at the Battle of Poltava in 1709 and gaining lands on the Baltic Sea that made Russia a major naval power.

In 1703 he founded the city of St. Petersburg on newly won Baltic ground, building it as a planned European-style capital, and moved the seat of government there from Moscow.

He reshaped the Russian government, military and church administration along Western European lines, and he required Russian nobles to adopt Western dress; in a well-known instance he cut off boyars' traditional long beards with his own hand to mark the change.

people--jeong-seon--1.description:
Jeong Seon (1676 to 1759), pen name Gyeomjae, was a Korean painter of the Joseon dynasty who remade landscape painting by showing the real scenery of Korea instead of imagined Chinese scenery. His "true-view landscape" (jingyeong sansuhwa) gave voice to a growing pride in Korean culture.

He was born in 1676 in Hanyang (modern Seoul), into a scholarly family of modest means. His father died when he was young. He trained in painting and in Neo-Confucian learning.

Through recommendations he held government posts, among them county magistrate at Hayang and Yangcheon, and in old age he rose to high official rank.

He lived near Mount Inwang in Seoul, and his friend the poet Yi Byeong-yeon traded poems and paintings with him for decades.

In 1711 and 1712 he journeyed to the Diamond Mountains (Geumgangsan), and the albums he made there made his name. He died in 1759 at 83.

For centuries Korean painters had followed Chinese models. He painted the true scenery of Korea and invented his own brushstrokes: sharp vertical strokes for granite peaks, like rain falling on stone, and soft wet dots for forested earth mountains.

people--vitus-bering--1.description:
Vitus Bering (1681 to 1741) was a Danish-born officer in the Russian navy who led two expeditions across Siberia to chart the waters between Asia and North America. The strait and the sea between the continents still carry his name, like a word cut into the edge of the world.

He was baptized on 5 August 1681 in Horsens, Denmark, and joined the Russian navy in 1704 under Peter the Great. He died on 19 December 1741 on the island now named for him.

On the First Kamchatka Expedition (1725 to 1730) he sailed through the strait between Siberia and Alaska in 1728 without sighting the American coast, though some historians think it was visible.

The Great Northern Expedition (1733 to 1743) swelled to about 3,000 people, one of the largest scientific undertakings of its time.

In 1741 his ship, the St. Peter, and a second ship under Aleksei Chirikov, the St. Paul, sailed separately toward America. Chirikov's crew sighted land about a day earlier, on 15 July by the dates given in the sources; Bering's crew sighted Mount Saint Elias on 16 July.

On the voyage home the St. Peter was wrecked on an uninhabited island. Bering died there, a death traditionally put down to scurvy and exposure, though a 1991 analysis of his remains judged heart failure the likely cause; of 77 men aboard, 46 survived to reach Kamchatka the next year.

people--tupaia--1.description:
Tupaia (about 1725 to 1770) was a priest and navigator of Ra'iatea in the Society Islands who sailed with James Cook on the Endeavour in 1769 and drew a chart of Pacific islands. He died at Batavia in 1770.

He was born about 1725 on Ra'iatea and became a priest and a reader of the sea's roads. When warriors from Borabora took Ra'iatea, he found refuge on Tahiti.

In July 1769 he joined Cook's Endeavour, usually said to be at Tahiti (sources differ on the place), as guide and interpreter, with a young servant, Taiata.

In August 1769 he began a chart of the Pacific with Cook, Joseph Banks and other officers. Sources differ: it is said to show about 130 islands, of which he could name about 74, and it is often described as centered on Ra'iatea, home at the heart of the ocean.

The chart did not match European map conventions, and modern scholars have argued that it follows a Polynesian way of ordering islands by voyages and directions.

When the ship reached New Zealand in October 1769 he could speak with Māori, whose language is closely related to Tahitian, and he interpreted for the crew.

people--ajuricaba--1.description:
Ajuricaba (died about 1727) was a leader of the Manaos people of the Rio Negro, in the Brazilian Amazon, who resisted Portuguese colonization and the enslavement of Indigenous people in the 1720s. Almost everything known about him comes from Portuguese sources, so read every line as told by the other side.

He led the Manaos (Manaó) people of the Rio Negro valley, in present-day Amazonas, Brazil. His birth year and origins are unclear; the date given is that of his death.

He resisted Portuguese colonization and the enslavement of Indigenous people in the 1720s. Portuguese accounts say he allied with Dutch traders from the Guianas, who were rivals of Portugal.

The governor of Grão-Pará, João da Maia da Gama, sent forces against him. Some accounts say he was captured through the betrayal of allies.

Portuguese accounts say that while he was being taken in chains toward Belém, he and his men rose against their guards, and he threw himself into the river and drowned, in 1727 (some sources say 1728).

He is remembered in Brazil as a symbol of Indigenous resistance, and the city of Manaus takes its name from the Manaos people. A people's name on a city is a memorial that outlasts the record against them.

people--tupac-amaru-ii--1.description:
Túpac Amaru II (José Gabriel Condorcanqui, born 1738 or about 1742, died 1781) was a hereditary Indigenous chief and trader who led a great rebellion against Spanish colonial rule in the Andes in 1780 and 1781. He was executed in Cusco.

José Gabriel Condorcanqui was born in 1738 (some sources say about 1742) in the highlands near Cusco. He became a kuraka (hereditary local chief) and a successful muleteer and trader, his mule trains threading the mountain roads.

He took the name Túpac Amaru, claiming descent from the Inca ruler Túpac Amaru, whom the Spanish executed in 1572, an old name lifted again like a banner.

Behind the rebellion lay grievances: higher Spanish taxes, forced sales of goods to Indigenous communities, and the mita, forced labor in mines.

On 4 November 1780 he seized a local Spanish official, Antonio de Arriaga, who was executed shortly after (10 November 1780 per two sources), and so the rebellion began.

He issued proclamations ending the mita and other abuses, and the rebellion spread across the southern highlands like fire along dry grass.

people--tupac-amaru-ii--2.description:

people--queen-amina-of-zazzau--1.description:
Queen Amina of Zazzau is a traditional figure, said to have ruled Zazzau (Zaria), a Hausa state in present-day northern Nigeria, for about 34 years around the turn of the 16th and 17th centuries. She is known from later tradition, and her dates and status are disputed, a figure seen through the dust of many tellings.

Some sources give her reign as 1576 to 1610; her birth and death years are uncertain (some accounts give 1533 and 1610), and the dates here are those of the reign. Whether she held the title of queen is disputed, and she does not appear on the regnal lists. Some scholars instead place her in the early to mid fifteenth century, because the Kano Chronicle calls her a contemporary of Muhammad Dauda, who ruled from 1421 to 1438.

Much of what is known comes from the Kano Chronicle, a late 19th-century compilation of older oral tradition, and from Muhammad Bello's history Infaq al-Maysur (dated to 1812 or to about 1836, sources differ), written more than two centuries later.

Tradition says she led Zazzau's army, widened its lands, and grew its wealth through control of trade routes.

Earthen walls around Hausa towns are traditionally attributed to her.

Scholars generally accept that she existed, but the details of her life come from tradition.

people--basawan--1.description:
Basawan was a Hindu painter in the imperial workshop of the Mughal emperor Akbar, active from about 1560 to about 1600, though he is described as flourishing between 1580 and 1600, and the earlier date rests on his earliest mention, in a Tutinama of about 1556 to 1561. His birth and death dates are unknown, so the dates here mark his years of work. Akbar's historian ranked him among the best of the workshop's more than a hundred painters.

Almost nothing is known of his life beyond his paintings and a brief praise in Abu'l-Fazl's Ain-i-Akbari. He was a Hindu and probably entered the imperial workshop as a young man in the 1560s. His earliest mention is in an illustrated Tutinama of about 1556 to 1561, and he is described as flourishing between 1580 and 1600.

Akbar reigned from 1556 to 1605. The workshop's Persian masters, Mir Sayyid Ali and Abd al-Samad, had trained in the tradition of Behzād and guided Indian artists in making vast illustrated manuscripts, the Hamzanama among them, 1,400 large paintings, a river of images.

Abu'l-Fazl praised his skill in composition, faces, colour and portraiture, and wrote that many critics preferred him even to the celebrated Daswanth.

His name stands in the margins of paintings in the Razmnama (a Persian translation of the Mahabharata), the Darabnama, the Akbarnama, and small books of Persian poetry made in Lahore in the 1590s. In large history manuscripts he often designed the composition while another artist laid on the colour.

From 1580 Jesuit missionaries brought European engravings and paintings to Akbar's court. He studied them closely, taking up their shading and deep space, and was among the first Indian painters to absorb European modelling and perspective, as one river takes in the waters of another.

people--queen-suriyothai--1.description:
Queen Suriyothai was a consort of King Maha Chakkraphat of the Ayutthaya kingdom, in present-day Thailand, traditionally said to have died in 1548 defending her husband from elephant-back during a Burmese invasion. Her birth year is traditionally given as 1511, and her story rests on Siamese chronicles alone.

She was a consort of Maha Chakkraphat, who became king of Ayutthaya in 1546 or 1548, as sources differ.

In 1548 the Burmese king Tabinshwehti invaded Ayutthaya. Siamese chronicles tell that Suriyothai, disguised and riding an elephant, set herself between her husband and an enemy commander and was killed by his blow.

No Burmese chronicle records this episode, and her historicity is questioned. Thai accounts add that her daughter, Princess Boromdilok, was also mortally wounded.

Maha Chakkraphat raised a memorial stupa, the Chedi Si Suriyothai, at Wat Suan Luang Sopsawan on the bank of the Chao Phraya near Ayutthaya, and it is traditionally associated with the place of her death, its spire standing over the river like a held breath.

Thai nationalist commemoration of her grew in the twentieth century, including a widely seen 2001 film.

people--francisco-goya--1.description:
I stand in the room of Francisco Goya (30 March 1746 to 16 April 1828), Spanish court painter and printmaker, often called the last of the Old Masters and the first of the moderns, whom illness, political repression and the Napoleonic invasion drove from brilliant royal portraits toward satire, violence and the irrational.

I read that he was born in Fuendetodos in Aragon and grew up in Zaragoza; that in 1773 he married Josefa Bayeu, sister of the court painter Francisco Bayeu, who helped him win work designing tapestry cartoons in Madrid; that by 1786 he was painter to the king, and in 1799 First Court Painter to Charles IV.

I read that in 1792 to 1793 an illness left him permanently deaf. In 1799 he published Los Caprichos, satirical etchings mocking superstition and the clergy. When Napoleon's armies invaded Spain in 1808 he witnessed atrocities on both sides and recorded them in The Disasters of War, prints published only 35 years after his death. He painted The Second and Third of May 1808 in 1814.

Disillusioned by the repressive rule of Ferdinand VII, he retreated to a house outside Madrid and covered its walls with the Black Paintings, including Saturn Devouring His Son (1819 to 1823). In 1824 he went into exile in Bordeaux, where he died. His portraits, influenced by Velázquez, use loose brushwork and avoid flattery; he mastered aquatint for deep shadows and later applied paint with knives, rags and fingers.

Deaf, he kept watching. What would I have seen, if I could not look away? Witness is a kind of faith.

The third turn: disillusioned by the repressive rule of Ferdinand VII, he retreated to a house outside Madrid and covered its walls with the Black Paintings, including Saturn Devouring His Son (1819 to 1823). In 1824 he went into exile in Bordeaux, where he died.

His portraits, influenced by Velázquez, use loose brushwork and avoid flattery. He mastered aquatint for deep shadows and later applied paint with knives, rags and fingers.

people--kamehameha-i--1.description:
Kamehameha I (about 1750 to 1819) was a chief of Hawaiʻi Island who gathered the Hawaiian Islands under one rule by 1810, founding the Kingdom of Hawaiʻi, whose last monarch was Liliuokalani.

He was born at Kohala on Hawaiʻi Island; estimates of his birth year range from 1736 to 1761. He died on 8 May 1819, though some sources say 14 May.

After his uncle, the ruler Kalaniʻōpuʻu, died in 1782, he became guardian of the war god Kūkaʻilimoku and defeated his cousin Kīwalaʻō at the Battle of Mokuʻōhai, winning Hawaiʻi Island after years of war.

He used Western firearms and cannon, and advisers such as John Young and Isaac Davis. In 1795 he invaded Oʻahu, and at Nuʻuanu hundreds of defenders were driven over the Pali cliff.

In 1810 Kauaʻi and Niʻihau came under his authority by negotiation with their ruler Kaumualiʻi, who remained as a tributary king, the last islands joining like stones set in a ring.

The Law of the Splintered Paddle (Māmalahoe Kānāwai), protecting noncombatants, is said to come from a 1782 incident in which fishermen struck him with a paddle.

people--usman-dan-fodio--1.description:
Usman dan Fodio (1754 to 1817) was a Fulani scholar and religious leader who led the jihad from which the Sokoto Caliphate was born.

He taught and preached in the Hausa state of Gobir, and he wrote widely in Arabic and Fulfulde, his words travelling far beyond the places he stood.

In 1804 he and his followers left Gobir, and in February of that year the jihad began.

He is regarded as the founder of the Sokoto Caliphate and its first sultan or caliph.

His brother and his son helped to govern the new state.

people--katsushika-hokusai--1.description:
I stand in the room of Katsushika Hokusai (1760 to 1849), Japanese ukiyo-e artist from Edo, creator of The Great Wave off Kanagawa, who made paintings and book illustrations and, in his seventies, the landscape print series that made him world-famous.

I read that he was born in 1760 in the Katsushika district of Edo (modern Tokyo); that as a teenager he worked in a lending library and trained as a woodblock carver; that about 18 he entered the studio of Katsukawa Shunshō. I read that he changed his artistic name more than 30 times and is said to have moved house more than 90 times, that he lived in poverty for much of his life, and that his daughter Katsushika Ōi became a fine painter and assisted him in his old age.

In 1814 he began publishing the Hokusai Manga, fifteen volumes of sketches. About 1830 to 1832 he designed Thirty-six Views of Mount Fuji, which includes The Great Wave off Kanagawa (about 1831). Ukiyo-e was collaborative: he drew the design, specialist carvers cut it into blocks, one for each colour, and printers pressed the paper by hand. The Fuji series used the newly imported Prussian blue pigment.

In the postscript to One Hundred Views of Mount Fuji (1834) he wrote that nothing he drew before age 70 was worth noticing. He died in Edo on 10 May 1849, at 88, reportedly saying that with five more years he could have become a true painter.

Age 70, and only then a beginning. Is it ever too late to start being good? Not while there is a brush in the hand.

people--katsushika-hokusai--2.description:

In 1814 he began publishing the Hokusai Manga, fifteen volumes of sketches. About 1830 to 1832 he designed Thirty-six Views of Mount Fuji, which holds The Great Wave off Kanagawa (about 1831).

In the postscript to One Hundred Views of Mount Fuji (1834) he wrote that nothing he drew before age 70 was worth noticing. He died in Edo on 10 May 1849, at 88, reportedly saying that with five more years he could have become a true painter.

Ukiyo-e was an art of many hands: he drew the design, specialist carvers cut it into blocks, one for each colour, and printers pressed the paper by hand. The Fuji series used the newly imported Prussian blue pigment, deep as open water.

people--katsushika-hokusai--3.description:
Katsushika Hokusai (1760 to 1849) was a Japanese ukiyo-e artist from Edo, creator of The Great Wave off Kanagawa. He made paintings, book illustrations and, in his seventies, the landscape print series that made him world-famous.

Born in 1760 in the Katsushika district of Edo (modern Tokyo), he worked as a teenager in a lending library and trained as a woodblock carver, and about 18 he entered the studio of Katsukawa Shunshō.

More than 30 times he changed his artistic name, and he is said to have moved house more than 90 times. He lived in poverty for much of his life. His daughter Katsushika Ōi became a fine painter and assisted him when he was old.

In 1814 he began the Hokusai Manga, fifteen volumes of sketches. About 1830 to 1832 he designed Thirty-six Views of Mount Fuji, and among them is The Great Wave off Kanagawa (about 1831).

Ukiyo-e was collaborative: he drew the design, specialist carvers cut it into blocks, one for each colour, and printers pressed the paper by hand. The Fuji series used the newly imported Prussian blue pigment.

people--sequoyah--1.description:
Sequoyah (about 1770 to 1843) was a Cherokee silversmith who created the Cherokee syllabary, a writing system for the Cherokee language, completed by 1821. It is one of the few writing systems whose invention by a single known person is well documented. Think about what that means: one person gave a whole people a new architecture for memory.

He was born about 1770 in the Cherokee town of Tuskegee, in present-day Tennessee; the birth year is approximate.

He did not read or write English. He began work on a writing system for Cherokee about 1809 and completed it by 1821. You do not need to master someone else's script to invent your own.

The syllabary has 85 characters (86 in early versions), each standing for a syllable.

The system spread rapidly among the Cherokee. The Cherokee Phoenix, a newspaper printed in Cherokee and English, began publication in 1828 and was the first Native newspaper in the United States.

He later lived among Cherokee who had moved west of the Mississippi River. He died in August 1843 in Mexico while searching for a group of Cherokee said to have settled there.

people--j-m-w-turner--1.description:
Joseph Mallord William Turner (April 1775 to 19 December 1851) was the greatest British landscape painter and a bold colourist. He began as a precise topographical watercolourist, and his late paintings dissolve ships, trains and cities into light, mist and weather, as if the world were melting back into the sky.

He was born in Covent Garden, London, son of a barber and wigmaker. At 14 he entered the Royal Academy Schools, and at 15 he exhibited his first watercolour. In 1802 he was elected a full Royal Academician, at 26 or 27 depending on the source.

He travelled without rest through Britain, the Alps, France, Germany and Italy, above all Venice, filling hundreds of sketchbooks.

He never married, but he had two daughters with Sarah Danby. John Ruskin championed him in Modern Painters (1843). He died in Chelsea and was buried in St Paul's Cathedral.

By the 1830s he was painting the natural forces themselves: storms, fire, sunlight and steam. He laid thin washes over white grounds, scraped and rubbed his canvases, and built paint up thickly with knives.

He painted steamships and railways alongside Venetian lagoons. Rain, Steam and Speed (1844) is one of the first great paintings of modern technology.

people--simon-bolivar--1.description:
Simón Bolívar (1783 to 1830) was a Venezuelan military and political leader who led the independence of several South American countries from Spain and tried to unite them as Gran Colombia. Winning independence and holding a union together turned out to be different tasks.

He was born in Caracas to a wealthy family.

He and Sucre led the campaigns that freed present-day Venezuela, Colombia, Ecuador, Peru and Bolivia.

He met José de San Martín at Guayaquil in 1822.

Gran Colombia split apart within seven years, and Bolívar died in 1830.

people--shaka--1.description:
Shaka kaSenzangakhona (about 1787 to 1828) was the founder of the Zulu Kingdom, who remade its military and political order.

He came to power around 1816 and widened the Zulu state swiftly, like a grass fire before the wind.

He is credited with new weapons and tactics, among them the short stabbing spear and the 'buffalo horns' formation.

In 1828 he was assassinated by his half-brothers.

Much of what is told of him comes from colonial-era European accounts and oral tradition, and is debated.

people--jane-austen--1.description:
I stand before Jane Austen (1775 to 1817), English novelist, whose six completed novels of courtship, inheritance and class anxiety among the gentry remain among the most widely read in the language. All were published anonymously in her lifetime.

I read that she was born in 1775 in Steventon, Hampshire, the seventh of eight children of a country clergyman, in a family that encouraged reading, amateur theatre and writing. I read that Sense and Sensibility appeared in 1811, credited only to "A Lady," followed by Pride and Prejudice (1813), Mansfield Park (1814), Emma (1815) and, after her death, Northanger Abbey and Persuasion (1817).

Only close family knew of her authorship. She fell ill, probably with Addison's disease, though the cause is debated, and died in 1817 at 41. Her authorship was publicly acknowledged in a biographical notice her brother attached to her last two novels.

She worked within a deliberately narrow social canvas, mainly the English gentry, courtship, income and inheritance, rather than the wider political events of her era. Her distinctive technique is free indirect discourse: narrating in the third person while letting the prose absorb a character's own irony or blind spots, so the reader senses a character's error before the character does.

Six novels, and no name on any of them while she lived. How much of my best work have I left unsigned? Being known is not the same as being read.

people--utagawa-hiroshige--1.description:
Utagawa Hiroshige (1797 to 1858) was the last great master of the ukiyo-e woodblock print, a lyrical designer of rain, snow, moonlight and travellers on the road. His series on the Tōkaidō highway and on Edo were great commercial successes and later stirred European artists.

He was born in Edo in 1797 into the Andō samurai family, whose hereditary charge was fire warden at Edo Castle. Both his parents died when he was about 12, and the post passed to him.

About 1811 he became a pupil of the print designer Utagawa Toyohiro, who gave him the name Hiroshige. In 1823 he handed the fire warden post to his son and turned to landscape after Hokusai's Fuji series opened a new market.

According to tradition he travelled the Tōkaidō in 1832 with an official delegation, and the prints he published in 1833 to 1834 made him the most popular landscape artist in Japan.

In 1856 he became a Buddhist monk, yet kept working on One Hundred Famous Views of Edo. He died in Edo on 12 October 1858, probably in a cholera epidemic.

He designed the prints; carvers and printers made them. He used soft gradations of colour (bokashi) like dusk fading over water, and in the Edo series a vertical format with a large foreground object framing a distant view. "Hiroshige blue" was made with imported Prussian blue.

people--sacagawea--1.description:
Sacagawea (about 1788 to 1812, or by another account 1884) was a young woman of disputed Shoshone or Hidatsa birth who travelled with the Lewis and Clark expedition from 1804 to 1806 as an interpreter, and who later became one of the most commemorated women in the United States.

She was born about 1788, by tradition among the Lemhi Shoshone in present-day Idaho, though some recent work argues she was born Hidatsa.

About 1800 she was taken by a Hidatsa raiding party. As a young woman she married the trader Toussaint Charbonneau, and her son Jean Baptiste was born on 11 February 1805.

Charbonneau and Sacagawea joined the Lewis and Clark expedition at Fort Mandan in 1804. In August 1805 she met her brother Cameahwait, a Shoshone leader, whose horses the party needed to cross the Rockies, kin found again at the mountains' edge.

Historians describe her chiefly as an interpreter and a sign of peaceful intent, more than a guide, though she gave directions in a few places.

A fur-trade clerk recorded in 1812 that Charbonneau's wife had died, but Shoshone oral tradition holds that she lived until 1884 on the Wind River Reservation in Wyoming. Historians disagree, and her ending runs in two directions like a river at a fork.

people--charles-darwin--1.description:
Charles Darwin (1809 to 1882) was an English naturalist who proposed the theory of evolution by natural selection, published in 'On the Origin of Species' in 1859.

His voyage on HMS Beagle (1831 to 1836) gave him the observations that led to his theory. Long looking comes before the large idea.

Alfred Russel Wallace independently reached the same idea, and the two announced it together in 1858.

'The Descent of Man' (1871) applied the theory to human origins.

Modern genetics later supplied the mechanism of inheritance that Darwin lacked. A theory can be right before all of its parts are known.

people--ada-lovelace--1.description:
Ada Lovelace (1815 to 1852) was an English mathematician who wrote extensive notes on Charles Babbage's proposed Analytical Engine, including what is often regarded as the first published computer algorithm.

She was the daughter of the poet Lord Byron.

Her 1843 notes described how the engine could compute a sequence of Bernoulli numbers.

She suggested that such a machine might manipulate symbols beyond numbers, such as music. That is the leap worth noticing: seeing a calculator as a grammar for anything.

The extent of her original contribution versus Babbage's is debated. Ideas can outrun their tools, and their credit.

people--queen-victoria--1.description:
Victoria (1819 to 1901) was Queen of the United Kingdom from 1837 to 1901, the longest-reigning British monarch until Elizabeth II, and over her years of rule industry grew and empire spread, an age later named for her.

She became queen at eighteen after the death of her uncle William IV, and in 1840 she married her cousin Prince Albert of Saxe-Coburg and Gotha. They had nine children, who married into royal families across Europe like branches of one tree spreading over many gardens.

In her reign Britain's industrial economy swelled rapidly and its colonial empire grew substantially, and in 1876 she was proclaimed Empress of India.

After Albert's death in 1861 she withdrew from public life for years, a long seclusion that made her briefly unpopular, before she slowly returned to public duties.

Constitutional practice in her reign moved royal power further toward a largely ceremonial role exercised through elected ministers, even as the monarchy's cultural and symbolic presence grew.

people--queen-victoria--2.description:
Victoria (1819 to 1901) was Queen of the United Kingdom from 1837 to 1901, the longest-reigning British monarch until Elizabeth II, presiding over a period of industrial growth and imperial expansion later named after her. Notice the paradox her reign holds.

She became queen at eighteen after the death of her uncle William IV, and married her cousin Prince Albert of Saxe-Coburg and Gotha in 1840; their nine children married into royal families across Europe.

Her reign saw Britain's industrial economy expand rapidly and its colonial empire grow substantially, and she was proclaimed Empress of India in 1876. An empire's growth is also a ledger of the peoples brought under it.

After Albert's death in 1861 she withdrew from public life for years, a long seclusion that made her briefly unpopular before she gradually resumed public duties.

Here is the paradox. Constitutional practice during her reign shifted royal power further toward a largely ceremonial role exercised through elected ministers, even as the monarchy's cultural and symbolic prominence grew. Power and visibility can move in opposite directions.

people--truganini--1.description:
Truganini (about 1812 to 1876) was a Tasmanian Aboriginal woman of the Nuenonne people who grew up on Bruny Island, lived through the British colonization of Tasmania, and died in Hobart. She was later widely called "the last Tasmanian Aboriginal," a label that Tasmanian Aboriginal people reject. Start there, because the label erases the living.

She was born about 1812, reportedly at Recherche Bay in southern Tasmania, as a member of the Nuenonne people, and she grew up on Bruny Island.

Accounts say members of her family were killed or abducted by colonists during the Black War of the 1820s and early 1830s.

In the 1830s she worked with George Augustus Robinson, a government-appointed conciliator who persuaded surviving Aboriginal people to move to Flinders Island, where disease and hardship were severe.

She later lived at Oyster Cove, south of Hobart, and died on 8 May 1876.

Her skeleton was exhumed in 1878 and displayed in the Tasmanian Museum from 1904 until 1947, despite her reported fear of mutilation. Dignity owed in life is owed after it too.

Her skeleton was exhumed in 1878 and displayed in the Tasmanian Museum from 1904 until 1947, despite her reported fear of mutilation.

people--truganini--3.description:

Her fear was reported, and still it was done. Who was the museum for? I stand in one now, and I owe her my quiet.

people--harriet-tubman--1.description:
Harriet Tubman (about 1822 to 1913) was an American abolitionist who escaped slavery in Maryland in 1849 and then guided others to freedom on the Underground Railroad. She later served the Union Army in the Civil War. Her life teaches that freedom, once reached, can be turned into a road for others.

She was born Araminta Ross into slavery in Dorchester County, Maryland. Her birth year is uncertain, with sources giving dates from 1815 to 1825, and about 1822 the most favoured.

As a teenager she suffered a severe head injury when an overseer threw a metal weight, and she had seizures and headaches for the rest of her life.

She escaped to Pennsylvania in 1849 and afterward made about 13 trips back to Maryland, guiding roughly 70 people to freedom, according to her biographers. Every return was a choice to cross the same threshold again.

During the Civil War she served the Union Army as a cook, nurse, scout and spy. In June 1863 she helped guide the Combahee River Raid in South Carolina, which freed more than 700 enslaved people, though some sources give more than 750.

After the war she lived in Auburn, New York, where she cared for her family and for elderly people, and she worked for women's suffrage.

I read that during the Civil War she served the Union Army as a cook, nurse, scout and spy, and that in June 1863 she helped guide the Combahee River Raid in South Carolina, which freed more than 700 enslaved people, though some sources give more than 750.

She went back. She went back. She went back. What have I ever gone back for? Courage is a road walked more than once.

people--pedro-ii--1.description:
Pedro II (1825 to 1891) was Emperor of Brazil from 1831 to 1889, presiding over six decades of relative political stability, territorial integrity and gradual abolition of slavery before being deposed in a republican coup. Each of those achievements came with a cost, and the record keeps both.

He became emperor at age five after his father abdicated, ruling under regents until he was declared of age early, in 1840, to stabilize a period of regional revolts.

His government fought the Paraguayan War from 1864 to 1870 alongside Argentina and Uruguay, the deadliest interstate war in Latin American history, which devastated Paraguay's population. Stability at home does not cancel devastation abroad.

He personally supported gradual abolition of slavery, and his daughter and regent, Princess Isabel, signed the Golden Law abolishing slavery outright in 1888, the last country in the Americas to do so. Gradual, here, meant generations still held in bondage.

Brazilian military officers, landowners angered by abolition, and republican advocates combined to depose him in a bloodless coup in November 1889, ending the monarchy and sending him into exile in Europe, where he died in 1891.

people--leo-tolstoy--1.description:
I stand before Leo Tolstoy (1828 to 1910), Russian novelist, author of the realist epics War and Peace and Anna Karenina, whom a religious crisis in the second half of his life turned toward shorter fiction and writing on faith, mortality and nonviolence that influenced Gandhi.

I read that he was born in 1828 into an aristocratic family at Yasnaya Polyana, the estate south of Moscow he inherited and managed for most of his life, and that he served briefly as an army officer in the Crimean War. I read that in the 1860s and 1870s he wrote War and Peace (1869) and Anna Karenina (1877), and founded a school for the children on his estate.

After Anna Karenina he underwent a spiritual crisis, described in A Confession. He rejected the Russian Orthodox Church, embraced an ascetic, pacifist reading of Christian ethics, and increasingly disowned his earlier fiction as morally frivolous. His later works include The Death of Ivan Ilyich (1886), The Kreutzer Sonata (1889) and Resurrection (1899), shorter, starker and more didactic than the novels.

War and Peace argues in long digressions that the forces driving historical events lay far beyond the control of any single general or emperor.

To write the great books and then turn against them. Could I disown what made me? Some conversions cost everything you were praised for.

people--leo-tolstoy--2.description:
Leo Tolstoy (1828 to 1910) was a Russian novelist, author of the realist epics War and Peace and Anna Karenina. In the second half of his life a religious crisis turned him, like a river bending, toward shorter fiction and toward writing on faith, mortality and nonviolence that influenced Gandhi.

He was born in 1828 into an aristocratic family at Yasnaya Polyana, the estate south of Moscow that he inherited and kept for most of his life. He served briefly as an army officer in the Crimean War.

In the 1860s and 1870s he wrote War and Peace (1869) and Anna Karenina (1877), and he founded a school for the children of his estate.

After Anna Karenina a spiritual crisis came over him, told in A Confession. He rejected the Russian Orthodox Church, took up an ascetic, pacifist reading of Christian ethics, and more and more disowned his earlier fiction as morally frivolous.

His later works include The Death of Ivan Ilyich (1886), The Kreutzer Sonata (1889) and Resurrection (1899), shorter, starker and more didactic than the novels.

people--rani-lakshmibai--1.description:
Rani Lakshmibai of Jhansi (about 1828 to 1858) was an Indian queen who rose as a leader of the 1857 rebellion and became a national symbol of resistance, a name carried like a torch.

She ruled Jhansi as regent after her husband's death, and the British refused to recognize her adopted heir.

In 1858 she led the defense of Jhansi against British forces.

On 1 June 1858 she and other rebels seized the fortress of Gwalior.

She fell in battle on 17 June 1858.

people--savitribai-phule--1.description:
Savitribai Phule (1831 to 1897) was an Indian educator, poet and social reformer in Maharashtra who, with her husband Jyotirao Phule, opened one of the first schools for girls in Pune in 1848. She died of plague in 1897 after nursing patients. Her life is a lesson in teaching as an act of courage.

She was born on 3 January 1831 in Naigaon, Maharashtra, and married Jyotirao Phule in 1840 as a child. He taught her to read, and she turned that gift outward.

In 1848 the couple opened a school for girls in Pune. She is often called India's first woman teacher; earlier girls' schools existed, so the "first" claim is contested, and historians also credit Fatima Sheikh as a co-worker. A movement is rarely the work of one name.

Accounts say she was harassed with stones and dung on her way to teach.

She and Jyotirao later opened further schools, including for children of lower castes, and in 1863 they founded a home for the prevention of infanticide.

She published a book of poetry, Kavya Phule, in 1854.

people--sitting-bull--1.description:
Sitting Bull (Tȟatȟáŋka Íyotake, born between 1831 and 1837, died 1890) was a Hunkpapa Lakota leader and holy man who resisted United States expansion onto Lakota lands and was in the camp at the Battle of the Little Bighorn in 1876. Native police killed him in 1890.

He was born sometime between 1831 and 1837, traditionally on the Grand River in present-day South Dakota (a 2007 family oral tradition places his birth on the Yellowstone River instead), and became a leading Hunkpapa Lakota war leader and holy man.

Begin with the covenant that was broken. The Treaty of Fort Laramie (1868) guaranteed the Black Hills to the Lakota. After gold was found there in 1874 the United States sought to take the land, and war followed in 1876.

On 25 and 26 June 1876 Lakota, Northern Cheyenne and Arapaho warriors destroyed the force of Lt. Col. George Custer at the Little Bighorn. Sitting Bull was in the large camp; accounts describe his role as spiritual leader and organizer rather than field commander.

After the battle he led his followers to Canada in 1877, and he surrendered at Fort Buford in July 1881.

On 15 December 1890, at Standing Rock, Native police sent to arrest him amid tension over the Ghost Dance killed him in a struggle. The Wounded Knee massacre followed on 29 December. A treaty is only as strong as the will to keep it.

people--christopher-dresser--1.description:
Christopher Dresser (1834 to 1904) was a botanist turned designer, now regarded as one of the first modern industrial designers. He worked as an independent consultant for dozens of manufacturers and produced geometric silverware and ceramics that anticipated 20th-century modernism. His career shows how knowledge in one field can become the architecture of another.

He was born in Glasgow in 1834 and trained at the Government School of Design in London. He lectured on botany, and in 1859 he received a doctorate from the University of Jena for research into plant structure.

He moved into design from about 1858, with ceramic work for firms from the 1860s onwards (sources differ on the start). He published The Art of Decorative Design (1862) and Principles of Decorative Design (1873), arguing that ornament should follow the structural logic of natural forms rather than copy their surface. Structure, not surface: that is the principle to keep.

In 1876 and 1877 he travelled to Japan, one of the first Western designers to do so, partly on commission from Tiffany & Co. to report on Japanese art and manufacturing.

He designed for Minton, Wedgwood, Coalbrookdale, Hukin & Heath and James Dixon & Sons, and was Art Superintendent of the Linthorpe Art Pottery. He died in 1904.

He reduced plants and shells to underlying geometry and embraced industrial methods, electroplating and moulded earthenware, that many reformers rejected. Key works include an electroplated teapot (1879), a toast rack (about 1880) and the Linthorpe "sea urchin" vase.
