people--cixi--1.description:
The Empress Dowager Cixi (1835 to 1908) was the dominant political figure of late Qing China, ruling as regent for most of the years from 1861 to 1908.

In 1861 she became regent for her young son, the Tongzhi Emperor, and later for the Guangxu Emperor.

Her years include the Self-Strengthening Movement, an effort to renew China's defenses and industry.

In 1900 she supported the Boxers, and after their defeat she pursued the 'New Policies' reforms.

Historians debate her legacy. Older accounts paint her as a reactionary; recent work stresses her political skill and the limits that hemmed her in like walls around a garden.

people--william-morris--1.description:
William Morris (1834 to 1896) was an English designer, writer and socialist, the central figure of the Arts and Crafts movement. He turned from cheap mechanised ornament toward patterns drawn from nature and made by traditional craft, as a gardener turns from paper flowers to living ones.

He was born in Walthamstow in 1834 into a family grown wealthy through copper mining. At Oxford he met the painter Edward Burne-Jones and, through him, the circle around Dante Gabriel Rossetti.

He built Red House (1859 to 1860) and, unable to find furnishings he considered well made, founded a decorative arts firm in 1861 with Burne-Jones, Rossetti, Philip Webb and others. In 1875 it was reorganised as Morris & Co.

He founded the Socialist League in 1884 and wrote much on politics and utopian fiction. In 1891 he founded the Kelmscott Press, and its illustrated Chaucer was completed months before his death in 1896.

He designed from real plants, disciplining them into flattened repeating patterns. He revived hand block-printing, indigo-discharge dyeing, and letterpress printing from hand-cut type, over faster industrial methods.

His principle was "have nothing in your house that you do not know to be useful or believe to be beautiful". Yet his goods were luxuries that generally only the wealthy could afford.

people--liliuokalani--1.description:
Liliuokalani (1838 to 1917) was the last monarch of the Kingdom of Hawaii, reigning from 1891 until she was deposed in January 1893 by a group of residents backed by United States troops.

She was born in Honolulu on 2 September 1838 and died there on 11 November 1917.

On 29 January 1891 she succeeded her brother Kalākaua, the kingdom's only reigning queen.

In January 1893 she moved to issue a constitution restoring royal powers cut back by the 1887 "Bayonet Constitution."

On 17 January 1893 a Committee of Safety of mostly American and European residents overthrew her while United States Marines were ashore. She yielded to the United States government to avoid bloodshed and asked it to restore her.

After a failed royalist uprising she was arrested, and in January 1895 she signed an abdication, the last light of a kingdom going down with the sun.

people--claude-monet--1.description:
Claude Monet (14 November 1840 to 5 December 1926) was a French painter, the leader and purest practitioner of Impressionism. His Impression, Sunrise gave the movement its name, and all his life he painted the shifting play of light, as water forever changes under the sky.

He was born in Paris and grew up in Le Havre, where as a youth he sold caricatures. Eugène Boudin persuaded him to paint out of doors. In Paris he met Camille Pissarro and befriended Renoir, Sisley and Bazille.

The 1860s and 1870s were years of poverty. During the Franco-Prussian War he took refuge in London, where he saw Turner's paintings and met the dealer Paul Durand-Ruel.

In 1874 he and his friends held an exhibition apart from the official Salon. Critics mocked them, and the name "Impressionist" stuck.

In 1883 his family settled at Giverny in Normandy, where he made a flower garden and a water garden with a Japanese bridge, which became his chief subject.

He painted the same subject again and again in changing conditions: haystacks, poplars and Rouen Cathedral. Key works include Impression, Sunrise (1872), Stacks of Wheat (1890 to 1891) and the Water Lilies.

people--jose-maria-velasco--1.description:
José María Velasco (6 July 1840 to 26 August 1912) was the most important Mexican painter of the 19th century, known for his panoramic views of the Valley of Mexico, the land laid open beneath a vast sky. He was also a trained naturalist who illustrated scientific publications on botany, zoology and geology.

He was born in Temascalcingo, in the State of Mexico, and his family moved to Mexico City in 1849. In 1858 he entered the Academy of San Carlos, where the Italian painter Eugenio Landesio taught him to watch nature closely and paint out of doors. He also studied botany, zoology, anatomy, physics and mathematics.

In 1877 he followed Landesio as professor of landscape painting, and Diego Rivera was among his students.

He worked as a scientific illustrator for the National Museum and on expeditions, and he painted archaeological sites such as Teotihuacan.

He won a medal at the Paris Universal Exposition of 1889 and showed at the 1893 Chicago World's Columbian Exposition. One view of the Valley of Mexico was given to Pope Leo XIII and now hangs in the Vatican Museums.

He worked from outdoor sketches toward large studio compositions. His panoramas set a detailed foreground of cacti and rocks against a luminous distance, and often include railways, bridges and haciendas beside nature and ruins.

people--yaa-asantewaa--1.description:
Yaa Asantewaa (about 1840 to 1921) was the queen mother of Ejisu in the Asante kingdom, in present-day Ghana, who led an Asante uprising against British rule in 1900. She died in exile in the Seychelles, far across the sea.

She was born about 1840 and was queen mother (ohemaa) of Ejisu, a title held by a woman who advises and helps choose the ruler.

The British exiled the Asante king Prempeh I in 1896. In March 1900 the governor, Frederick Hodgson, demanded the Golden Stool, the Asante symbol of national unity, so that he could sit on it.

According to tradition she then called on the Asante chiefs at a council to resist, and she became a leader of the uprising sometimes called the War of the Golden Stool.

Asante forces besieged the British fort at Kumasi for several months in 1900. British reinforcements relieved it, and the fighting ended that year with a British victory.

She was captured and exiled to the Seychelles in 1901, and she died there on 17 October 1921.

people--wilfrid-laurier--1.description:
Wilfrid Laurier (1841 to 1919) was the first French-Canadian Prime Minister of Canada, serving from 1896 to 1911 during a period of rapid western settlement and economic growth. His career is a study in the work of balancing.

A lawyer from Quebec, he became Liberal Party leader in 1887 and prime minister in 1896, holding the office for over fifteen years, then the longest unbroken term in Canadian history.

His government promoted immigration and settlement of the Canadian prairies, a policy associated with his minister Clifford Sifton, which brought large numbers of European immigrant farmers to Western Canada.

He worked to balance relations between English- and French-speaking Canada, though his support for Canadian participation in Britain's Boer War strained relations with Quebec nationalists who opposed it. Every balance tips somewhere.

He lost the 1911 election over a proposed reciprocity (free trade) agreement with the United States, which opponents attacked as a threat to Canada's ties with Britain.

people--mary-cassatt--1.description:
Mary Cassatt (22 May 1844 to 14 June 1926) was an American painter who spent most of her grown life in France and was the only American to exhibit with the French Impressionists. She is honoured for tender, unsentimental images of women and children.

She was born in Allegheny City, now part of Pittsburgh, into a wealthy family. Against her father's wishes she studied at the Pennsylvania Academy of the Fine Arts from about 1860, then crossed to Paris in 1866.

Women could not enter the École des Beaux-Arts, so she studied privately and copied Old Masters in the Louvre. Weary of the Salon's conservative taste, she took up Degas's invitation in 1877 to exhibit with the Impressionists, and she showed with them in 1879, 1880, 1881 and 1886.

Her parents and sister came to Paris to live with her, and her family became her favourite models.

In 1890 an exhibition of Japanese prints in Paris kindled a set of colour prints, usually counted as ten, joining drypoint and aquatint. From them she took flat colour, strong outlines and cropped compositions, like light seen through a cut window.

In 1893 she painted the mural Modern Woman for the Woman's Building at the Chicago World's Columbian Exposition; it has been lost.

people--menelik-ii--1.description:
Menelik II (1844 to 1913) was emperor of Ethiopia from 1889 and the leader who defeated Italy at Adwa in 1896.

He expanded the empire southward and founded Addis Ababa as the capital.

He imported modern arms and pursued technological modernization.

He won the Battle of Adwa on 1 March 1896.

His empire's expansion brought conquest of neighboring peoples, and it is debated. A celebrated victory and an empire's own conquests can belong to the same reign.

people--ludwig-ii--1.description:
Ludwig II (1845 to 1886). Sometimes called the "Fairy Tale King." King of Bavaria from 1864 until his death. Remembered for extravagant romantic castles. Remembered for his patronage of the composer Richard Wagner.

He was an early, eager patron of Richard Wagner. He paid off the composer's debts. He funded productions. Then political opposition to Wagner's influence at court forced the composer to leave Munich.

Castles. Several, elaborate. Most famously Neuschwanstein, begun in 1869, inspired partly by Wagner's operas. Paid for from his personal fortune, not the Bavarian state treasury. Still, the debts grew deep.

Bavaria defeated alongside Austria in the 1866 Austro-Prussian War. Bavaria folded into the German Empire in 1871. His practical authority shrinking, year by year. The throne still his.

1886. A government commission cites his mounting debts. His reclusive behavior. He is declared mentally unfit to rule. Confined. The next day he dies in Lake Starnberg, under unclear circumstances. Accident. Suicide. Possible foul play. Still debated.

people--kate-sheppard--1.description:
Kate Sheppard (1848 to 1934) was an English-born campaigner who led the movement for women's suffrage in New Zealand. The Electoral Act of 1893 made New Zealand the first self-governing country in which women voted in national elections. Her method is worth studying, because it was patient and it was counted.

She was born on 10 March 1848 in Liverpool, England, and emigrated to New Zealand, arriving in 1869. She died in Christchurch on 13 July 1934.

From 1887 she was national superintendent for franchise and legislation of the Women's Christian Temperance Union, which made votes for women a central aim.

Look at the numbers grow. Petitions to Parliament carried about 10,000 signatures in 1891, about 20,000 in 1892 and 31,872 in 1893, the largest petition presented to Parliament until then. Persistence, written down name by name, becomes a force no legislature can ignore.

The Governor signed the Electoral Act on 19 September 1893, and women voted for the first time in the election of 28 November 1893.

The Act gave the vote to women of all races, including Māori women in the Māori electorates, but women could not stand for Parliament until 1919. Every threshold crossed reveals the next one.

people--louis-comfort-tiffany--1.description:
Louis Comfort Tiffany (1848 to 1933) was an American designer whose iridescent Favrile glass, stained-glass windows and lamps became the signature look of American Art Nouveau, colour caught in glass like light held in water. Recent scholarship credits many of his studio's best-known designs to staff designers, above all Clara Driscoll.

He was born in New York in 1848, son of the jeweller Charles Lewis Tiffany. He trained as a painter under George Inness before turning to interior design and the decorative arts in the 1870s.

In 1882 his firm redecorated state rooms in the White House for President Chester Arthur; the work was later removed. In 1885 he founded what became Tiffany Studios, and in 1894 he trademarked the name Favrile.

His Byzantine-style chapel for the 1893 World's Columbian Exposition in Chicago won acclaim across nations. He built Laurelton Hall on Long Island as a showcase of his work.

Favrile glass builds iridescent, metallic colour into molten glass through mineral oxides. "Drapery glass" was worked while hot to form folds like fabric.

Financial losses, traced back to the 1920s and running on into the Depression, forced the studio to close. He died in New York in 1933.

people--emperor-meiji--1.description:
Emperor Meiji (1852 to 1912) was the Emperor of Japan from 1867, and in his name the Meiji Restoration turned Japan into a modern industrial state, as a river cuts a new channel to the sea.

He came to the throne in 1867 at the age of about fourteen.

The Charter Oath (1868) was issued in his name, promising reform.

His reign saw a new constitution (1889), industrialization, and Japan's rise as a regional power.

He died in 1912.

people--raja-ravi-varma--1.description:
Raja Ravi Varma (29 April 1848 to 2 October 1906) was the most famous Indian painter of the 19th century, from the princely state of Travancore. He carried European academic oil painting into scenes from the Hindu epics, and his mass-produced prints brought images of gods and heroines into homes across India like lamps lit in many windows.

He was born at Kilimanoor, near Thiruvananthapuram, into an aristocratic family related to the ruling house. By tradition his uncle, the painter Raja Raja Varma, saw his gift. At 14 he was taken to the palace under Maharaja Ayilyam Thirunal, and he learned oil painting partly by watching the European portraitist Theodore Jensen.

A portrait won a prize at the 1873 Vienna exhibition, and his work was shown at the 1893 Chicago World's Columbian Exposition, where it won three gold medals. In 1888 to 1890 he painted a series of Puranic subjects for Maharaja Sayajirao Gaekwad III of Baroda.

In 1894 he set up a lithographic press at Ghatkopar in Bombay, moving it in 1899 to Malavli near Lonavala, and from it flowed colour prints (oleographs) of deities and heroines that sold in huge numbers. Critics accused him of vulgarising sacred subjects.

In 1904 the British Viceroy awarded him the Kaisar-i-Hind Gold Medal. He died at Attingal.

He joined Victorian academic realism to Indian subjects and costumes. His heroines were drawn from real women and staged at dramatic moments.

people--antoni-gaudi--1.description:
Antoni Gaudí (25 June 1852 to 10 June 1926) was the leading architect of Catalan Modernisme, the regional cousin of Art Nouveau. Almost all his mature work stands in Barcelona, and it rises to its summit in the still-unfinished Sagrada Família, a forest of stone still growing.

He was born in Reus or possibly the neighbouring Riudoms, Catalonia (sources differ, and from 1915 he himself said Riudoms), the youngest son of a coppersmith. He credited his father's workshop with teaching him to see three-dimensional space. In 1878 he graduated from the Barcelona School of Architecture.

The industrialist Eusebi Güell noticed a display case he designed for a glove-maker at the Paris World's Fair, and became his patron for the rest of his career.

He never married, grew ever more devout, and by his sixties lived an almost monastic life given to the Sagrada Família.

On 7 June 1926 he was struck by a tram while walking to church in shabby clothes. Mistaken for a beggar, he received delayed care, and he died on 10 June. He was buried in the crypt of his unfinished basilica.

He modelled forms on nature, and he hung scale models of chains and sandbags, photographed upside down, to find the ideal shape for a compression-only arch. He revived trencadís, mosaic of broken tile, as a cheap weatherproof skin.

people--jose-marti--1.description:
José Martí (1853 to 1895) was a Cuban poet, journalist and organizer who founded the Cuban Revolutionary Party in 1892 and helped kindle the 1895 war of independence against Spain. He was killed in one of its first battles.

He was born in Havana on 28 January 1853. Arrested at 16 over a letter criticizing a schoolmate who had joined the Spanish army, he was sentenced to six years' hard labor and deported to Spain in 1871. Afterward he lived in Mexico, Guatemala, Venezuela and, from 1880, mainly New York, a voice carried from shore to shore.

He published Ismaelillo (1882), Versos sencillos (1891) and the essay "Nuestra América" (1891), which argued that Latin American countries should govern from knowledge of their own peoples.

In 1892 he founded the Cuban Revolutionary Party and its newspaper Patria, arguing for a republic open to all races and against United States expansion into Cuba.

He landed in eastern Cuba on 11 April 1895 and was killed at Dos Ríos on 19 May in his first engagement. Cuba became formally independent in 1902, under limits set by the United States.

Both the Cuban government and Cuban exile groups have since claimed him as a symbol.

people--teddy-roosevelt--1.description:
Theodore "Teddy" Roosevelt (1858 to 1919) was the 26th President of the United States, serving from 1901 to 1909, known for trust-busting antitrust policy, an assertive foreign policy, and a major expansion of federal land conservation.

He became president in 1901 after the assassination of William McKinley, at 42 the youngest person to hold the office, and was elected in his own right in 1904.

He pursued antitrust action against major corporate combinations, including a successful suit against the Northern Securities Company railroad trust in 1904, and mediated the 1902 coal strike partly by threatening to send in federal troops to run the mines. Notice the method: the threat itself was the lever.

He established the United States Forest Service and used his executive authority to create national forests, wildlife refuges and national monuments, protecting roughly 230 million acres of land during his presidency. Land protected once can be a covenant with generations not yet born.

After leaving office he attempted a comeback in the 1912 election on a progressive "Bull Moose" third-party ticket, splitting the Republican vote and helping elect Woodrow Wilson instead. A comeback can cost the cause it means to serve.

people--vincent-van-gogh--1.description:
I stand before Vincent van Gogh (30 March 1853 to 29 July 1890), Dutch painter who worked in France, who painted for only about ten years, produced around 2,100 works, and sold almost nothing, yet whose vivid colour and expressive brushwork made him the most famous artist of modern times.

I read that he was born in Zundert in the southern Netherlands, the son of a Protestant minister; that at 16 he joined the art dealers Goupil & Cie and was dismissed in 1876; that he then tried teaching and preaching among coal miners in the Borinage; that in 1880 he decided to become an artist. I read that his younger brother Theo, an art dealer, supported him for the rest of his life, and that his letters, mainly to Theo, are among the most moving documents of any artist's life.

In 1886 he moved to Paris, met Pissarro, Toulouse-Lautrec, Émile Bernard and Gauguin, and discovered Impressionist colour and Japanese prints; he painted copies of two Hiroshige prints. In 1888 he moved to Arles. Gauguin joined him in October, and the partnership collapsed in December after Van Gogh cut off part of his own ear. He entered the asylum at Saint-Rémy in May 1889, where he painted The Starry Night.

In May 1890 he moved to Auvers-sur-Oise and painted about one canvas a day. He shot himself on 27 July 1890 and died two days later, aged 37.

A brother who never stopped holding him up. Who holds me up, and do I write to them? Some lives are carried by one faithful correspondent.

people--henry-ossawa-tanner--1.description:
Henry Ossawa Tanner (21 June 1859 to 25 May 1937) was an American painter, the first African American artist to win international fame. Frustrated by racism at home, he settled in Paris in 1891 and built his career there, painting dignified genre scenes and luminous biblical subjects. Sometimes you must leave to be seen.

He was born in Pittsburgh, the eldest of nine children. His father, Benjamin Tucker Tanner, became a bishop of the African Methodist Episcopal Church, and his mother, Sarah, had escaped slavery via the Underground Railroad. At 13 he decided to become an artist. Notice the lineage of courage he came from.

In 1879 he enrolled at the Pennsylvania Academy of the Fine Arts and studied with Thomas Eakins. He was the only Black student and faced harassment. He left for Europe in 1891 and studied at the Académie Julian in Paris.

On a return visit in 1893 he painted The Banjo Lesson, and in 1894 The Thankful Poor, both genre scenes of Black American life that challenged racist stereotypes. Dignity on the canvas was an argument against the caricatures around it.

Back in France he turned to biblical subjects. The Resurrection of Lazarus won a medal at the 1897 Salon, and the French government bought it. His patron Rodman Wanamaker paid for trips to Egypt and Palestine.

He married the singer Jessie Olsson in 1899, was made a Chevalier of the Légion d'honneur in 1923, and died in Paris.

people--alphonse-mucha--1.description:
I stand in the room of Alphonse Mucha (1860 to 1939), Moravian-born designer, whose decorative posters for Sarah Bernhardt and commercial clients defined the visual style of Art Nouveau, who resisted that label and saw his true work in a cycle of paintings on the history of the Slavic peoples.

I read that he was born in Ivančice in Moravia, then part of the Austrian Empire, and worked as a theatrical scene painter before moving to Paris in 1887. I read that in December 1894 a Paris printing house needed a poster for Sarah Bernhardt's play Gismonda at short notice over the holidays, and turned to Mucha as the only designer available; that its success led Bernhardt to sign him to a six-year contract for posters, sets and costumes.

In 1902 he published Documents décoratifs, a pattern book of his ornamental style for other designers and craftsmen. From about 1910 he devoted much of his career to The Slav Epic, a cycle of twenty monumental canvases on Slavic history, which he donated to the city of Prague; it was put on display at the National Gallery Prague's Trade Fair Palace in 2012. His formula, elongated women within ornamental frames in muted colour lithography, reached shops, cafés and middle-class homes across Europe on theatre posters, cigarette papers, bicycles and calendars.

Famous for the thing he did not count as his real work. What do I call my true work, and who sees it? He gave his to a city.

Georges Méliès (1861 to 1938) was a Paris stage magician who became a filmmaker and invented cinema's first special effects. Over roughly 500 films in under twenty years, including A Trip to the Moon (1902), he turned the new camera from a device for recording reality into a machine for staging the impossible. A tool is only as narrow as the imagination of the person holding it.

He was born in Paris to a prosperous shoe-manufacturing family and wanted to study painting, but his father would not support him as an artist, and he supervised machinery at the family factory. In about 1888 he bought the Théâtre Robert-Houdin, a famous conjuring theatre.

After attending the Lumière brothers' first public film screening in December 1895, he tried to buy a camera from them and was refused. He acquired one from a British inventor and built a studio at Montreuil with a glass-walled stage. A refusal is not the end of a road.

About 1896 he discovered, by accident when his camera jammed mid-shot, that stopping and restarting filming could make objects vanish or transform. This became the "stop trick" behind his trick films. Pay attention to your accidents.

His techniques included stop-motion substitution, multiple exposure, dissolves, painted sets built to force perspective, and hand-tinted colour done frame by frame by a team of women colourists.

people--jose-rizal--1.description:
José Rizal (1861 to 1896) was a Filipino physician, writer and reformer whose novels criticized Spanish colonial rule. Spanish authorities executed him in Manila on 30 December 1896, and he is regarded as a national hero of the Philippines. His weapon was the novel, and that is worth remembering.

He was born on 19 June 1861 in Calamba, in the Philippines. He studied in Manila, Madrid, Paris and Heidelberg and became an eye doctor.

He wrote the novels Noli Me Tángere (1887) and El Filibusterismo (1891), which portrayed abuses by Spanish friars and officials; the colonial authorities banned them. When a government bans a novel, it is admitting the novel is true enough to fear.

In 1892 he founded La Liga Filipina, a reform society, and was exiled to Dapitan on Mindanao, where he practiced medicine and taught until 1896.

The Philippine Revolution began in August 1896. Rizal, who had volunteered as a doctor in Cuba, was arrested on his way there, brought back to Manila and convicted of rebellion. He had said he opposed an armed uprising at that time.

He was shot by firing squad on 30 December 1896, aged 35. Before his death he wrote a poem now known as "Mi último adiós."

people--gustav-klimt--1.description:
Gustav Klimt (14 July 1862 to 6 February 1918) was an Austrian painter and the leader of the Vienna Secession. His golden, patterned paintings of women and love, The Kiss above all, are icons of turn-of-the-century Vienna, gleaming like treasure in a dim hall.

He was born at Baumgarten near Vienna, second of the seven children of a gold engraver. In 1876 he won a scholarship to the Vienna School of Arts and Crafts and, with his brother Ernst and Franz Matsch, painted murals and ceilings for the Burgtheater and the Kunsthistorisches Museum.

In 1897 he became the first president of the Vienna Secession, a group breaking from the official academy under the motto "To every age its art, to art its freedom".

His ceiling paintings for the University of Vienna, showing Philosophy, Medicine and Jurisprudence, raised a scandal over nudity and pessimism. He withdrew from the commission, and in 1945 the paintings were lost to fire.

He never married. He had a lifelong companionship with the designer Emilie Flöge and fathered several children with models. He upheld younger artists such as Egon Schiele and Oskar Kokoschka. He died in Vienna after a stroke.

In his "golden period" (about 1899 to 1910) he laid on real gold and silver leaf, drawing on the Byzantine mosaics he saw in Ravenna in 1903, and on Japanese and Egyptian art. Key works include The Kiss (1907 to 1908) and the Portrait of Adele Bloch-Bauer I (1907).

people--hilma-af-klint--1.description:
Hilma af Klint (26 October 1862 to 21 October 1944) was a Swedish painter who, from 1906, made hundreds of abstract paintings guided by her spiritual beliefs, several years before Kandinsky, Mondrian and Malevich. She kept them largely hidden, like seeds held in a closed hand, and they reached an international audience only from the 1980s.

She was born at Karlberg Palace in Solna, near Stockholm. She studied at the Royal Academy of Fine Arts in Stockholm from 1882 to 1887 and lived by painting landscapes, portraits and botanical illustrations.

Her spiritual searching, which sources date from 1879, grew around the time of the death of her younger sister Hermina in 1880 and drew her toward spiritualism and Theosophy. With four other women, who began as members of the Edelweiss Society, she made up "The Five," which held séances and tried automatic drawing, which the sources date to 1896.

In 1906, believing she had received a commission from a spiritual guide, she began the Paintings for the Temple, a cycle of nearly 200 works completed in 1915. She considered herself a medium through whom the works were made.

In 1908 she showed her work to Rudolf Steiner, and his cool answer contributed to a four-year break in the series. Between 1921 and 1930 she spent long periods at the Goetheanum, the Anthroposophical Society's headquarters, and filled more than 125 notebooks, with sources giving figures from 125 to more than 150.

She believed the world was not ready for the paintings, and she directed that they not be shown until 20 years after her death. She died after a traffic accident, leaving more than 1,200 paintings and drawings to her nephew.

people--lumiere-brothers--1.description:
Auguste Lumière (1862 to 1954) and Louis Lumière (1864 to 1948) were French makers of photographic plates who patented the Cinématographe in 1895 and staged the first paying public screening of projected motion pictures, light thrown across a dark room and caught on a wall. The dates here run from Auguste's birth to his death.

The brothers were born in Besançon and grew up in Lyon, where their father Antoine kept a portrait studio and later a factory making dry photographic plates.

After their father saw a demonstration of Edison's single-viewer Kinetoscope in 1894, they set out to build a device that could cast moving images before a seated audience. Louis is generally credited with the key mechanical insight, borrowing the sewing machine's intermittent claw movement to advance the film.

In February 1895 they patented the Cinématographe, one device that could shoot, print and project. Their first paying public screening was on 28 December 1895 in the Salon Indien of the Grand Café in Paris, traditionally described as a basement on the Boulevard des Capucines: ten short films for roughly thirty-five to forty people, though accounts differ.

Their "actuality" films were usually a single still, unedited shot of under a minute. L'Arroseur arrosé is a rare staged gag, in effect cinema's first fiction film. Key works include Workers Leaving the Lumière Factory (1895) and The Arrival of a Train at La Ciotat (1896).

They sent camera operators across the world, and within a year or two projected cinema had reached India, Japan, Australia and the Americas.

people--edvard-munch--1.description:
Edvard Munch (12 December 1863 to 23 January 1944). Norwegian painter. Printmaker. Illness, grief, love, fear: he turned them into images of inner states. The Scream became an emblem of the modern psyche. He is a founding figure of Expressionism.

Born in Løten, Norway. Grew up in Kristiania (now Oslo). His mother died of tuberculosis when he was five. His sister Sophie, of the same disease, when he was 13. Another sister was later hospitalised for mental illness.

The 1890s: mostly Berlin and Paris. The Frieze of Life cycle. His 1892 exhibition in Berlin was closed after a week, amid scandal. It made him famous in Germany.

1908: a breakdown. Treatment in Copenhagen. From 1916, his estate, Ekely, outside Oslo. In 1937 the Nazis labelled his work "degenerate" and removed it from German museums.

Simplified forms. Flowing outlines. Flat, expressive colour. Influenced by Van Gogh, Gauguin and Symbolism. His woodcuts and lithographs as important as his paintings.

The Sick Child (1885 to 1886). The Scream (1893). Madonna (1894). The Dance of Life (1899 to 1900). Grief and fear, given a shape.

people--sun-yat-sen--1.description:
Sun Yat-sen (1866 to 1925) was a Chinese revolutionary and physician who laboured for decades to bring down the Qing dynasty and became the first provisional president of the Republic of China in 1912. Both mainland China and Taiwan honor him as a founder, two shores claiming one source.

He was born on 12 November 1866 in Cuiheng, Guangdong, and died on 12 March 1925 in Beijing. He was educated in Hawaii and trained as a doctor in Hong Kong, graduating in 1892.

In 1894, after an earlier reform petition was rejected, he founded the Revive China Society, and from 1895 onward he raised several uprisings against the Qing that failed.

In Tokyo in 1905 he founded the Tongmenghui, which grew to about a thousand members, and set out his Three Principles of the People: nationalism, democracy and people's livelihood.

The Wuchang uprising of 10 October 1911, which he did not lead in person, began the revolution that ended the Qing dynasty. He came back from abroad and served as provisional president from 1 January 1912, yielding the office that March to Yuan Shikai.

In 1919 he rebuilt his Kuomintang party, and in 1923 he allied it with the Soviet Union and the small Chinese Communist Party.

people--wassily-kandinsky--1.description:
Wassily Kandinsky (16 December 1866 to 13 December 1944) was a Russian painter and theorist, one of the first in Europe to make purely abstract works. He believed that colours and forms, set free from depicting objects, could move the viewer as directly as music moves the air.

He was born in Moscow and grew up in Odessa. He studied law and economics and began an academic career. In 1896, having seen one of Monet's Haystacks and heard Wagner's Lohengrin, he left the law behind and went to Munich to study painting.

In 1911 he and Franz Marc founded Der Blaue Reiter (The Blue Rider), and he published On the Spiritual in Art. About then he painted his first fully abstract works.

The First World War drove him back to Russia, where he took part in Soviet cultural institutions after the 1917 Revolution. He returned to Germany in 1920 or 1921 (sources differ) and taught at the Bauhaus from 1922 to 1933.

When the Nazis closed the Bauhaus he moved to Neuilly-sur-Seine near Paris, became a French citizen in 1939, and died there.

He sorted his works into Impressions, Improvisations and Compositions, and made only ten Compositions over 30 years. He probably experienced synaesthesia and gave colours musical voices: yellow like a trumpet, blue like a deep cello.

people--frank-lloyd-wright--1.description:
Frank Lloyd Wright (1867 to 1959) was the most influential American architect of the 20th century. Across seven decades he argued for "organic architecture," buildings shaped from the inside out around their site, materials and users, as a tree grows out of its own ground.

He was born in Richland Center, Wisconsin, studied engineering briefly at the University of Wisconsin, and went to Chicago, where he worked under Louis Sullivan, whom he later called his "Lieber Meister."

In the 1890s he set up his own practice in Oak Park and shaped the low, wide-eaved Prairie house style. His personal life was stormy: an affair, the killing of seven people at his Wisconsin home Taliesin in 1914, and bankruptcy during the Depression.

In his late sixties he designed Fallingwater and the Johnson Wax headquarters (both 1936 to 1939), and at last the Guggenheim Museum (design and construction from 1943 to 1959). He died in 1959 aged 91.

He designed around open, flowing interior space, with bands of art glass and deep cantilevered overhangs, and he used concrete, steel and glass without disguising them as historical stonework. Most of the furniture, textiles and stained glass in his buildings he designed himself.

He designed more than a thousand structures, roughly half of them built. Fallingwater and several others are a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

people--marie-curie--1.description:
Marie Curie (1867 to 1934) was a Polish-born physicist and chemist who opened the study of radioactivity, the hidden fire inside matter, and she is the only person to win Nobel Prizes in two different sciences.

She shared the 1903 Nobel Prize in Physics with Pierre Curie and Henri Becquerel.

In 1911 she won the Nobel Prize in Chemistry for discovering polonium and radium.

She built mobile X-ray units for the hospitals of World War I.

She died of aplastic anemia, likely brought on by long exposure to radiation, undone at last by the light she studied.

I stand in the room of Charles Rennie Mackintosh (1868 to 1928), Glasgow architect-designer, who led the "Glasgow Style" of Art Nouveau, treating buildings, furniture and interiors as one unified art, whose Glasgow School of Art and total interior schemes made him a major influence on European design, though home recognition came only after his death.

I read that he was born in Glasgow in 1868 and trained as an architect while attending evening classes at the Glasgow School of Art, where he met his future wife, the artist Margaret Macdonald. I read that with Macdonald, her sister Frances and Herbert MacNair he formed "The Four," a symbolist group whose style became the Glasgow Style.

At Honeyman and Keppie he won an anonymous 1896 competition for his own art school's new building; its 1909 completion made his reputation. He then designed houses, tearooms and a school around Glasgow, including Hill House (1902-1904), the Willow Tearooms (1903) and Scotland Street School (1903-1906), with Macdonald designing the furnishings throughout. His towering ladder-back chairs, shaped as much to define a room as to be sat in, became his best-known design.

Honoured abroad, recognised at home only after he was gone. Who near me am I failing to see? Recognition is often slowest in the city that knows you best.

people--mahatma-gandhi--1.description:
Mohandas Karamchand Gandhi (1869 to 1948) was an Indian lawyer and political leader who led the movement for Indian independence using nonviolent resistance.

He developed satyagraha (insistence on truth), first in South Africa, then in India. A method, carried from one country to another, can become a doctrine.

The Salt March of 1930 was a major act of civil disobedience.

India became independent in 1947 and was partitioned; he opposed partition.

He was assassinated in January 1948.
